div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
THE PRICE OF MILK.

The Warrington Milk Dealers' Association have raised the retail price of milk to 4d. a quart. In Lymm and district the price has been raised to 44d. Milk dealers of Spalding (Lincs.) and district have announced an increase in the price from 3d. to 4d. a quart to date from the Ist October. Boston and other Lincolnshire dairymen will charge, 4d. ft quart during the winter.
The Farmers' Union has ,fixed the minimum wholesale price of milk in South Wale-4 fof the coming winter at 13d. per gallon, delivered in

towns. It is announced by advertisement, in which no name or address is given, that "in consequence of the increased price paid to farmers owing to the enhanced cost of production, London dairy- men are compelled to raise the price of milk to 541. a quart" from Sunday last (the 3rd inst.). At Birmingham and Liverpool on the Ist of October, the retail price of milk was raised to 541. a quart. An important development, due probably to labour difficulties, is shown at Liver- pool, where only one delivery a day is to be made.

div.head: NEW REGULATIONS CONCERNING
div.p: THE NEW REGULATIONS CONCERNING
CALF SLAUGHTER.

Farmers should note that the new rules con- cerning the slaughter of calves, as set out in the Maintenance of Live Stock Order of the Board of Agriculture, came into operation on the Ist inst. These rules have been set forth fully in our columns. No calves, with the exception of those of certain breeds specified, and also some that are held to be not worth rearing, are to be sold until the first permanent molar tooth is visible. That means for practical purposes until it is approximately six months old.

div.head: LIQUID MANURE.
div.p: LIQUID MANURE.

A great source of waste in these days is the liquid manure on the farms. I was on .a small farm not long since and saw one of the best farmed little holdings I ever saw. The .farm was barely 80 acres,-all grass, and yet it carried a herd of 37 slapping big dairy Shorthorns. First-class Cheddar cheese was made and pigs were fattened. The land had been got into good condition by basic slag supplemented by farmyard manure, but what struck me most was his arrangement for conserving his liquid manure. The liquid tank was outside the yard, and he had constructed alongside it a small compound of beaten clay, slightly raised, plump in the middle, surrounded by a smallgutter that drained into the tank. The land was somewhat wet and the cattle had to be housed a great part of the winter. All the manure from the stalls that was not hauled direct on to the land was carted out daily en to this -prepared Place and all the soakings ran into the tank and was pumped out and hauled over the grass land. There was no waste here, but on 90 per cent. of our English farms the liquid manure and the soakings of the manure heaps are absolutely wasted entirely. On the farm I have described the farmer was lucky in having his manure tank in such a position that he could take advantage of it. Liquid tanks are often placed where they never ought to be; what should be done is that the manure from all cattle should 'be placed in covered pits, the drainage there- from to be carried -direct to -the liquid tank together with the drainage from the stalls. With nitrate of soda standing at its present price, and not procurable always, •the liquid manure is worth saving now. There is no in- ducement at present from the practical farmer's point of view in ploughing land for wheat—it is to the improvement and upkeep of our pastures that the British farmer must look, for there can be no doubt that the future of successful British farming lies in stock farming mostly on grass.—Somerset Farmer in "Farm and Home."

div.head: TAKE CARE OF IMPLEMENTS.
div.p: TAKE CARE OF IMPLEMENTS.

At a time when all are urged to save in every possible direction, attention should be given to the storing away of farm implements for the winter. The annual loss .caused by neglect of this precaution is said to be very great, and it is a loss easily prevented.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
ROSES AND THEIR CULTURE.

Having been frequently asked how to grow roses, perhaps the following notes will help beginners from worrying themselves and finally giving roses a wide berth. I do not propose to give any remarks that have not been proved by myself both in soils and 'growth. Of course roses will not thrive in bleak places, one facing south, south-east or south-west being the best, and it must be sheltered from high winds. Some people say you cannot grow roses without marl or clay; this is a silly idea. My roses grow in land that is quite sandy, one spade- blade deep (Orford), and I may say I have had blooms well up to exhibition standard. Such soils require to be made heavy by adding turf well rotted, and plenty of pig or cow dung added; or remove some of the worst soil and break up the other and add your turf and manure. The bed should be raised from the ground about 61n. or 9in. and boarded round to make a neat job of. it, and should run from north to south if possible, .so as to get all the available sun. In the case of clayey or manly land (like Cheshire for instance), roses ought to grow without much attention; this soil suits them best. Make your beds about 11. to !.,,ft: deep, getting the manure well down and plenty of it, if possible, because once the bed is made 'there is no chance of manuring underneath. Now to planting and see that you get good stuff from a reliable-nursery, and budded on to the wild briar (the dog rose I mean), because. this class of briar is very hardy and vigorous. Insist on having your plants budded on this class of briar. A few good firms are Bee's, Ltd., Liverpool; Clibran's, Altrincham; Tittering- ton's, Preston; and Caldwell's, Knutsford. These firms all use the English briar and grow good strong stuff. When planting see that no manure comes into contact with the roots., A good method is to put a handful or two of potting soil in the hole before spreading the roots out. See that you spread the roots well out, and any long ones may be cut back with. a sharp knife to make. them Somewhat even. Cover up to 2in. above the scion or joint and stamp well down to make the tree firm. When the bed has settled down the joint will be about level with the surface. Don't put any manure on the surface, because the plants will get all the nourishment they require from the soil. A little bone-meal might, be added, .say, a small handful around each tree, and lightly pricked in. in the spring. /. I think I have made everything clear, so next come the varitties to grow. If you want a good variety don't look at. a trade exhibition at flower shows, but rather go to the niirseries- and see for yourself. Failing to do thiS you will find the following roses will suit all purposes, and are good doers and grand flowerers. I. will split them up ,in their respective ' sections' so that no mistakes will be made :

Hybrid Perpetuals.—This class is very vigor- ous and can withstand the English winter and embraces our largest roses and our best reds. Hybrid Teas.—This class is greatly on the in crease on account of ,the beautiful colonrings, fragrance and shape. This class is obtained by crossing the Tea with the Hybrid Perpetual, and is the best seetion of all the roses.

Teas.—This class is very, fragrant and hardly as hardy as the Hybrid Teas, and should be mostly grown in pots, although some do very well outside. Some of our best"' yellows are in this section. Then there are various classes., such as Pernettiana, China, Polyantha and Wich- uraiana and others, but these need not be men- tioned. because the foregoing classes ,are the best. The following varieties will suit this dis- trict very well. Hybrid Perpetuals.
Frau Kari Druschki.—The largest white rose
MILLING'S SELL " BLUE BAND " MAR- GARINE. The Perfect Butter Substitute.--Advt.

div.p: in existence; vigorous grower and great bloomer. For best results the crown bud should be re- tained, the others picked off. Its only draw- back is, it has no smell. Hugh Dickson.—A fine large crimson rose, a worthy companion to the above, very vigorous grower, should be pegged down, very fragrant. Captain Hayward.—A fine crimson scarlet, fragrant, very floriferous, vigorous grower, best results when grown in partial shade. Mrs. R. G. Sharman-Crawford.—A grand pink, nice Ihape, nearly thornless, and flowers all through the summer and autumn; vigorous in growth and nice foliage. In bloom with me yet. Mrs. J. Lang.—A fine soft pink, large and good form, fragrant and vigorous. A great favourite. Commander Jules Gravereaux.—Velvety red, shaded maroon, long pointed buds and large full flowers; vigorous. Prince Camille de Rohan.—The darkest of all roses; medium in size, long pointed blooms and full, vigorous in growth and very sweetly scented. Just a word about dark roses. There ;are no black roses, but there are some that have so deep a tint of maroon that they are .generally taken for black. For the benefit of our readers I will give in some other issue about six of our(dairkest roses.

div.head: Hybrid Teas.
div.p: Hybrid Teas.

There are so many grand roses in this section: that it is very hard to say which ,are the best fifteen, but the following will want some beat- ing for 81.1-round varieties : Caroline Testout.—Satin rose, brighter centre, large, full and globular, prolific bloomer, and very sweetly scented; very vigorous. Should be in every garden. Lady Ashtown.—Pale rose, shaded yellow at base, long, pointed blooms, each petal running to a point; vigorous ,in growth, very free flowerer. I find no fault in it anywhere. Madame A. Chatenay.—Carmine and fawn, pointed petals, large and full, vigorous in growth but sometimes erratic, a grand variety and very sweetly perfumed. A nice buttonhole, like the above.

Mons. J. Hill—Salmon pink and copper, a beautiful tint, large, full, vigorous, free flowerer, sweetly scented, lovely bronze foliage and flowers erect on thornless stems. A superb variety. Liberty.—Brilliant velvety crimson, medium in size, full, sweetly scented, moderate in growth but very hardy. The best crimson buttonhole. Richmond.—Pure red scarlet, hardly full, vigorous and sweetly scented, larger than Liberty, a good buttonhole rose. A sport from Lady Battersea. Lieu Chaure.—Velvety crimson red, large blooms hardly full, vigorous in. growth, fragrant, does very well anywhere.

British Queen.—A new pure white rose, large blooms and beautifully pointed, with a deep lasting fragrance. Not so vigorous as F. K. Druschki, but very .brancing and floriferous. Well worth its place with Druschki. Duchess of Wellington.—ln my estimation the best deep yellow rose we have. Hardly full, blooms similar in shape to Killarney, and very deeply scented; grand robust growth, and should be in every, collection. Deep saffron yellow, outer petals stained crimson. Madame Ravary.—Deep yellow, deepening to orange yellow; semi-globular in shape, large and full, sweetly scented. Does very well in. towns, and robust in growth. A great favourite. Pharismr.—Rosy white, shaded salmon, lovely pointed blooms and well formed, large and full; fairly vigorous. Antoine Revoire.—Creamy flesh, bordered with carmine; vigorous growth, large full blooms. A grand variety. Betty.—Fawn centre, outside carmine, fairly full, vigorous growth, very long buds; flowers from May till frost comes. Grand buttonhole rose and very sweetly scented. La Tosca.—Silvery pink, deeper centre, globu- lar blooms, sweetly scented, very large and full; a thornless rose. Does well in towns. It has no fault.
Laurent Carle.—Brilliant velvety carmine, very large, vigorous grower, sweetly scented; good for exhibition or garden decoration and a full flower.
Of course, there are others, but these do well around Warrington, and are mostly sweetly scented.
Pernettianas.

This is a new class produced by Mons Pernet Dueller, France, by crossing the Austrian briars with other varieties. These roses are most beautifully coloured, and have a delightful fra- grance. They have only one drawback, and that is some of the best shoots are apt to die down, but the plants are very hardy. The best of this section are:—

Lyon •Rae.—Shrimp pink, coral and yellow, large, very full, and delightful fragrance. This plant will give different coloured blooms, and is somewhat 6preading in habit and vigorous in growth. Willowmere.—Supposed to be an improved Lyon rose; better grower thari Lyon, large red thorns. Blooms resemble Lady Ashtown and Lyon crossed; beautiful shape and very flori- ferous. Should be in every collection. Rayon d' Or.—Sunflower yellow, very full and very deeply scented; has the fault of dying down. Maiden shoots are the best. Does very well- when established: Very hardy and worth growing, but Duchess of Wellington has my pre- ference.

Teas.—The following I find do very well out- side, and aro quite hardy, but in winter a good plan is to draw some soil and leaf mould about 6in:: over the crown. Should the winter be severe the tops may die, but the covered portion will be quite safe. Harry Kirk.—A grand sulphur yellow rose, large and full, very fragrant and a nice shape; very hardy and vigorous in growth, and very long thorns. In bloom now with me. Lady Hillingdon.—A beautiful deep apricot yellow, very floriferous and a fair grower, semi- double, a first-class buttonhole rose, and an easy doer.

Lady Roberts.—A beautiful sport from Anna Olivier; colour apricot and coppery rose, a lovely shade, hardy and moderate grower; exception- ally good as a pot rose. Anna Olivier.—Rosy flesh shaded with buff, identical with the above except colour. White Kaman Cochet.—A beautiful sport from Main. an Cochet, pure • white and cream, lovely shape and vigorous, fragrant, best seen under glass. Molly S. Crawford.—Another good white, shaded lemon white; when opening and finish- ing a pure glistening white. Very hardy and almost thornless; blooms globular in shape and very sweetly scented; best under glass. The best results from tea roses are obtained in pots in greenhouse or conservatories, but the above will do fairly well outside shaded from cold winds.

div.head: Climbers For Arches And Pergolas.
div.p: Climbers For Arches And Pergolas.
These need no describing, because everyone must have seen them flowering in great clusters around gardens, walls and arches. I will just name a few of the best.
Dorothy Perkins.—Shell pink.
White Dorothy.—White. Minnehaha.—Rose. Crimson Rambler.—Crimson. Hiawatha.—Single, crimson-white centre. Bouquet d' Or.—Pale yellow, coppery in centre, large, full. Glorie de Dijon type.

div.head: Climbers For Walls.
div.p: Climbers For Walls.

Glorie de Dijon, Ards Rover, Climbing Caro- line_ Testout, Bouquet d' Or, Climbing F. K. Druschki and Madame A. Carriere. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
WOMEN LIBERAL WAR WORKERS.
Winter's Sewing .Campaign Inaugurated By
Ward Teas,
SIA A. H. AND LADY CROSFIELD'S eNCOURAGEMENT.

The members of the War Sewing Class in connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association—who last winter sent out thousands of acceptable articles of wearing apparel to the brave British lads who lined the trenches and who during the warmer months have been busy getting ready for the oncoming cold spell which is Once more to try the mettle of the campaigners—have this week been hold- ing a series of three ward tea meetings and concerts in aid of their funds. "More and still more" money is required in order that the good work may this winter not only be, "dime as satisfactorily as it was last, but may be accomplished on an even more lavish scale. The socials have, without exception, been dis- tinct successes, and they have been .raced by -the presence of 'Sir Arthur and Lady bCrosfield, who-,have- thus made their first public •appear- ance among *their friends and admirers of the Liberal party since' Sir Arthor's elevation to a baronetcy.

div.head: WHITECROSS WARD.
div.p: WHITECROSS WARD.
How Women Are Backing Up
The Soldiers.

The first of the three meetings and concerts was ixrolnoted in connection with the White- cross Ward—of which Mrs. Percival is the captain—and was held in the spacious and artistic Crosfield Memorial Hall on Monday evening. Between 300 and 400 ladies and :gentlemen attended and took tea together, their wants. being attended to by a large body of ward auxiliaries, under the charge of the ward captain, who had the able and valued assistance .of Mrs. Edmund Osborne, the popular honorary secretary of the Women's Liberal Association.
„In between the tea and the concert came some speech-making, ever which Lady Crosfield grace- fully presided and to which she also contri- buted in characteristic vein.

AFTER WORK, A LITTLE RELAXATION. First the Honorary Secretary had a few words to say. Many things, said Mrs. Osborne, had happened since the occasion of their last ward tea. The country had been plunged into war, and hundreds of thousands of young lives had been lost. Matters concerning the war were continually before one's notice, and the women who were left at home were backing the efforts of their brave soldiers by supplying them with warm comforts. Many sewing meetings had been held, but, that night, those who had been so busily engaged on that work were afforded an opportunity of a little relaxation, and that meeting would be the means of spurring them on to equally good work in the futurei That night they were specially honoured. She remembered a short time ago a meeting at which one of the members, at the close, called for three cheers for Lady Crosfield. A lady of different political persuasion replied, as caustically as she could: " H'm; she's not Lady Crosfield ; she hasn't got a title." "Well," replied the Liberal worker, "if she hasn't got a title, she is a lady." Congratulating The New Baronet.

"To-night," said Mrs. Osborne, "there can be no possible doubt about it, and as our Presi- dent we have the greatest possible pleasure in congratulating her and Sir Arthur upon the honour which has been conferred upon them, and on the town, through them. We are proud, very proud, to have Sir Arthur and Lady Cros- field with us." (Cheers.) _ _ - -

They were also glad to have with them Miss Truda Crosfield. It was many months since she was in Warrington. She had been engaged doing noble work in France. They had hoped to see Mrs. John Crosfield, whose kindly dis- position and sweet womanliness were 60 well known throughout the town and district. She very rarely came to Warrington—a place which she dearly loved—without bestowing upon it mime 'favour. They were indebted to her for the magnificent building in which they were gathered, and that afternoon she had handed over to the Mayor—who, by the way, they were glad to learn had accepted that high position for another year—a memorial bust of the late Mr. John Crosfield. (Applause.)

div.head: Take Care of the Pence
div.p: Take Care of the Pence

Later on Mrs. Osborne took the opportunity of bringing before the notice of the gathering the Penny Bank which had been started in connection with the Women's Liberal Associa- tion. Deposits of a penny and upwards, she explained, would be received and the money would be invested in the Warrington Savings Bank. Each depositor would be furnished with a bank book free of charge; and, as soon as the amount paid in by any depositor reached a sovereign, interest was paid on it. Strict secrecy was observed respetting all deposits, which were audited by the cashier (Councillor Osborne) every week. The committee of the association had asked her (the speaker) to take the post or secretary and treasurer, and she had consented to do so and would be in attend- ance at the Memorial Hall every Thursday afternoon from 2.30 to 5 o'clock.
Id. a Day-30s. a Year!

The bank was instituted \ for the personal benefit of the members of the association, and they were not to be ashamed to bring their pennies along, remembering that a penny a day saved meant 30s. in the bank at the end of the year. It was the desire of the officials of the association to help their members all they could, and, as one means to that end, they cordially invited on and all to join the Penny Bank. Mrs. Osborne also referred to the im- pending visit to the town of Miss Petty, "the Pudding Lady," and said that it was very essential, with food prices going up and up, that the women should attend the lectures and demonstrations shortly to be held at the Co- operative Hall, and take advantage of the hints which the lady lecturer would give.

div.head: STOCKING-KNITTING COMPETITION.
div.p: STOCKING-KNITTING COMPETITION.

A feature of the gathering—as also of the other two which have followed—was a stocking- knitting competition. This had attracted a large number of entrants and the level of the work entered was very good indeed. The prize-winners were Mrs. Denmard, Aikin-street, .and Mrs. Henry Osborne, of St. Barnabas'- place. The wool for the stockings exhibited was supplied by the War Sewing Class. The prizes were given by Councillors Roberts, Bar- ton and Dale.

During the early part of the• proceedings a parcel of a dozen and a half towels was handed up to the platform to be sent to some of the soldiers at the Front. The towels were the gift of Mrs. Payne, of Hood-lane, who has previously contributed similar gifts to the supply of comforts sent out by the association.

div.head: TIME FOR DEEDS, NOT WORDS.
div.p: TIME FOR DEEDS, NOT WORDS.

Lady Crosfield presided and was supported by Miss Truda Crosfield and Sir Arthur. Her Ladyship's speech, which formed the prelude to the music, was brief, for, to use her own phrase, the present is no time for words, but for deeds: She went on to commend the work which the Liberal women of 'Warrington had already done, and then proceeded to talk of work which she had herself undertaken in connection with a military hospital in Highgate —the Metropolitan suburb in which Sir Arthur and her Ladyship have their town residence.

div.head: EXCITING EXPERIENCES.
div.p: EXCITING EXPERIENCES.

Miss Truda Crosfield, who has been rendering splendid service in connection with a hospital established at Cherbourg, France, said that she had -recently received a low, letter from her brother,. Major Crosfield, and as many of those present must have • sons or other relatives at the Front, it would, no doubt, interest them to hear *hat the Major had to tell. They knew that the ' 4th South Lancashires were in that terrible gruelling on June 16th, and since then there had been something in the nature of a long lull. The Germans had consolidated 'their trenches on their side and the British had con- solidated theirs, until they, had made them almost impregnable. Then 61214 the big attack of the other week-end, the story of which had thrilled them all. Miss Crosfield went on to recount some exciting stories of the Major's ex- periences at the Front. Councillor Pale said a, few words of thanks to
• MILLINErS SELL. "BLUE BAND" MAR- GARINE. The Perfect Butter Substitute.--Adrt.

div.head: SPARTAN WOMEN OUTDONE.
div.p: SPARTAN WOMEN OUTDONE.
Sir Arthur's Praise For Mothers ,And Wives.

Sir Arthur Crosfield, who, on rising, was greeted with hearty applause, then addressed the gathering, his remarks being frequently punc- tuated by outbursts of hand-clapping. Count cillor Dale, he remarked, had said several striking and important things, and what he said was very true, too. His reference to the women of Sparta was so absolutely appropriate; it was not a bit exaggerated. They had sterner con- ditions to face to-day than, were faced •in the small inter-state wars of Spartan days, magni- ficent and immortal as was the heroism shown by the men of that far-off time. Great as were the sacrifices made by the Spartan women, the women of Old England were sacrificing just as much at the present time. He did not underrate, nor had he ever underrated, the fact that the men had to make sacrifices; they might as well -suggest that the Englishman Was going to funk difficulties and tarn back when he was in a tight place. The Britisher did not do that! No, he went through with the job—and he conquered. (Hear, hear.) The, War .and—Posterity.

He did not believe that the man was born whose imagination could grapple with the pro- blem as to what this war would mean to the future generations of the race—as to the inspir- ation and the lessons they would draw by look- ing back on the achievements of the present time. He'knew perfectly well that there were pessimists who would tell them that war, devastating, destructive and infamous as it was, was bound to continue for all time. People who talked like that might just as well try to make them believe that because, in the early 'sixties, there raged a terrible civil war in the United States of America, that the States had got to look for- ward to another North and South War; that the wastage and bloodshed of strife was to continue for ever in the great Western Repub- lic. The fact was, as all who thought and understood must know perfectly well, that that ,awful struggle between North arideuth would never be repeated, for the reason -that it was- so awful. Americans were not going- to have an experience like that twice. It had taudht them wisdom, and they had absorbed the lesson'iso well that he believed that whatever differences might in the future arise between them and this country it was arbitration that ,had got to settle those difficulties and .not bloodshed. The War and Ourselves aril the U.S.A.

They were fast approaching the point when the Statesmen of the British Empire and of America would realise that a. war between the two countries would be an unthinkable crime against civilisation—a crime that was never again to be permitted.. , The present great war was the overshadowing topic; they thought of little else and wondered how soon it might be possible to bring it to an issue ! The :struggle must not be for nothing, and when.',Fhe read of the leading Statesmen of Britain and the Allies—men of vast experience and political sagacity—speaking of a glorious and a permanent peace—well, he was thankful to be enough of an optimist to believe that that was not mere talking in the air.

div.head: Unless The Victory Is Decisive –
div.p: Unless The Victory Is Decisive -

But unless the Allies achieved a decisive supremacy and made it clear to Europe and to the whole world that they, as civilised people, would not tolerate the reckless infamy of the military gamblers of Prussia ; unless they could so far establish their supremacy as to make that clear : then, he was afraid, it was only too true! that either they, in their lives, or the children of the coming generation, as they grew up, would see another struggle—perhaps as had; perhaps even worse! That was why the pre- vious speaker had appealed to the women that night to use their incalculable influence with the men who still remained in the old country and who were availnble for service at the Front. Of course, nobody wanted to send to the Front the men who were doing good service in turning out in one form or another the munitions and equipment of war—the things that were a sine qua non, both for the soldiers of this country and of our Allies. But, at the same time, there were still many young fellows who could go, and it was upon them that th,e womenfolk could exercise their persuasive in: fluence.

div.head: Chance of Centuries!
div.p: A Chance of Centuries!

The most enduring source of satisfaction in life was useful, valuable, honourable achieve- ment. And thousands of years might pass and never again, in all that long period,' might it be the privilege of any of this islathl race to play a part in so great and blessed an achieve- ment as that which would result in the Fiping out of the vile system of Junkerism. The man who went into "this job" and did "his bit," facing risk and hardship, would occupy the proudest position in the land. If the young men who had yet to go and win their_ spurs. wanted anything further in the way of induce- ment, they had only to look around and note. the example of their own kith and kin .who were already "out there "; who had fought like the heroes they were, not merely on one occasion, but on twenty occasions. They should be pleased and proud that the opportunity of lending a helping hand was theirs, and that theirs was the privilege of going out and back- ing up with all the force at their command the brave lads who were already in the battle arena. The programme was sustained by the follow- ing :—Mrs. Dutton and Messrs. W. H. Rigby, A. Dutton and Poole, and Master Hannan..

div.head: FAIRFIELD WARD.
div.p: FAIRFIELD WARD.
Lady Crosfield's Call To The Women. •

On Tuesday came. Fairfield's turn and the Liberal ladies of the ward rose in goodly num- bers to the special opportunity afforded them of once more evincing their interest ,in the work of the Women's\Sewing'Class, there being an excellent- assembly round the tea tables and at the concert which followed. Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield and Miss Truda Crosfield graced the proceedings with their 'presence, her Ladyship, occupying the chair.

div.head: HOW WOMEN MAY HELP TO KEEP THE FLAG FLYING I
div.p: HOW WOMEN MAY HELP TO KEEP THE FLAG FLYING I

Lady Crosfield, who was accorded a splendid ovation,- said that it was a ,great pleasure to her to come again to Warrington after the summer holidays and to find, the Liberal women all looking so fit and well and prepared for work again. At the same time one could not but feel sad that the occasion which prompted their meeting was that of so terrible and far- reaching a war. however, it was hest to jut a good face on things, though she 'could irot disguise from herself the fact that they had to face another winter of terrible warfare. Con- sequently it behoved them to prepare, straight- away, comforts for the men at the Front, and all varieties of warm clothing similar to that which was Sent to their men last winter and which was such an aid to them throughout that cold and dreary, time. The number of articles sent by the members of the class last year amounted to 4,4so—(applause)—Wliicli. she thought, was a very good total. To all those

who took a hand in making those comforts it inust be a source of gratification to know that , tl)ey ,were helping to alleviate the discomforts I,of those who were so bravely fighting for the people at home. The men at the Front, were keeping, the flag bravely flying; and those at hOme must keep it flying also. The womeu could not fight; but they could work—in fact, they could do their " bit " jil p§ the menfolk were so well doing theirs in Franm AbCYe all others, this was a time when women could ;:ros-T_ what tht- were Iy9rth At what work I thy•could do, 6i MititOi Ovoqb y kiln* t.IIO women could kop linti*--(laughter)—and that they could thirSte but women had nowadays discovered that. they could 'do a great many Other things which, hitherto, they had never tried their hands at, and which nobody felt certaip that they could do even if they tried— until they did it!

div.head: War's Service to the Women !
div.p: War's Service to the Women !

The war had brought the women to the fore, and now was the time for them to show that they could set their hands to almost everything —and, moreover, that when they set their hands to a thing they could •do it as well as .the men: As one went about London—so far, it was less va in Warrington—one could not help notsicing a cvmplete change in regard to the posts formerly 'occupied by men. When she went shopping she found that outside many of the large shops there were women to call the carriages and hand the shoppers into them, or to fimi their Motor cars for them. They did the—work splendidly—they never made a mistake-4/aughter)—and they did their work with smiling faces; a decided contrast to the .somewhat glum faees with which the men used to perform similar services. (Laughter.) Again, they found the women working on the trams and in the lifts; 'indeed, practically all the lifts in the city were now manned by women. Women were also 'to :be found at the railway stations, acting as tidket collectors, and, moreover, they were in different parts of the country taking. charge of the cleaning of the carriages—and at that point it might be mentioned that passengers who had need to use the railways were very pleased with the way in which the carriages were cleaned—the windows had been made to look brighter than ever they, had looked before— (laughter and applause)—und moreover the women, wore a very neat and picturesque cos- tume.
Peeresses Making Munitions.

Why, some-of ;the peeresses were even engaged making munitions—a wonderful thing and a very, very praiseworthy one! (Applause.) Think of those ladies who had been brought up in the lap of luxury—used to their breakfasts in bed and to-staying there until 11 or 12 o'clock in 'the morning—and-who were waited on hand and foot, going out and working, on night shifts, at making ammunition. A great many women had enlisted Mr Women's Special Service, among them Mrs. Osborne's daughter, who had been studying at an agricultural college and had learned to dO dairy work—and to sell the pro- duce at a profit. (Laughter and applause.) Of course, the women of France set the example to the women of England, for in the country of their ally across the Channel every woman able to leave her home was actively engaged on some piece of -work. The women of this country who could not find time to go to Work, could, at least, go to sewing meetings and help to supply the soldiers with the warm socks and clothing which they would need so badly during the bleak, cold winter which was ahead. Grateful " Tommies."

Her Ladyship then proceeded to read two letters -of thanks from soldiers who had received presents made by the members of the Associa- tion. The first of the twain wrote that it was a pleasuie to'-know that they had left some people.. at home who .thought of those at the Front. The second letter was from a man in hospital, who was suffering from abscess and partial lock-jaw, and who wrote, after express- ing his thanks, that in the tent in which he was quartered; "we were all ten Warrington boys together." (Applause.) Most of them were in the glorious charge last Saturday. 'From the letters which she had received, and the scores of similar lettePs which had reached Mrs. Osborne, they ,could see how greatly the things they had worked were appreciated by the soldrrs. WOMEN AND THE WAR.

What It Has Helped Them To Show The Men! Miss - Crosfield, who was loudly applauded, said that thet war had given the women the opportunity of provink that they could not only sew and stitch, but that they could also reap and mow. In war time agriculture was one of the most important new spheres for women. She was talking to a lady in London the other day and the lady told her that north of the Border, in Scotland, they saw more women than men in the fields doing the work and getting in the harvest. But, when she got back into sleepy, old England, no longer did she find the women working in the fields. There was a sphere of work open to women which Lady Crosfield had not mentioned—they could work as tram con- ductors or as 'bus conductors. She had put the question as to why women were not being taken. on at that work and a male conductor had in- formed her that it was not the Trade Union that prevented it, adding "But, if you saw the ' drunks ' that get in on Saturday nights you ,would not like to think of any woman having to collect fares from them !" Glasgow, however, had tried the experiment of having women con- ductors', and there the women were doing simply splendidly. Miss Crosfield went on to talk of. a. letter she had received from her brother, Major Crosfield, who is at the Front with the Warrington Territorials, and who wrote of the determination of the British to push the enemy back as speedily as possible. They all knew- and admired the splendid work which the. local Battalion had been doing; they. all recalled how in the tremendous scrimmage of. June 16th they put in thirty-six hours under shot and shell. The • work on which they were recently engaged was the repairing, at nights, of the trenches which happened to 'be blown to pieces during the day. Miss Crosfield went •on to talk of her experiences in France and of *the shortage of socks that had 'been encountered, especially by the French. The French ladies had. appealed for wool, but as they could not give them that in the ordinary way the English workers had unravelled other woollen goods and had given them the wool to knit up into the articles they, most required. sfi.wanted to do all she could to encourage those present to make socks and stockings for the soldiers;, those were .the articles they appreciated, and those, were articles which were and would be sorely needed. Once she saw a vessel full of French soldiers come into harbour • and the feet of the soldiers had been frozen. They had been in a irench half-full of water, and one Sunday night .sharp frost had set in! She asked a great French surgeon what he thought of the men, and he said that he hoped that in most cases they would recover the use of their feet.

div.head: COUNCILLOR'S PRAISE AND PROMISE.
div.p: COUNCILLOR'S PRAISE AND PROMISE.

Councillor Locker, called on by Lady Crosfield to make a few *remarks, said he knew that the articles 'which had been made had been appre- ciated • at the Front, and he was •glad. to .have ithat opportunity of thanking the ladies who had spent •so much of their time in constructing them. . They all knew how their friends 'and relatives on the Continent were fighting for them, and the least they could do in return was to prepare for them such little articles as would make them comfortable and help them to go on with their splendid work. Tie would always he delighted to do all he could to help on any move- ment for the well-being of the soldiers who were doing 'do much' for the people at home. (Ap- plause):

div.head: SIR .IRIIIUR'S WISH.
div.p: SIR .IRIIIUR'S WISH.
One Great Thing Women iCan Do !

Sir Arthur Crosfield said he hoped they would all give -a very good account of themselves—in whatever sphere they happened to be—in the matter of carrying out the work to which their Association had set its hand, viz., the working .np, of very necessary garments for the soldiers. Luxuries were not being asked for—merely necessaries! The fine work which the women were doing; nay, the inestimably valuable work, was deeply appreciated by those ,on whose be- half it was accomplished. There was another direction in which the Womenfolk could help; and that was by using their illimitable influence to help on the great cause of recruiting. lie knew that, it • meant sacrifice., But, if ,it meant sacrifice to the men, in how many eases did it not mean ,more sacrifice to the women? For moment let them think of the case of the woman at home; the woman to whom every postman's knock was ,like a stab at the 'heart. The men who went to the Front had to face hardship and risk, but they had the sustaining knowledge that they were fighting for a just cause—a cause which would bring to every one'of ,them glory;

not only in their own times, but for endless cen- turies to come. Theirs would be the privilege of enjoying a meed, of glory such as had never been equalled in English history and suth as was not likely to be exceeded in the future. Look- ing back 2,500 years, across the mists of history, to the glorious days of ancient Greece, they fg4Pitt the deeds of the warrior heroes of those fap,ol duo shone as brightly in this year of grace as they 441 itt time when they were ,?o valorously perforatpai

div.head: Priceless Compensation.
div.p: Priceless Compensation.

It Would be the same in the case of the men who had gone, and were going, to serve their country in this great war, and the thought should be a priceless compensation to every man who had the ..pluck and the manhood to go and do his duty. Britain owed it as a matter of national honour—as a fundamental principle of national honour—not to allow weaker and friendly peoples to be snuffed out; not to allow the vile Teuton gospel of force to dominate Europe! Germany preached that gospel, and the whole essence of their policy and their actions was not to, • spiritualise the material things of the world, but to materialise its spiritual things. (Hear, hear.) No heavier in- dictment could be brought against a nation., They gave the Germans all the credit—if credit were due—for the preparations they had made for the dark work on which they were at present engaged; they gave them all the credit to which they were entitled for their capacity for organisation. They gave the German soldier credit for believing that he was fighting in a worthy cause; although, of course, they knew that he had been woefully misled by the men in authority in his country. Of course, they could not tell how long he would go on believing that ' he was fighting a worthy fight. The Military Gamblers.

He (Sir Arthur) gave the German soldier credit for being misled, as well as for courage and patriotism; but there were no words of condemnation that human tongue could utter, that were strong enough—severe enough—for the military gamblers who had staked the whole of Germany; nay, the whole well-being of Europe and the peace of the world, on the gamesters' throw. Their criminal folly was beyond descrip- tion. It was the duty of all who were able to put forth every effort to defend not only their hearths and homes but, also, the healthy national life of old England as they knew it. Had this country played a pusillanimous and miserable part and had left France and Belgium to their fate, as some people—happily, very few! —would have had her do, her turn would have come next—" and," added Sir Arthur, amid applause, "I for• one think we should pretty well have deserved it !" (Hear. hear.) In con- clusion, Sir Arthur expressed the thanks of the company to Mrs. James Locker, the ward cap- tain, and all the ladies who had assisted her, as well as to the artistes.

The 'evening's entertainers were Mrs. E. A. Sanders, the Misses Winstanley and Weston, and Messrs. J. Hannan, W. Rigby and A. Dutton, with Mr. E. Hannan at the piano. The prize winners in the knitting competition were :-1, Mrs. Ryder, 57, Hume-street; 2, Mrs. Houghton, 18, Algernon-street. The prizes were given by Councillor and Mrs. Locker.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD.
Sir Arthur Crosfield And The
Unspeakable Turk,

On Thursday evening was held the St. John's Ward tea party and concert—attended by suc- cess every whit as great as its two forerunners. After full justice had been done to an excel- lent tea, a splendid concert and some rousing speeches were listened to by a crowded hall. Before the commencement of the items Mrs. Osborne again took the opportunity of ex- plaining and advocating the Penny Bank, her words once more being attentively hearkened to: Despite a severe cold, Lady Crosfield took the chair for the greater portion of the pro- gramme, Mrs. Osborne afterwards taking her place.

div.head: EXAMPLES IN CHEERFUL COURAGE.
div.p: EXAMPLES IN CHEERFUL COURAGE.

Lady Crosfield expressed her sincere pleasure at again Meeting all the ladies after the summer vacation, and only wished that the object which had called them together had been other than war. They cQuld, however, follow the example of the brave men at the Front in being courageous, watchful and cheerful'. "Yesterday I was paying a visit to Lord Derby's War Hospital," continued her Lady- ship, "that wonderful hospital which most of you have seen and of which certainly all of you have heard. We visited the bedsides of all those soldier-boys—some from Warrington, some from other parts—and it was touching to see the cheerfulness with which they all bore their pain and suffering and the courage with which they spoke of the trials they had en- dured. There was not a single word of com- plaint from any of Mein; and I thought 'Well if that is the morale of our soldiers, then victory is certain for us!'" .(Applause.) Nothing counted so much as morale; it in- fluenced rulers, leaders, soldiers and women alike; and nothing kept up one's spirits so much as work. During the last year they sent 4,500 garments to the soldiers, and this year she hoped fhey would beat even that! (Applause.)

and children into exile, stripping them of every mortal thing they posses and sending them to tramp the road to some unknown destiny, driving the women mad by the hundred with their sufferings, so that they actually kill their own children in their madness—it would be hell let loose upon earth! The Damning Fact.

"But mark this damning fact! Germany is now trying to pretend that all this was brought about because there was some little insurrection by those unfortunate Armenians! It is a friends, like a good deal else that has come front Germany. (Loud applause.) • Here is the iwfu/ fact and the awful responsibility that is piling up on the shoulders of those criminals in Prussia: Everybody in Europe knows that if the Kaiser had lifted a finger he could have stopped the Turks committing these atrocities! Friends. the finger has not been lifted. The Kaiser lets the gospel of frightfulness go on. And you and I in our own small sphere have got to do all that lies in our power to bring about at the earliest possible moment the day when those criminals should be brought up for reckoning. (Prolonged applause.) • Entrancing Music.

The second half consisted of a beautiful quintet "The Rosary," followed by two quartets "A Little Tommy" and "Nellie Was a Lady." Mrs. Sephton followed with "When You Come Home," and Mr. Dutton with "Thy Sentinel Am I." Then came the duet "A Night In Venice," by Mrs. Dutton and Mr. Sephton. "God ,Save the King" concluded this, most successful function.

div.head: SPLENDID ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: SPLENDID ENTERTAINMENT.

The programme, for which the talented Brooklyn Concert Party were responsible, started with a male quartet, "Come where my love lies dreaming." Mrs. Sephton then sang rousingly "England," and Mr. Sephton followed with that most beautiful of Irish love songs, "Moira, my girl." Mr. Hopkins, having been encored for "I followed her," gave capitally "Ef yo' Then followed the mixed quartet, "A regular Royal Queen "—from "The Gondoliers "—splendidly given. Mrs'. Fairhurst and Mr. Trow, whose musical gifts cannot be gainsaid, concluded the first half with the overture, "Die Italiererin in Algier." SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD ON DOING OUR SHARE.

. Sir Arthur 11. Crosfield, who was received with rounds of applause, began. by offering, in the company's name, as well as on his own account, inost hearty thanks to the ladies and/gentlemen who gave the delightful entertainment, together with the ward captain, )frs. Dutton, and all the lady auxiliaries of St. Johns Ward, who were to be immensely congratulated upon their most excellent organisation. (Loud applause.)

.!` Now," continued Sir Arthur,- "Lady Cros- field spoke of our victory at the end of this great struggle as being certain. Well, friends, I am a. bit of an optimist myself; I have no patience with the pessimistic few as to the ultimate outcome. But I am equally certain That we can only make the most of it by each and all of us doing our share. Allusion has been made to the women's widening opportunities, and to those who are willingly facing hardships and risks—and who in only too many cases are laying down their lives for our country. And I think it is up to us all to exert ourselves in using our influence to persuade those who are still' able to go, and have not gone, to lose no time in going and helping their heroic kith and kin at the Front. (I fear, 'hear.)

div.head: One Word—Must.
div.p: One Word—Must.

Never forget how far-reaching is this cause that they are fighting for! Some of us felt only too sadly the awful consequences that were bound to follow this infamous military gamble in Prussia, and only in the last few days you have been reading perhaps the most hideous example_ of it aIL You remember in the great days of Mr. Gladstone how he said of the ,un- speakOle Turk that there was only one word the Turk would listen to—the word 'Must!' If only we had used it to the Turk in those day,, as the great Gladstone used to urge—and' as urged, I. may say, in our .own .local sphere by my father—if we had only had the courage to deal with the scoundrel then and send him bag and baggage about his business; there would have been, a great deal less horror perpetrated thaq there is being done now. Why, it is a cash of Herod out-Heroding Herod! Only past night you had Lord Bryce, one of the best in- formed men -in the 'country, stating seriously in the' House of Lords that it was quite possible this awful estimate of eight hundred thousand children, women and men who have been deliberately and in cold blood most horribly butchered—ig not an exaggeration! Well, friends, if it was only half that number treated as the Turks know how to treat them—torturing many before they kill them, sending the women

div.head: YEAR AGO!
div.p: YEAR AGO!
(It is just a year since Messrs. James, Dale, Beech, Savage, and Furness enlisted.)
year ago! A year of war's alarms has fled ,into the fast-forgetting past, A year ago since our men sprang to arms, - And left their classrooms at the clarion's blast.
Nor fiery cross, nor fear of conscript's ban. Had need to urge our men to duty's call, They went as free men in the foremost van, Free to do manly deeds, or, freely fall.
Not tears but cheers bade them a-fighting go, To cross clean swords against the frightful Hun,
And cleanse the world of such a carrion foe, And so they changed their chalk sticks for 5 gun.
And now their lots are cast, East, South and West, _
Their country's need the onry "Schemes " they know. Each plays a real man's part, the only test, Of manhood when war's drama is on show.
Thus we, the weak and women left behind, More than admire the patriots' part they play, And daily pray the Saviour of mankind To guard and guide our teachers 'midst the fray.
Another year God grant them "homeward
pass," A safe return when war and strife shall end; That each may greet the laddies of his class, And each be greeted "hero," yet still "friend." * W. 31.
(Re-printed from "The Beamont Mrald of September 17th, 1915. Written by Mr. Mason the head master, in commemoration of Oa anniversary of the "joining up" of five members of his staff.)
A poet says that in this life one Must lief either anvil or hammer. Lots of us; however, are only bellows.
Very Game. Mrs. Nicholas Longworth, at a dinner in. Cincinnati, told a quaint story about a pre- cocious boy.

"They are very precocious, indeed," she. said, "those little chaps from Eton or Rugby,_ with their round, sober faces and their quiet air. A very pretty- American girl was talking. one evening in London to one of these urchins. "'And _have you got a sweetheart yet,. Tommy?' she said playfully. " ' No,' said -Tommy—' still I'm game enough- for a bit of 'spooning if that's what you're after.'"
Have you
er thought how little food is absorbed in liness,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
1.4 Y 'VI M
Dr. Kenneth De Jong.—Private Joseph Clare, of the Royal Engineers, writes to his mother at Booth's Hill to say he has seen Dr. Kenneth De Jong in France.

Word from Capt. Ridgway.—We are pleased to hear that Captain Tom Ridgway, of the 4th South Lancashire Regiment, and of Wilders- moor, Lymm, came safely through the great advance—in which he played a strenuous part.

Soldier's Memorial Service.—At the Primitive Methodist Church on Sunday the Rev. R. W. Ferguson conducted a memorial service to Ser- geant George Appleton, of the 9th Rifle Brigade, and of Statham, recently killed in action.

"Whom God Hath Joined."—Two marriages recorded in the Parish Magazine are: Septem- ber 4th Frank Smith (St. John's, Altrincham) to Evelyn Platt (Lymm); and September 18th, Harry Jones to Martha 'Ann Shaw (both of Lymm).

"Our Day."—The National Red Cross move- ment, fixed for October 21st, arid • known as "Our Day," will be held in Lymm, as else- where, and we understand that Mrs. Watkin has the arrangements well in hand. On the pre- ceding day a grand musical concert to aid the hospital funds will, as • last year, be given in the Drill Hall. Well-known Chorister Married.—At the Parish Church on Monday morning, the Rector con- ducted the wedding of Mr. G abert Bowen, of Lymm, and Mrs. hal (widow of the late Mr. Wm. Hill), of Lymm Bridge. The bridegroom is a well-known member of the church choir, to which he has belonged for about four years. Previously he was one of the baritone singers in the Manchester Cathedral.

Death of Mr. H. Percival.—Very suddenly on Sunday, morning, we regret to state, the death took place from heart failure at 9, Moston-street, of Mr. Henry Percival. He had been unwell for a week, and under the care of Dr. L. Thorpe. Aged about 58, he was employed by Mr. Holt, builder.—At the Parish Church 'ow Wednesday afternoon the funeral was conducted by ;the Rector. The deceased leaves one son—Corporal Richard Percival, now abroad with the Lymm Territorials.

Lad's Club In War Time.—lt has been de- cided that an attempt shall be made to run the Lymm Lads' Club till Christmas to see- if in war time it can get along with its usual swing. If the lads can possibly "carry on." they will do so, under the leadership of Mr. J. C. Lister- Farrar and with Mr. G. W. Jones as secretary. All the usual attractions—gymnastics, billiards and shooting—are provided. Intending members should apply at. the Drill Hall on Monday nights.

Italian Voluntaries.—At the Parish Church during this month the voluntaries played by Mr. William Cooke will he by Italian corn- posers: "Marcia Religiosa " (Edoardo Perelli), "Andante Cantabile" (Marco A. C,esti), "Valli Profonde" (Marco Da Gagliano), "Alla Marcia" (Vincenzo Righini), " Offertorio" (V. A. Petrali), "Cantata" (Alessandro Scarlatti), "Organ Sonata" (P. Funiagalli), " Grave " (Arcangelo Corelli), " Aria " (Giovanni B. Martini), and " Aria " (A..:Sacchini). At an organ recital the pieces will be Caro mio ben" (Giordani), " Capriccio " (Filippo Capocci), " Intermezzo " (Pietro Mascagni), and "Marcia di Processione " (Enrico Bossi).

Congregational Harvest.—The Rev. Dr. R. Cantrill Scurrah (father-in-law of the new minister, who commences his pastorate a week to-morrow), conducted the Congregational harvest festival on Sunday. This was the most successful festival of its kind during he 51 years of the church's history. The collections realised over £6. The morning text was "Thou crowneth the year with Thy goodness (Psalms), and that of the evening "War a. good warfare" (Timothy). The choir rendered splendidly the anthems "Thou Visitest The Earth" .(morning) and "-Ile Watereth The hills" (evening); Both anthems were composed by Jamouneau. The evening solo part was taken by Miss M. J. Appleton., Mr. Albert Leather presiding at the organ. On Monday evening Dr. Scurrah lectured in the school on "Some Mistakes In Measuring Men," his dis- course being directed against those who judged men by the length of their purses. The school was well filled.

Of War-Time Harvest Festivals.—The Rector says: "We are now in the second year of the most terrible war in history; the somewhat confident and amateurish way in which we regarded that war a year ago, so far as we were ourselves concerned, has disappeared and many an illusion has been dispelled. We are still, thank God, confident and our confidence ! during the past few days has been shown to have some solid foundation, but the country has needed much awakening, and we are now fully alive to the task which lies before us, and to the serious peril in which we stood last winter on account of our unpreparedness and our grievous want of men and munitions. The harvest thanksgiving services should, there- fore, have a wider and deeper meaning to us than in ordinary years of ,peace.. Our minds have been broadened by the experiences of recent months, and while we thank God for the bountiful harvest of the fields that has been so mercifully bestowed on Us this year we must not forget the greater harvest in the spiritual world that God has vouchsafed to us in this war. We who look not on the things that are seen but on things that are not seen, we who have the faith in Christ to dwell not merely on the temporal but also on the eternal, have an abundant harvest of joy to thank GU for in allowing us to witness the brave, noble and unselfish deeds, countless and beyond number, of those young men who have gone out from among us, and who are fighting our battles with such courage and endurance in foreign lands. And for those, our heroes, we shall not cease to pray that an abundant harvest may be granted to that seed that they are sowing in pain and weariness, aye, and with their irery lives, in a world renewed, restored, a world of true liberty and freedom for all races of man- kind, which will be the priceless heritage for those who come after."

twelve months, from Urging the claims of the Church on your attention except from a spiritual standpoint; I have been unwilling to appear even in the smallest degree to do or say anything that would seem to arrest the full flow of generosity in money or in personal services into the new channels, created .by the necessities of the war; and. I think I recognised at a very early stage that the expression so freely bandied about of Business as usual' was a ridiculous one in face of- the' very grave and exceptional difficulties that the nation was so suddenly called upon to encounter. Ido not see any reason for, departing from that attitude at the present time, except to voice a little warning which is not oritinal, but expresses a sentiment that many earnest-minded persons must be feel- ing. War tends,- and especially in these days of cheap newspapers, to become an obsession, that is it tends to oce_upy the whole mind and for the time everything else suffers and is crowded out by the one dominant thought. This when pushed to the extreme by those who perforce must remain quietly at home may become very harmful, especially when it is the domain of religion and religious duties that is thus threatened. And so it comes to pass that except in the case of those whose religion is closely connected with their life, religion passes into the background ready perhaps to assert itself again in more favourable times. I have no hesitation in saying that this danger has shown itself in Lymm, as no doubt it has in many other places. I would ask you most earnestly to give this matter your serious consideration, and to ask yourselves if this has been the case with

div.head: " STOPPED " CHEQUE.
div.p: " STOPPED " CHEQUE.
Pony Exchange Leads To Warrington County Court. Case.

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, before Judge-J. Scott Fox, ,K.C., James Shepherd, tobacconist, of Bridge-Water- street, Lymm, made a claim against James G. Westbrook, poultry dealer, of ,Sandy-lane, Lymm, for £6—on a cheque given by West- brook .to him on an arrangement for the ex- change of ponies. The payment of the cheque had been stopped. Westbrook brought a counter claim for £l2 6s. He alleged that on the exchange of ponies plain- tiff wanted the pony, which heisold defendant. Mr. T. S. Steel (of Warrington) appeared for plaintiff, whilst Mr. Rhodes (of Manchester) represented defendant. Mr. Steel said that on Tuesday, August 24th, plaintiff went to defendant's- house with the object of purchasing some poultry. Westbrook expressed admiration of his pony, and after some conversation it was arranged that they should exchange ponies, Westbrook paying £6 to boot. For this sum he gave plaintiff a cheque, which was afterwards stopped at the bank. In taking the pony, added Mr. Steel, de- fendant tested it for himself. • • Mr. Rhodes maintained that Shepherd war- ranted the pony not to be lame; but that after- wards defendant found it was very lame and not fit for work. After hearing considerable evideneio from both sides, his Honour came to the conclusion that on the plaintiff's own statement he had war- ranted the pony all right. Judgment was, there- fore, given for defendant, and on the counter- claim for .t 9.

div.head: PRIVATE J. FRED. PERCIVAL.
div.p: PRIVATE J. FRED. PERCIVAL.
Grappenhall Tanner Wounded In Fore- Finger Of Right Hand.

Private James Frederick Percival, of Canal Bank, Grappenhall, and the son-in-law of Mrs. Statham, 12, Moston-street, Lymm, has, while serving in France with the 2nd Cheshires;been wounded in the ,forefinger of his right hanol.
PRIVATE J. FRED PERCIVAL.
Wounded.

div.head: PRIVATE JACK STATHAM.
div.p: PRIVATE JACK STATHAM.
Airs A Grievance—But Postal Author- ities Are To Blame.

Private Jack Statham, of the 6th South Lan- cashires, after being slightly wounded in the head whilst serving at the Dardanelles, *rites to his wife at 11, Moston-street : lam in the best of health just now. •Well, We had some very hard fighting, and on the-6tll of August 1 was hit by a shrapnel bullet, but it was fiot, very bad. Now 1 am ready to go back—and the sooner the better. We have to work jolly hard here, for we are getting a base ready for the

troops. "I suppose you have either heard or seen Joe Daniels by now, for he left Alexanaria for Eng- land about three weeks ago, and I was more than disappointed at not seeing him, before he went. But we have got to put up- With a lot worse than not seeing a friend go home; for, you kflop, it is jolly hard lines when YOU see a Chum getting put off altogether,' never to be seen again. . . "We have now been left England , three rupiahs and I have never had a line from any- Now, put things the other way. Say I never sent -'a line for three months, you would jump to conclusias and think that something had happened to me. Well, it is just the same with -me, for you know accidents ca4n happen in England just as well as out here, and it makes one think something has happened when they don't hear from home." It may be added that Mrs. Statham has writ- ten frequently to „lier..husband. . . •
one.

div.head: Rector On_" These Days Of Cheap
div.p: Rector On_" These Days Of Cheap
Newspapers..."
The Lymm Citizens' Sunday is being arranged for October 17th or 24th. In the current Parish Magazine the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) writes :

"The Citizens' Sunday was instituted some seven years ago by the Tradesmen's Association, the object of its promoters being to gather together all parishioners once a • year in an act of united worship. It was a great conception, and undoubtedly has been, of much blessing to the village and neighbourhood. The inspiration which this service gives to all will be warmly welcomed at this .time of trouble and anxiety; we shall haVe united with us in spirit our many brave lads on active service, and our prayers will go up for them and their safety. "But the inspiration from a gathering like this should not cease with the service. I know not what is the case among other religious denominations in Lymm, but I do know that some of our own Church people have grown lax and careless. Let then this Citizens' Sunday stir us all up to 'better endeavours, ad make us more earnest in our worship of Almighty God, the value of which to our national spirit is inestimable at the present crisis of our country's ' history. "A Ridiculous Expression." •
"I have purposely refrained during the past
FROM
The news that he had been wounded 'first reached his wife, staying at Lymm, on Wednes- day, and .from him Mrs. Statham also has received a card.

Aged 32, Private Percival was born at Lymm and brought up at the village school under Mr. Oddie's headmastership. After7leaving, he first became a fustian-cutter for the. late Mr. F. 0. Moston, but has been a tanner at Lortg's Tan 7 yard, Grappenhall, for about nine years. He attends the C;rappenhall Church, and has two little boys. He joined the 2nd Cheshires early this year. Previously he was in the Reserve, having at one time belonged to the Warrington Militia. To the Continent he crossed a few weeks after enlisting.

div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
OPTIMISTIC LETTER FROM PRIVATE HENRY BROOKES.

*vale Henry Brookes,. of the 1/sth Cheshire Teiiriterials, writes from the Front to his mother, Mrs. Taylor, at 1,. West Hyde:— " Juet a few lines to say I am well, contrary to the false report ;11/hielt had gained currency in Lymna. Of course you, knowing that we were in the midst of these' such terrible dangers diay after day, are easily led to believe Such reports until you receive some self-written note Which altogether is to the contrary. Last week only Iliad a leffer. from a gentleman, in which it said how Awonderfully preserved we had .been ;sci far,. seeing that we have been in the thick of it. I thought how true this was, and I Must say we have much to be thankful for.

div.head: Great Events To Take Place.
div.p: Great Events To Take Place.

"Well, I suppose that the good news- which has appeared in the English panels about the much-waited-for: advance has livened things up a bit, and peopf will be, looking forward for greater events to :take place. Our Allies, the French, are making splendid progress, especially in the -Argonne and Champagne dis- trict—where their: consistent artillery bombard- ments have wrought havoc among the German trenches. The CroWn Prince's army, which is in opposition round that region, is having a very hie and trying time.

div.head: Hopeful Prophecies.
div.p: Hopeful Prophecies.

"You no doubt will hear of the great doings of the Cheshires in the near future. If we keep on as we are doing we ought to have them out of France and Belgium very soon. "We have had a very bad spell of wet weather round here tlis last week, much of it being due to the heavy _rumbling of the big guns during the bombardments. ",I had a letter from my master this week, and he told me that Mr. Harry [Champ, of Cheadle], had come out, to France with the Royal Engineers. I should like to see him if he comes down our way. I arii glad to see that Ernest Shaw is still keeping well, as I saw a letter of his which appeared in one of the papers. We have met a good number of the Scottish Regiments since we came out here; we have .not had the goad fortune of seeing him yet, but hope to do so before very long.

div.head: Dwindling Numbers.
div.p: Dwindling Numbers.

"When we came out here there were well over thirty Lymm fellows in our platoon, but to-day we only muster about a dozen. One by one they have gone, and times seem so different with the absence of the • dear old faces. Through many rough storms we have 'trudged, to and from the trenches in all-sorts of weather, but- nevertheless happy, and singing on our dreadful- journey—never knowing who was to he the next to leave this good company. But still, we were aware of the -bitter times which surely must come, and we wore these trying thoughts down with the hope of some day returning home victorious, knowing that-we were clear of the' scorn which some time the slacker would have to face. We are now but few, but hope to see the day when we shall push the Kaiser's 'fragments' over the running waters of the Rhine.

div.head: Gift of Books.
div.p: A Gift of Books.

" I hope Jim's arm is improving, and that I shall soon have a line from him. The books you sent were very interesting, and you must thank my Uncle Heywood for them if he gave them to you." It is .interesting to note that Private Brookes
has received from the Lymm ' Tradesmen's Association a letter of congratulation on having beeu awarded by the Tzar an Order of the Cross of St. George.

div.head: SAPPER. PERCY, CL.NRE VISITS HOME.
div.p: SAPPER. PERCY, CL.NRE VISITS HOME.

Sapper Percy Clare, of the Lymm Territorials, but since a month ago attached to the Royal Engineers—on Saturday morning arrived home from France on six days' leave—having left his duties early the previous morning. When he had been at home two days there arrived several letters written by him four days before leaving. On Thursday afternoon "The Examiner" man chatted with Sapper Clare at his home on Booth's Hill, and IVarn`ed that the 'leave had been granted at one day's notice. On Wednes- day night of last week they went up ,to the trenches as usual, and that was his last , night in them. By train he had a good journey down to the coast, and (after a short wait at the port for. the boat) a good journey across. Follow Advancing Army.

Until, in response to a request for volunteers, he joined the Mining Section, Sapper Clare saw plenty of fighting which went well in favour of the Allies. Now, however, he does not see Much fighting, because as soon as "anything is going to come off" the miners leave the trenches. As the army. advances they follow it. As soon as a trench is taken from the Germans they.. are sent for. Of course they also help in the taking of the trenches, because when a trench is to be taken they do the dynamiting, and then in the attack the officers explode the mines. Mining is risky and rather dangerous; but it has its compensations. Rats are encountered only in small numbers. The advantages are demonstrated not only by the fact that Private Clare is looking splendier, but also because during .the last four weeks there have only been half a dozen casualties amongst the hundred men of his section. And these casmi- ties took place not when the mei,/ were, -doing their work, but when they were leaving the trenches. The Germans have the miners marked, and as they vacate the trenches send over aerial torpedoes and. mortars. The men, however, can see them coming and so have a chance to get out of the way.

div.head: Star-Shells At Night.
div.p: Star-Shells At Night.

All night the enemy send star-shells to try and ascertain their pbsition. As soon as they get well into the air these shells burst, and whilst they are blazing the whole scene is light as day for a few minutes. Then they fall to the ground and fizzle out. At the worst a man could otijy receive burns from them: they are like children's sky-rockets.

div.head: Spare Hours.
div.p: Spare Hours.

They have eight hours in the trenches dnd twenty-four out. Spare hours they spend in a town which has been altogether shelled, but in which a few civilians still remain. What the, do for a living the miners do not know, although they see them regularly. A good proportion of the men's spare time is spent at a hut which has been erected since three weeks; and which is visited once a week by a minister, who con- ducts a service. The room is used for writing letters in, and a piano ale is provided. As some of the miners can play this. excellent con- certs are got up. This is one of the men's chief amusement resorts.

The coming winter has not yet emphasised it- self so far as they are concerned; happily the summer has been a prolonged one, marked on the whole by good weather. Rains, of course, have come at times, rendering the trenches sloppy and muddy; but unlike the condition in the early stages of the war, to n great extent it now drains off.

Sapper Clare does not think the war will last long. Private Joseph Clare is also mining along with his cousin, an.d finds it a pleasurable change to be in the trenches without having continually to crouch in fear of one's life from snipers and shells. A Gardener. -

Aged 22, Sapper Percy Clare was born and brought .up at Lymm, and is in peace times a Primitive Methodist and a gardener for Mr. Houghton, West Leigh. The Territorials he joined four and a half years ago, and was called up on the war outbreak.

Private H. Cadman in Scotland.—Private Henry Cadman, of the Mining Section of the Royal Engineers, has for a month been in hos- pital in Scotland s,uffering from asthma. - Writ- ing home to tell how comfortable and well-cared- for he is, he adds: "It is-a big gentleman's house that we Are quartered in, and we, are only allowed out in the grounds. Still there are plenty of '()Ames for us when it is fine weather we get fed up with playing them every day !" He is progressing well, and in another letter tells of motoring to the picture theatre and finish- ing up at night with a grand concert at the hospital !
