div.head: " BEECHAVOOD " HOME.
div.p: THE " BEECHAVOOD " HOME.
Satisfactory Report Published By Belgian Refugees' Committee.

Mr. Alfred Watkin, on behalf Of the Execu- tive Committee of the "Beechwoodt" Belgian Refugees' Home (of which he is chairman),. publishes the following report : "The total receipts. to June 30th fast were ..f..8401185. lfdL and the. erpendiiture .41540 3e. lid., leaving a balance in hand of X. 300) Is.. From this, however, must be deducted a sum of ap- proximately of-80 for June accounts unpaid at the date of this account.

"It will be remembered that Sir W. H. Lever, Bart., early in October,: kindry offered the free use of :Beechwood' for a Refugee Home, and with generous contributions of furniture, &c., from local residents, the Home was completely furnished within seven days' at very little cost to the fund, and was opened on October 27th, when the first guests arrived:- The committee, after careful consideration, de- cided to offer hospitality to thirty-five ref ugees-,. and approximately this number has been, in continual residence.

div.head: Working Or With The Colours.
div.p: Working Or With The Colours.

"In all, 78 refugees have been sent to Lymm, and of these several have joined the Col Ours, others have found occupations- in gitglandi, and a few unsuitable cases have been returned to the War Refugees' Committee. There .are at present in residence 37 Belgians, of whom five are wounded soldiers, discharged as unfit for further duty. The other men are all over military age, and have hitherto'. been found- occupation in cultivating the gardens, and, at local farms. All these. have -now- been regis- tered for employment at- the Labour Exchange. Most of the other guests, (about thirty) are wives and children of Belgian soldiers now :serving at the Front. Several of these latter, ,while on leave, have visited their families at' ithe Horne, and have all. expressed thei;,grlti- .tude for the care and attention they re- ceived. Several of- the men, who have found ,eMployment out of the diStriet often visit the 'Home at week-ends.

div.head: "To Ccrntributts To- Their Support"
div.p: "To Ccrntributts To- Their Support"

"In compliance with a request from the Local Government Board that the refugees in receipt of money should make some contribu- tion towards their support, the Executive Committee have the matter under • considera- tion.

- "The Exec. utiVes COmmittee• wish to place on record their appreciation- of the services of Miss Healey, the first Hon. Matron of the Home. The present Hon. Matron- (Mrs. Dorling), with the assistance of the House Committee, which meets every Friday, has managed the Home efficiently and economically. The guests are well looked after, they are most comfortable, and complete harmony- prevails; "It is probable that the Home Will have to be continued for some considerable time yet, and although Sir W. H. Lever is liberally sub- scribing to the fund, it iS still imp6rative that further subscriptions should be received. The committee thank all who have contributed in money or kind, and trust to receive a con- tinuance, of their • kind. support. Visitors will be heartily welcomed and allowed to view the Home at any time on application to the Hon. Matron!'' To Whom Hcnour Is Due.

The Executive Committee is as follows : Mrs. Parmiter, Mrs. Watkin, Messrs. F. Clarke, G. A. Cook, Thomas F. W. Dixon, F. E. Evans, H. T. Mercer and T. J. Ridgway, the Rev. G. .B. Thurston and Mr. Alfred Watkin. Their splendid report—a matter of hearty congratu- lation—has been circulated amongst subscribers to the Home.

div.head: TEMPERANCE WOMEN CONFER.
div.p: TEMPERANCE WOMEN CONFER.
Two liundred'Cheshire Delegates Visit The Township.

In connection with the National British Women's Temperance Association, the Autumn Conference of the Cheshire County Union was held on Wednesday in he Primitive Methodist Church at the invitation of t/he Lymm Branch, of which Mrs. Welford is secretary. From all parts of the County about-itwo hundred dele- gates attended. The morning session was mainly devoted to the transaction of business—in which a lively interest was taken. Luncheon was provided in the adjoining schoolroom, after which a "Y" Conference' was held in the vestry and a devotional meeting, conducted by Miss Stanier, of Northenden. A time of real refreshment and help was experienced. At 3.30 an open conference was conducted by Miss Agnes Dutton, when the speakers were Mrs. Boston, of Crewe (" Branch Difficulties and Failures"); Mrs. Brooke, of Hazel Grove (" How We Won the Banners"); Mrs. Vacher, of Birkenhead ("Temperance Essay Scheme"); and Mrs: Walt. Walker, of Preston ("B. Respon- sibility for'Y' Work"). By all the day's proceedings were highly enjoyed and voted a huge success.- Much praise was given to the local branch for the very admirable way in which it had catered for it visitors, and helped to make the visit so successful. •

div.head: NEW SESSION OPENED.
div.p: NEW SESSION OPENED.
On Wednesday evening the opening meeting of the Lymm Branch's new session was held amid a large attendance of members and friends. _ _ _

The chair was taken by Rev. G. S. Tudor- Evans, rector of Oughtrington, who, in a short and able address expressed his deep sympathy with the work—particularly at the present time of urgent need. Miss Cherry (hop. secretary of the County Union) spoke most highly of the work of some 8.W.T.A1 workers in the canteens, after which Mr. George Wilson (secretary of the U.K.A.) spoke on "Drink and Economy." A highly in- formative and lucid speech, this was listened to with keen interes4by all. At the close Mrs. F. 0. Moston, in a few well chosen words, expressed the thanks of all to the Chairman, speakers, and last, but not least, to Mrs. Worthington, of Warrington—who had enriched the proceedings by singing three appreciated songs. The meeting closed with encouragement to all temperance workers—who felt that the branch had had a very good "send off" for the winter's work.

Parish Church Harvest Festival—The morn- ing preacher at the Parish Church harvest fes- tival on 'Sunday was the Rev. B. Percival (vicar of St. Peter's., Warrington) and the evening one the Rev. G. S. Tudor-Evans (rector of Ought- rington). Offertories were taken from the large congregations on behalf of the choirlund, whilst at the afternoon children's fruit and flower service, fruit,. Veigetables and eggs were collected on behalf of the Red Cross Hospital.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL. CHESHIRE VOLUNTEER REGIMENT.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL. CHESHIRE VOLUNTEER REGIMENT.
Grappenhall Detachment.
_ Orders for week commeneing_Oetober .11th :

Wednesday, October 13th.—Musketry instruc- tion, 7.45 p.m. Fall-in at Headquarters 7.40 p.m. sharp. Saturday, October 16th.—Companyll, 3.30 p.m. Fall-in at Headquarters at 3.25 p.m. sharp. Recruits Still Wanted.—A strong apPeal is made to all men beyond military age, or those engaged on munition or similar work for the Government, to enrol in a Volunteer Corps, and undertake such 'work as will enable the men of the Regular +Army, now engaged in Home Defence, to be utilised for other and more use- ful purposes.. ApplicatioW should be made for enrolment at the Headquarters (the Large Room) any time the same is open for drill.

div.head: ORFORD.

div.head: LOST HAND.
div.p: A LOST HAND.
Boy Cable-Worker Sues For Compensation.
FIRM WILL FIND FRESH WORK.

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day morning, before his Honour Judge. J., Scott Fox, K.C., an interesting case under the Work- men's Compensation Act was heard, the appli- cant "'being Sidney. Bodle, aged .47, of 165, Knutsford-road, and the respondents \ the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company, Bank Quay. The applicalit Sought' coMpensation for the 1014 of his left hand. Mr. Edward Acton (instructed by Messrs. Arthur Browne and Co.) was for the applicant, and Mr. Wingate Saul (instructed by Mr. John Taylor, of Blackburn) for the respondents.

div.head: CASE FOR THE APPLICANT.
div.p: THE CASE FOR THE APPLICANT.

In opening the case, Mr. Acton said that the applicant was a youth, seventeen years .of_ age, but at. the date of the accident—April 26th of the present year—was only sixteen. It. was on April 6th that the lad began to work for the respondents, his wage being a guinea a week, plus a war bonus of 10s. a month. When he was engaged his instructions were that he was to do whatever was put before him; there appeared to have been no definition of the limit of his duties. What, in fact, he was set to do was to render assistance in various ways in the process of sheathing cables with rubber. On the day of the accident Mr. Hopley, who was the fore- man of the cable department, told the appli- cant and certain other workers engaged on the same task that they would have to werk until 8 o'clock. Accordingly, between 7 and 8 o'clock the applicant was at his work, and a cable was being sheathed, the mixing machine—in which the-rubber was mixed—and the spewing machine —which coated the cable with the rubber—being both running. For some reason, the mixing machine man—" who rejoiced in the well-known name of John Burns "—had gone home, and there was accordingly nobody left to warm and soften rubber, in case any more was required for the sheathing of the cable. An Important Point. That was an important point, for unless the sheathing machine was kept running con- tinuously until the whole of the cable was sheathed so much of the cable as might be sheathed when the supply of rubber came to an end would be wasted. The applicant was engaged in cutting the warm and softened rubber, at a table close to the spewing machine, into such a size that that machine could deal with it. Towards 8 o'clock he noticed that he was getting very near to the end of the rubber which he had, and he asked the man in charge of the spewing machine whether he would require more, the man replying that he would. The applicant, accordingly went to the mixing machine to get some more rubber, but when he got there he found that the man in charge had gone, and that there was no rubber in the mixer.
How The Accident Happened.

He thereupon went_ to the spewing machine and gathered some waste rubber, which he took to the mixing machine. Under those circum- stances he was in a dilemma, especially as the foreman under whose orders he worked had also temporarily left the workshop. He did not want to see the cable spoilt, and he knew that by putting the rubber which he had gathered into the mixing machine and then drawing it aut from underneath he could in- stantaneously Supply himself with the where- withal to complete the sheathing process. In order that he might get the rubber that was so urgently needed out of the mixing machine the lad put his right hand under the machine and with his left hand held on to a single-rail guard. Whilst he was drawing the rubber out the lad's left hand slipped from the rail into the rollers, being drawn in and crushed so badly that it had to be amputated. HAD DONE IT BEFORE!

In the witness box, the applicant said that he had, in the absence of the man in chargw; put rubber in the mixing machine before, his idea being, as on the occasion of the accident, not to interfere with the sheathing process. Mr. Wingate Saul, in cross-examination, elicited from the lad the fact that at the time of the accident the spewing machine was not engaged on cable Work at all, but on the making of dialite cord. Mr. Saul: And when you are working on this cord you can stop the machine at any time without spoiling the job in hand.. Witness: I did not know' that. His Honour (to applicant): Your story was that the work you werip on was the work of sheathing cables, .and no you remember that it was dialite cord. It is rather funny how you came to tell your counsel that it was sheathing work, isn't it? Applicant: I had forgotten for the moment what it was. In answer to further questions, the applicant stated that on the day in question he WO, engaged in cutting for cable-sheathing up to about 5.30. He knew that the dialite cord pro- cess on which the machine was engaged at the time of the accident might safely be inter- rupted. LAD'S MOTHER'S EVIDENCE.

Mary Ann Bodle, mother of the boy—whose father, she Said, left her many years ago and had not been seen since—deposed to interviewing Mr. Seymour, the manager of the Cable Co after the accident, and said that that gentle- man assured her that the firm intended to give the lad half wages during the time he was in the Infirmary, and to find. him job in the works when he was better. • Mr. Seymour also said that the firm Would buy him a false hand. CASE FOR THE RESPONDENTS.

Called for the respondents, Mr. Edwin Shirley Sqiuour;,the company's manager, said that the firm only put experienced men on the mixing machine, and the applicant had no right what- ever to do anything with the machine. •: As a matter of fact it transpired after. the , accident that, for the class of workiw,hand; he had fed the wrong kind of rubber into the machine. On the risumption ,k,f; the case .after the luncheon interval, Mr. Saul called Frank Hopley, the foAman 111 the cable department of the works, :who .said that the lad had no right whatever to do any, work in connection with the mixing machine. If he had seen the lad inter- fering with the mixing machine he would have warned him the first time and have "cleared him out of the shop" the second time. OWN SENSE OUGHT TO HAVE TOLD HIM! Mr. Acton: The lad has stated that he was engaged to (16 whatever was found him to do? Witness: Yes; under the charge hand, of course! In; reply to .the Judge, the witness added that he lad's Own sense might to have told him notito go near to the mixing machine. Henry Montt, 'a-charge-hand at the works, said ht had the inthrfering with

div.head: COUNSEL'S SUBMISSIONS.
div.p: COUNSEL'S SUBMISSIONS.

In his address to the Judge, Mr. Acton sub- mitted that even if the applicant had done soniething that was not strictly in his employ- ment it was, not done for his own benefit, but for the benefit of his employers, and that he was not cheelied In the doing thereof. Mr. Wingate Saul argued that the boy's own words negatived' his learned friend's argument; for the boy expressly stated that when he was engaged he was told to do what he was found to do, and adinitted that on the occasion of the accident he was not told to go and feed the machine which crushed his hand. It might be—boys often did silly things for the
same reason—that the applicant was putting the rubber in the mixer for "the fun of the thing." The boy was not doing anything he had a right to do; nor anything that arose out of his employment.

div.head: JUDGMENT.
div.p: THE JUDGMENT.

His Honour found that applicant had not made out his case, and gave judgment for the respondents. Mr. Saul said that the firm would, as soon as possible, find the applicant a clerical job in. the works. His Honour: X am glad to, hear you say so!

div.head: CHURCHMEN'S SOCIETY.
div.p: CHURCHMEN'S SOCIETY.
Entertainment And Protection
Of Soldiers.

Following out resolutions of the Church of England's Men Society, Warrington and Dis- trict, to hold future federation meetings every two months on fixed dates, there took place last Saturday in the Vestry of St. Paul's Church, Warrington, a meeting of the Warrington and District Federation of the Church of England Men's Society. Thirty delegates attended from each of the branches forming the Federation, representing some hundreds of members. The Rev. Mr. Greenham ' (vicar of Halton), presided. The Rev. G. C. Briggs (vicar. of Latchford), a past chairman, also attended. Mr. Tegg (secretary) said that the usefulness of the Federation could be greatly improved by printing and supplying each 'delegate with a syllabus which would clearly set out particulars of meetings, Sic., arranged by each branch as their programme for a few- monthe ahead. He also expressed his view that interest in the branches would be stimulated by occasional friendly visits of the Chairman and others. It was resolved to print a- time table, in skeleton form for the present, giving as much informa- tion as possible of work going on in various branches and as far as possible ahead. The Chairman also particularly asked for invitations to be sent to him, giving definite dates upon which it would be convenient to spend an even- ing with each branch. Reference was made to an item in the C.E.M.S. current magazine, in which Bishop Montgomery urged all members to use their influence in sup- pressing pernicious literature circulated with the object of encouragirig immorality during the war. The Federation Secretary was instructed to write C.E.M.S. Head'quarters, asking whether they had any information relating to Warring- ton and district, and* how the delegates. could best help; which they 'pledged themselves to do. A resolution was proposed and carried that a committee should consider and report how best the Federation could initiate and assist in the provision of suitable entertainment and recrea- tion for soldiers passing ,through and stationed at Warrington. Mr. F. NeWhOld, Sankey Branch, was deputed to call together a pro- visional and elect a permanent committee for that purpose. A suggestion that extempore prayers should form a part of each Federation meeting was deferred for consideration at the next meeting. Mr. Smethurst (a Church officer), on behalf of St. Paul's Parish, heartily welcomed the dele- gates and explained that his Vicar was absent in France, and invited those present to partake 9f the hospitality certain ladies had provided. He took the opportunity of mentioning that the Church House was most suitable, and was avail- able at a nominal charge for future Federation meetings. The Chairman gratefully accepted the invitation and thanked him and St'. Paul's Branch members for their kind provision of meeting place and refreshment. It is an- nounced that the December gathering will be I held at St. Thomas', Stockton Heath Branch.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD.

Sir Arthur Crosfield and Lady Crosfield have had a busy week in Warrington. As a pre- liminary, they turned up unexpectedly at the Town ,Hall on Saturday night to witness the military tattoo, and the worthy Baronet made a rousing recruiting speech, which proved him to be in fine oratorical form. Speaking with his usual earnestness, and with great emphasis, his voice carried well over the great lawn, and was clearly comprehended on the far side of the crowd, for they cheered his words most heartily. On Monday Sir Arthur, on behalf of Mrs. John Crosfield and the family, presented to the town a fine marble bust of his father, which, originally intended for the Memorial Hall, was, at the request of the Council, diverted to the Town Hall, where it now stands next to the bust of the late Mr. George Crosfield. The fact that two brothers are thus represented in our muni- cipal headquarters is sonic indication of what this particular family have been to, and done for, Warrington. The Liberal. women workers have been set upon their winter's work by Lady Crosfield, who also paid a visit to the wounded soldiers at the Lord Derby hospital.

div.head: REV. T. T. JAMES RETURNS TO THE
div.p: REV. T. T. JAMES RETURNS TO THE
FRONT.

The Y.M.C.A. authorities, under whom the respected Pastor of the Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church has laboured among the soldiers at the Front duiing the present summer', hav- ing pressed Mr. James to return to their aid, the reverend gentleman, with the consent of his people, has undertaken to go upon another period of active service, and will prob- ably start for the Front next Thursday.

div.head: DEARTH OF ORATORY.
div.p: DEARTH OF ORATORY.

A month ago the sitting of the Town Coun- cil lasted only four minutes and constituted something like a record. On Tuesday night the business was quite as rapidly transacted, but, the holidays being over, there was more of it. Quarter of an hour proved sufficient to confirm all the, minutes that were submitted, as none of them called for any extended re- marks. The only subject that might have resulted in an orator's:.-field day was, fortun- ately, given the cold should& altogether. It will be remembered that the Education Com- mittee decided to appeal .to the Board of Education against the decision of the Health Committee and the Town Council not to allow them a voice in the election of their school medical officials, and a hint was given that the Town Council would not sanction the

appeal. As a matter of fact all the Education Committee minutes, like the minutes of the other committees; were confirmed en bloc, and the request for light from London goes on its way free and untrammelled. ' Of course, there is no election in November this year—and there was no need to make speeches at the October meeting.

div.head: "OUR DAY."
div.p: "OUR DAY."

We call attention to an article which appears in another column setting out the pro- gramme by which the friends of the Red Cross Society and the St. John Ambulance Associa- tion are about to celebrate the anniversary of the amalgamation of their forces for the purposes of the war. These missioners of mercy deserve all the help we can give them. Everything that can be done to alleviate the sufferers and to prevent unnecessary suffer- ing on the part of those who are fighting our battles these champions of the hospitals— field, base or home—are more than willing to do. They are burning with eagerness to do it. All they require is the necessary financial assistance—and who will be so mean in mind as to measure their purses against such a cry for help? We hope the programme will be well studied and well supported. Let us make October 21st a red-letter day in our annals of charity as well as a Red Cross day.

div.head: "OUR DAY."
div.p: "OUR DAY."
To Celebrate An Important Amalgamation Of Forces.
FRIENDS OF THE SICK AND WOUNDED.
Thursday, October 21st will be the first anni- versary of the amalgamation for war purposes of the British Red Cross and the Order of St. John (better known as the St. John Ambulance) Association.

An appeal is being made on the anniversary which will be known as "Our Day" through- out Great Britain and Greater Britain for our sick and wounded sailors and soldiers at the Front, and all money collected will be devoted' to the magnificent work of the Society abroad. With another winter campaign before the Navy and Army the need for a large fund is urgent. Warrington is taking her part in this worthy object. The first general meeting of the local committee was held on Tuesday at the Town Hall, under the chairmanship of his Worship the Mayor. There were also present the Mayoress, Miss Sylvia Broadbent (vice-president Daresbury Division), Mesdames Mocatta (War. rington Township Leader), Willis, Dakin, Segar Owen, Wheeler, Trampleasure, Fletcher, Bower, Birtles and Fox, Miss Burgess Colonel Mogg- ridge, Alderman Bennett, Mr. J. E. Birtles, Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Rev. Irvine Lister, Bandulaster Cahill. Mr. A. T. Hallaway (deputy town. clerk) and Mr. Thos. H. Spinks (assistant town clerk).

div.head: WARRINGTON PROGRAMME.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON PROGRAMME.

The Mayor explained that the object of the meeting was to devise ways and means for War- rington to assist in this Empire-wide movement. No words of his were needed to emphasise, the necessity for all to co-operate. Warrington had done well in all the various funds—more re- mained to be done, as whilst the war lasted the calls from all. sources were increasing. He would call upon Miss Sylvia Broadbent and Mrs. Mocatta to go into the proposals and suggestions for Warrington to take its part. Miss Broadbent informed the meeting that Warrington formed a part of the district com- prised in the Daresbury Division of the Red Cross Society, and whilst each outlying town- ship had its township leader, up to recently Warrington had no official head. Mrs. Mocatta (the wife of Colonel D. E. Mocatta, the recruiting officer) had very kindly under- taken the position of township leader for War- rington, and Miss Broadbent expressed the hope that all present would assist , her in making "the day" one worthy of the town and dis- trict.
Mrs. Mocatta gave the meeting numerous suggestions and proposals for raising funds, and the following items, were, after discussion, agreed upon by themeeting:— Concert in the Parr Hall.

That the.Theatres, Hippodrome and Kinema houses be approached for a percentage of their takings to be given. . Employers of labour be invited to contribute and to ask their employes to contribute sums of penny and upwards._ - _

All Elementary Schools, Technical, School, Grammar School, Training College, Priory and other Private Schools be asked to help. Any private individuals who care to give' private entertainments, whist drives, &c., and to devote proceeds of collections or charges to the fund are asked-to communicate with Mrs. Mocatta.

Outlying Districts.—The various details were left to the township leaders, a suggestion being made that a house-to-house collection be under- taken by responsible officials of the townships. Sub-committees were appointed to carry out the various schemes, and it is hoped, as a result of _these efforts, to secure a substantial sum.
Alderman Bennett Mentioned the interesting fact that the 21st October was "Trafalgar Day."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
MAYOR'S EULOGY.
Man Of Firm Convictions And Intolerant Of Meanness.

The Mayor, in accepting the bust on behalf of the town, said he felt that no apologies were due from him for having allowed that ceremony to take place in this year of war. Anyone who knew the late Mr. John Crosfield would recall that some years ago, when the Armenian atrocities were being committed, he, amongst a good many other stalwarts, laboured hard in an attempt to get a stop put to the horrors that were being perpetrated in Eastern Europe. To-day the long-suffering Armenians were again going through trouble, but it was trouble in a magnified form. One particular reason why Warrington should • accept that bust to the memory of Mr. John Crosfield was that this was the year 1915! Perhaps not all present were aware that it was in the year 1815, that the great firm of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons was 'karted. Therefore, they could, in a sense, cele- brate the centenary of the firm by accepting the bust, at the hands of the family, of one of the best known of its distinguished members. He (the speaker) had had several letters and tele- grams from gentlemen who knew the late Mr. John (7rosfield, among the telegraphic messages being one from Sir John Brunner, Who said, "I greatly regret my inability to attend at the un- veiling of the memorial bust of my old friend, John Crosfield, this afternoon, and I beg you to make my apologies to Mrs. Crosfield and to all the family.

div.head: Noble Citizen of an Historic Town.
div.p: Noble Citizen of an Historic Town.

"He was a noble citizen of a town with a great history, particularly as regards education, natural history and literature." (Applause.) The name of Crosfield, his Worship continued, had been long associated with the municipal life of the borough. Nearly a century ago, to be exact, on the 25th of July, 1817, Joseph Crosfield, the founder of the family, was appointed one of the Commissioners of the borough at a meeting held at the Nag's Head Inn. Warrington in those days was governed by Commissioners appointed under an Act of 1813 for regulating the town of Warrington: and they had apparently greater powers in those days than the Town Council had to-day. (Laughter.) Mr. John's brother. George, was also appointed a Commissioner on the 21st of Decem- ber, 1843, four years before the borough was incorporated. Mr. George Crosfield was also ap- pointed in 1845 on the Board of Surveyors of Highways—corresponding at the present time to the Paving and Sewerage Committee—and he was one of the first councillors elected on the incorporation of the borough in 1847. Mr. John Crosfield came to join his father in business in 1847, but it was not until 1866 that he entered the Town Council as a representative of the old South-West Ward. ,
Why Lord Winmirleigh Left.

In 1871 Lord Winmarleigh—then the Right Honourable John Wilson-Patten—who, he (the Mayor) believed, was born in the building in which they were assembled, and who had lived there until that year—determined to leave the borough. It was said that the smoke from the chimneys, which were growing up on most sides of his estate, including those at Cros- field's Works across the road—(laughter)—to- gether with the advent of the Cheshire Lines Railway, which cut off a big slice of. land on the north side, were the determining factors which drove Lord Winmarleigh from Warring- ton. As soon as his Lordship's decision became known, Mr. John Crosfield joined a body of gentlemen with the object of securing his Lord- ship's residence and the lands surrounding it for the town. Mr. John Crosfield took a very active part in securing the property, and there was little doubt that it was owing to his in- fluence; with his brother, George, that the latter, in October, 1872, gave £9,500 towards the purchase of the recreation ground, coupled with a conditibn,that "it should be used for no other purposes, and that no open-air preaching Or political meetings should be held therein," conditions which he (his Worship) could assure those present had been carefully fulfilled. In 1874 Mr. John‘Crosfield was appointed a Justice of the -Peace for the borough, '.and ten years later a county magistrate. In 'lBB2 he was elected.Mtior of this borough, and an alderman in 1885. (Applause.)

div.head: Many Acts of Generosity.
div.p: Many Acts of Generosity.

His year of office as Mayor , was marked by many acts of generosity. He .gave to the town the new clock in Trinity Tower; he looked after the creature comforts of the civic dignitaries by providing and fitting pp the kitchen in this building with a complete cooking range • at a cost of nearly X 300; and he subscribed the handsome sum of £l,OOO towards the erection of the existing School of Art. It was, perhaps, outside his province to refer to Mr. John Cros- field's generosity in other directions; but he wonld just, like .to refer to his great liberality for many years to the funds of the People's College and to the Bank Quay Working Men's Mission, in connection with which he built a handsome Infant School at Bank Quay; indeed, his generosity to nearly all the voluntary schools in Warrington was unequalled, his idea being to keep out the Board Schools of that time. (Applause.) The late Mr. Crosfield was an ideal Mayor, and his purse and help were available for all., Those who knew him intimately found behind his firm manner—he had almost said stern manner—a kindly disposition, with deep sympathies for the poor and those who asked for his help. Having referred to the fact that in 1903 Mrs. John Crosfield presented the cot*rvatory in the Park to the town, his Worship went on to say that Mr. John Cros- field was a man of firm convictions, with a strong intolerance of all that was mean. He never ,permitted isentiment to divert the course he had decided on, and, as an illustration of his practical businesslike views, it was while he was Mayor of the borough, and when the ques- tion of increasing the accommodation in the Town Hall building for the officials and its use by the public was under consideration, that he unceremoniously suggested that the wisest course would be to pull down the present build- ing and build a new Town Hall on its site. He was strongly of opinion that it would be a mistake to interfere with the existing building by attempting to enlarge it. (Hear, hear.) A Bold Proposition.

It was before the Ship 'Canal was thought of, that Mr. Crosfield,. standing 9n the steps in front of the Town Hall, boldly proposed that a new wide road should be constructed, from the front of the Town Hall over Arpley meadows into Cheshire. That would have got the town out of the difficulty with the level crossing at Wilderspool -s— (applause) a difficulty which would some 'day cost more to get rid of than the new road the late Mr. Crosfield proposed. To complete Mr. John Crosfield's municipal history, one ought to refer to his appointment as Chairman of the Town Hall and Park Committee, which was constituted In 1872 on the acquisition of the Town lall. He had previously held the 'chairmanship of trre Ceme- tery Committee for nany years, being appointed so long ago as November,. 1869. Ii fB9, when the Manchester Ship Canal was being first talked about, he was appointed Chairman of the Rivers Committee, which was constituted for the purpose of looking after the interests of the borough. The town did itself honour in admitting Mr. John .o.°A:eh" to be an honorary freeman in April, 1891. Mr. Crosfield had left the Council in October of the previous year; but he was re-elected for his old ward (renamed St. Austin's) in 1897, and finally severed his connec- tion with the Coincil—after 35 years of useful service—in 1900.
As we all know, he died in the following year, and was buried at St. Thomas' Churchyard, Stockton Heath. "On behalf of the Town
Conrmued In next column,

div.head: LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD.
Marble Bust Presented To The Town By His Family.

div.head: UNVEILED BY MRS. CROSFIELD.
div.p: UNVEILED BY MRS. CROSFIELD.

A marble bust of yet another Warrington worthy now adorns the spacious vestibule of the Town Hall—that of the late Mr. Jolla Crosfield, father of Sir Arthur H. Crosfield, and one of the borough's most illustrious and successful citizens. There is peculiar appositeness in the fact that the bust should be placed in the Town Hall, for Mr. John Crosfield was one of the gentlemen, who, when the late Lord Winmar- leigh decided to remove from the town, took a prominent part in securing to the inhabitants his lordship's stately residence, which is now used as the Town Hall, and the ornamental and other grounds surrounding it. The bust was unveiled on Monday afternoon by the widow of the gentl‘man whose memory it will help to perpetuate, Mrs. John Crosfield being accompanied by Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield and Miss Truda Crosfield.

div.head: SPLENDID LIKENESS.
div.p: A SPLENDID LIKENESS.

The bust—a splendid example' of the sculptor's art and a speaking likeness of the well-remem- bered public man and benefactor, as he appeared in the hesy-day of middle life—is the work of Mr. Henry Pegram, A.R.A., and it is. mounted upon a graceful pedestal made by Messrs. Robert Garnett and Sons from British oak, grown near Frodsham, on the Asfon Hall estate, and felled in the year 1911. The subject of the bust was, at, the tin* of .his death, managing director of the world-famous firm of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, soap makers, and under him the business grew and prospered 'greatly. Yet, multifarious as were his business

div.head: BUST UNVEILED.
div.p: BUST UNVEILED.
Mrs. John_Crosfield, who was applauded, at the request of the Mayor, who presided, unveiled the bust.

div.head: SIR ARTHUR PRESENTS 111 E BUST.
div.p: SIR ARTHUR PRESENTS 111 E BUST.
Sir Arthur Crosfield, who was received with applause, presented the bust to the town and said:—

Ladies and Gentlemen,—While there .will be many here to-day who knew my father, and knew him well during middle life, there will be very few vhio knew him in early manhood, and perhaps no one at all who knew him in his school days. It has occurred to me that a few incidents in those years, and a few reference: to his predecessors might be interesting this afternoon as 'helpful to explain characteristics of my father which were familiar to all of us. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Crosfield Ancestry.
div.p: Crosfield Ancestry.

The earliest record of my father's ancestors goes back to about the year 1530, and from that time onwards they dwelt in the Lake District. It is a pleasing fancy that from those who so long sojourned among the hills and dales of that beautiful part of the country my father inherited his great love of mountain scenery. 'George Fox had been preaching for only a few years when the family joined the Society of Friends, and Friends they remained through many generations—stern, God-fearing men, scions and ardent advocates of Peace, who were themselves Upon occasion net , incapable of manifesting, righteous indignation. I dare say more than a few here. will agree with me that this capacity for expressing with no in-

div.head: hotograph by 13irtles.
div.p: hotograph by 13irtles.

occupations, the late Mr. John Crosfield found tune to devote to public work and played a leading part in the municipal .and educational life of the borough. For many years he sat on the local governing body, mut in 1882 was elected to the highest civic office6—lhe Mayoralty. In 1891 his services to the town weTe recognised by his coadjutors in its public life, for they decided to add his name to the short list of those upon whom the signal distinction of the hone • freedom of the ancient borough has been con- ferred. WAR CALLS CAUSE ABSENCES.

Had circumstances rendered it possible, other members of the Crosfield family' -would have been present on so memorable an occasion, but, to their regret, they found it impossible to put in an appearance, `'some of them principally," as Sir Arthur phrased it, "owing to the calls made upon them due to the war." Those who were thus regretfully and unavoidably absent included Major George R. Crosfield—who is nobly playing his part at the Front with War- rington's plucky Territorials—nod Mr. J. J. Crosfield (brothers of Sir Arthur); Mrs. Ryan (Sir Arthur's eldest sister), Mrs. Eales .(another sister, prevented from attending owing to indis- position), Dr. and Mrs. Dickson, and Mr. and Mrs. E. M. Crosfield.

div.head: "TRUEST AND/ MOST LOVABLE."
div.p: "TRUEST AND/ MOST LOVABLE."

Mrs. Dickson, in a letter to Sir Arthur, wrote "We both remember him (Mr. John Crosfield) with undiminislled affection—one of the truest and most lovable men we .have ever been privi- leged to know t"

div.head: HATED OPPRESSION.
div.p: HATED OPPRESSION.

Mrs. Bales, Sir Arthur's second sister, wrote: "This is a fitting time to unveil this marble bust of our father. He hated oppression and injustice, and. I remember so well how enthusi- astic he was in the cause of the poor Armenian peoples, hunted from place to place by the brutal Turks. He took us to the meeting in Warrington in support of Gladstone's appeal. throughout England to help the Armenians to throw off the yoke of the demoniacal oppressors. Gladstone had no fear nor had our father. . . . We now find ourselves fighting against these cruel Turks, encouraged by equally cruel Ger- mans. May victory soon crown our efforts that we may libertte these wretched Armenians, as well as the Belgians and Poles. How many, many years have the Armenians waited for de- liverance! We ought to have done our duty long ago, when men like Gladstone and our father urged that the Turks should be compelled to cease these massacres for ever."
The Deputy Mayor (Dr., Joseph) also _wrote regretting his enforced fibsence, owing to having been suddenly called out of town.

div.head: OLD WORKMEN PRESENT.
div.p: OLD WORKMEN PRESENT.

There was a large and representative attend- ance of Warrington citizens, who were feceived in a committee room prior,, to the ceremony proper by the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peacock), Mrs. John Crosfield, Sir Arthur Crosfield, Bart., and Lady Crosfield, and Miss Truda Crosfield. Most of the members of the Corporation and Education Committee (accompanied in many instances by their wives), the local magistrates, the- Rector and Mrs. Willis and many other clergy and ministers and their ;wives, Colonel Moggridge, Captain Mathams and Captain Eric Fairclough were among those who had accepted invitations.

The Mayor, at . the special request of Sir Arthur Crosfield, invited several of the old em- ployes of the firm of Joseph Crosfield and Sons, and amongst those who attended were Messrs. George Gleave (whose length of service has reached 63 years), Peter Lythgoe (50 years). Jos, Hall, Nathan Hough, T. G. Brideson, John Rose, J. Flood, and Mr. John Willett.
The firm was also represented by Mr. R. F. Jones (one of the directors), and Mr. C. H. Hamilton (a director of Messrs. Gossage and Sons) was present.

div.head: BUST.
div.p: THE BUST.

considerable amount of vigour, righteous • indig- nation in 41 just cause was by no means the. exclusive possession of my father's predecessors. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Their habit of life was severely simple, and my . grandfather, for instance, -during the thirty years he lived at Bank Quay would have utterly"' scouted the notion of having a piano in the house. One might be inclined to wonder, • therefore, how my father could have inherited his great love of music, but for the fact that I know that both my grandfather lend grandmother had a pro- found admiration for Milton and Byron, so that if they were at all deficient in the sense of tone, they were evidently by no means lacking in their appreciation of cadence and rhythm. On a Sunday morning my grandfather was accustomed to drive the entire family over to the old Quaker Meeting House. at Framley, and it is recorded that upon those mornings on which the Spirit did not move any of the Friends to speak, my grandfather, who had surrepti- tiously slipped a copy of "Paradise Lost" into his fop hat--(laughter)—was accustomed there- with to Supplement his own pious_ meditations.-

, He was interested in half a dozen different businesses, and did a great deal of public. work into . the bargain, but at ten o'clock of an evening, after a sufficiently strenuous day, he wduld commence reading, and read till two in the morning. That was the example of strenuous work my IVather had before him in all his earlier years.
Mr.. John Crosfield's School Days.

At nine years of age my fatlu-r went to a Quaker School at York, where he spent five Pars, coming home once every twelve months for the holidays. The scholars at York school- led a frugal and hardy life. .In the winter for in- stance, when one black stove made a- wholly ineffectual attempt to warm the schoolroom, it was the regular custom of the schoolboys to pull off their shoes and stockings and -race round the playground in the snow barefooted to warm themselves. That hardy regime suited my father's robust constitution well. The fare at the school was of the leanest and poorest descrip- tion, and therefore the rare occasion of the arrival of a hamper from home was a very great event. It is on record that on one occasion when my grandmother sent a hamper containing nine mince pies of the largest size, they were consumed one after another the instant they arrived. (Laughter.) Amongst -other things, a -study of botany was included in the York curriculum, and the scholtirs were encouraged to -explore 'the sur- rounding neighbourhood, and make their .own little collections in the field of natural history. That encouraged natural tendencies in my father's character, and developed' that love of Nature and natural scenery which remained with him all his life. Some of my earliest recollections are associated with our scrambles together among 'rocks and along the cliffs of the beautiful ISland-of Arran in search of ferns.

div.head: Enters Bank Quay.
div.p: Enters Bank Quay.

Eighteen months at the High School at Glas- gow completed the senior's education, and it was in 1847—the year as it happens in which our borough was incorporated—that he entered the ofd firm at Bank Quay, of which my Uncle George and my Uncle Morland already had charge. Year after year my father worked at the business with zeal and assiduity, and year by year, as the time came round for the fort- night's summer holiday, my fatherS shouldered his knapsack and tramped the hills of Bonnie Scotland, or assailed the peaks, passes and glaciers of Switzerland. I have never known a man with a greater love of mountain scenery. As I have alluded to some early recollections, I might mention among them the laying of the foundation stone for the first Mission Chapel at Bank Quay in 1871 by my dear mother—one of the events, the remembrance of which one specially cheeishes. I have many a time heard my father say he never spent money on anything in his life that gave him so much pleasure as the results of his outlay at Bank Quay, where
the Mission has so long and so well thriven and prospered. (Applause.)
Bust for the Town Hall.

When Mrs. Cmsfield• told me she intended to build the Memorial Hall in Bewsey-street in remembrance of my father, I felt that having regard to his life long connection with Warring- ton, and the character of that connection. nothing could be more appropriate, and it was at once proposed that members of our family should place a bust of ray father in the Memorial Hall. It was then that members of the Town Council here were good enough to suggest that the bust should be placed in the Town Hall—and that is how I come.to make this presentation to-day. I can assure his Worship the Mayor and all the Aldermen and Members of the Council, as well as the large and repre- sentative gathering we have the privilege of meeting here to-day, that Mrs. Crosfield deeply appreciates the honour paid to ray father's memory, and I can assure you, Mr. Mayor, it is no less deeply appreciated by other members of our family. (Applause.)

div.head: CAL TELLIGENCE.
div.p: CAL TELLIGENCE.
Return Train Tickets. The return half of tram tickets can now be used on the motor 'buses.
More Precedents. At Wednesday's County Petty Sessions:— Defendant (having questioned witness): Now, don't contradict me!

div.head: Last Consideration.
div.p: A Last Consideration.
The Cemetery Committee have decided to forego the fees for lettering for an existing tomb- stone in cases where the deceased has died in the service of his country.

div.head: Coincidence.
div.p: A Coincidence.
• Many smiles were noticed at Tuesday's Police Court, when Councillor Henry Roberts presided, for the first case called on was that of Harry Roberts, an absentee from His Majesty's Forces.

div.head: Widening Howley-lane.
div.p: Widening Howley-lane.
The Street Improvement Committee were authorised by the Town Council on Tuesday night to pay £lO to the Union Tanneries, Ltd., for a strip of land for the widening of Howley- lane.

div.head: Loans to the Museum.
div.p: Loans to the Museum.

The Museum Committee have returned /to their owners the following collections: Seventy- five paintings and drawings lent by Miss Gaskell in October, 1891, and 140 Japanese sword guards lent by Mr. C. P. Peak.

div.head: New Bridge Claim.
div.p: A New Bridge Claim.

A letter from Messrs. Webster and Fitz- Simons containing a claim for extra fees for pre- paring fresh bills of quantity during the con- struction of the New Bridge was read at a recent meeting of the Bridges Committee, 'and the claim was not entertained.
This decision was approved on fuesday by the Town Council.

div.head: White Heather Day Result.
div.p: White Heather Day Result.

The net proceeds of the White Heather Day Fete held on the Cricket Ground on Saturday, the 21st of August, amount to about £157. At a meeting held at the Lion Hotel on Thursday evening it was decided to give £BO to the Infirmary (X4O to the Maintenance -Fund and £4O to the Special War Fund), ..f..35 to the Dis- trict Nursing Association, and £35 to the Poor Children's Camp Fund.

div.head: At Council Meeting.
div.p: At Council Meeting.

The following attended the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening :—The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), Aldermen Smethurst, Bennett, John Evans, Tinnion, Jas. Evans; Councillors Locker, Henshall, Dale, Barton, Lindley, Wilkinson, Halliwell, Skelland, Broadhurst, Roberts, Jenkins, Dickenson, Gough, Cunnington, Chantler, Chrimes, Archer and McKee.

div.head: Rev. H. Hands and St. James'.
div.p: The Rev. H. Hands and St. James'.

We record with great pleasure the ordination of Mr. H. Hands, of Downing College, Cam- bridge, and Ely Theological College, says the St. James' Parish Magazine. Mr. Hands re- ceived the holy order of a deacon from the Bishop of Southwark in his cathedral on the sixteenth Sunday after Trinity, September 19th, and was subsequently licensed to the curacy of St. Paul, Newington, London, S.E., of which the Rev. A. Eglington, who has preached several times at St. James', is the vicar. To the Rev. H. Hands, who, for a considerable time, has given, as opportunities have occurred; valuable help in the parish, we offer our congratulations and best wishes. St. James' parish, within the last three years, has supplied three candidates for the sacred, ministry; we believe that each of them will do good work for Christ and His Church.
A Gallant and Distinguished Constable.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday, the Chief Constable reported, through the Watch Committee, that an intimation had been received that P.C. 22 Walter W. Cooke, now serving as Corporal in the 2nd Life Guards, had had conferred upon him by the Emperor of Russia the Cross of the Order of St. George, 4th class, for "gallantry and distinguished service in the field." It was decided that the fact be placed on record, Alderman Bennett saying the town was proud of the man who had proved himself worthy of so exceptional an honour. (Hear, hear.)

The Watch committee had also resolved with respect to a plucky act in civil life:—" That P.C. 31 Coombs be commended for his prompt and plucky conduct in stopping a valuable horse which had bolted in Bridge-street on the 19th of July."
P.C. Skinner has been granted permission to join the R.A.M.C.

div.head: Shortage of Gas Workers.
div.p: Shortage of Gas Workers.

The Gas Committee, having considered a report of the General Manager that he is under difficulties with regard to the manufacture of gas owing to the shortage of workers, and that the position will become serious if any more men enlist, as he would be unable to replace them, resolved "That the Town Clerk give notice to employee thut as the works had been exempted by the Secretary of State, under the Defence of the Realm (Consolidation) Regula- tions, 1914, as amended by Orders in. Council, as necessary to secure the carrying on of the work which is required in the national interests, no workmen would be permitted to enlist without permission. and that the allowances made by ,the Council to employes under the resolutions of the Ist September, 1914, 6th October, 1914, and the 10th September, 1915, could not, there- fore, extend to employes leaving the service of the Corporation without the required permis- sion."
To Save Churches From Defacement.

Application is shortly to be made to the Con- sistory Court. of Chester for a faculty authoris- ing the intrgduction of electric light into St. James' Church. It will be news to some of our readers, says the Rev. H. B. Firth, in his Parish Magazine this month, that such a course of procedure is necessary; however, it is necessary and rather expensive, for faculties are not granted without the payment of fees. But the system is not by any means disadvantageous. If the clergy and churchwardens had an absolutely 'unfettered hand in making altera- tions and additions to their churches it is con- ceivable that in certain cases where their com- bined wisdom was not great and their 'artistic sense deficient, much irreparable damage might be done. It is therefore necessary in making structural alterations in one of our churches first to obtain the consent of the pitrishioners at a vestry meeting summoned for that purpose to the proposed alterations, and later to submit plans and specifications to the Chancellor of the Diocese. If he approves he issues his faculty and the vicar and churchwardens are at liberty to proceed with the work. . . . Electric light shoild tend greatly to reduce the heat of the church, which, in autumn and winter evenings, when all the gas jets are turned on, is very oppressive. The removal, too, of the old gas. standards from the body of the church will be a decided convenience, and in many other ways there will be an increase of efficiency and com- fort.
THE LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD
—continued.

Council; in fact, on behalf of the town itself,"' concluded the Mayor, I have much pleasure in accepting this bust of Mr. Crosfield, and of offering a permanent home for it in the build- ing which; during many years, he spent much of his time?' (Applause.)

div.head: MUSIC.
div.p: THE MUSIC.

An orchestra, under the conductorship of Mr. A. 'rrow, gave a selection of music; and Madam St;ara ksilcock, who was in perfect voice, sang "For you alone" and "A birthday.' Refresh- ments were served in the Council Chamber, Mrs. Mitchell's catering giving', as usual', the utmost satisfaction to all.

div.head: OFFICIAL RECORD.
div.p: OFFICIAL RECORD.

At the Town Councill on Tuesday night, The Mayor reported that on the previous day a bust of the late Alderman John Crosfield was presented to the town and unveiled' by his widow in the Town Hall. He thought it proper that an official record should be made in the proceedings of the Council. (Hear, hear.) This cows° was adopted.

div.head: Thanks to Needlework Guild.
div.p: Thanks to Needlework Guild.

The Guild of Help acknowledge with grateful thanks a parcel of clothing from the West Cheshire Needlework Guild, per Mrs. Lyon. The Matron of the Infirmary begs to acknow- ledge with grateful thanks the receipt of thirty articles of clothing from the West Cheshire Needlework Guild.
Primitive Methodists' Harvest Festival.
Harvest festival services will be held in the Primitive Methodist Church, Knutsford-road, to- morrow, when the special preacher in the after- noon and evening will be the Rev. G. Curtis.

div.head: "The Voice of God."
div.p: "The Voice of God."
At the Friends' Meeting House, Buttermarket- street, to-morrow evening, Mr. H. A. Lacon. of Birmingham, will give an address on "The Voice of God," all interested being invited to attend.

div.head: Footballer Licensee.
div.p: Footballer Licensee.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions' on Wednesday, Edward Bullen, 148, Hood-lane, Sankey, the well-known professional footballer of Bury, was granted the licence of the Rose Inn, Hood-lane. The previous tenant was Mrs. Mary Craske.

div.head: To the Fruit Trade.
div.p: To the Fruit Trade.

Under the auspices of the Warrington and District Retail Fruiterers' Association, a meeting will be held at the Royal Oak Hotel, Bridge- street, on Wednesday evening next, when Mr. W. Powell, of Fearnhead, will preside and addresses will be given by members of the National Federation Council.

Philomathic Society. At a recent meeting of the Council of the Warrington Philomathic Society it was decided that, owing to the war, no further meetings should be held during the present year. In the event, however, of /an early termination to the war, the Council intend to make arrangements for the second half of the session.

div.head: Military Gymkhana.
div.p: The Military Gymkhana.

Captains Mathams and iii-C-17airclough write to use on behalf of Colonel Moggridgo and Lieutenant-Colonel Mocatta to thank all those who helped them to make the military rally last Saturday a success. A special letter of thanks has been sent to the Warrington Football Club.

div.head: Week's Deaths.
div.p: A Week's Deaths.

Last week there were 22 deaths in Warring- ton, against 32 in the corresponding week last year. They arose from the following causes Scarlet fever, 2; diarrhcea, 1; enteritis, 1; phthisis, 4; other tubercular disease, 1; can- cer, 1; bronchitis, 1; pneumonia, 2; premature birth, 1; all other causes, 8.

Church Society's Anniversary. The anniversary service in connection with the Warrington Church Society will he held at the Parish Church on Friday evening next, when the Rev. F. W. Cooper (rector of Prestwich) will be the preacher. There will be a special early celebra- tion of Holy Communion the same day.

div.head: Assistant Librarian "Joins Up."
div.p: Assistant Librarian "Joins Up."

Alderman Bennett reported to the Council that the sub-librarian, Mr. John McAdam, had patriotically decided to serve his country by enlisting in the Liverpool Scottish Battalion for home defence, and the Museum Committee had resolved to continue to pay his salary less his Army pay and allowances. This decision was confirmed.

div.head: Munitions Tribunal.
div.p: Munitions Tribunal.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway presided at the second sitting of the local Munitions Tribunal, held at the Labour Exchange on Monday afternoon. With him, as assessors, sat Mr. H. Collin, of Warrington, and Mr. T. Bebbington, of Run- corn. Mr. G. F. F. White was present as clerk. The business was purely formal, there being no cases for hearing.

Congregational Sale of Work. On Wednesday, Thursday and Friday of next week a sale of work. is to be held in connection with the Elmwood-avenue Congregationa/ Church. On the first day the sale will be opened by Mr. Frank A. Haworth, and Sir Arthur Crosfield has promised to preside. On the second day the opener will be Mr. Peter Travis, of Bispham, and at 6.30 on the Friday evening Mr. J. Phcenix will conduct "a grand children's opening."

div.head: Band In The Park.
div.p: Band In The Park.

The following programme will be played in Bank Park to-morrow (Sunday) at 3.15 by the Brick-Btreet Mission Brass Band :—Hymn, "Abide with me," W. H. Monks; march. "La Busse," W. Rimmer ; selection,- " Zampa," Herold; air vane, "Edwinstone," J. Ord Hume; selection, "Songs of Wallace," W. V. Wallace; overture, "Diamond Cross," J. Greenwood; "God Save the King." Conductor, Mr. C. Yorke.

Ladies' War Bowling Main. In aid of the War Sewing Fund, Mrs. Percival on Wednesday afternoon organised a ladies' bowling main at the Brookland Hotel, Lovely- lane—the prizes kindly being bought by Coun- cillor Barton. At the conclusion Miss Barton gracefully presented the prizes in the following order: Mesdames Straw, Pritchard, Wilcox. Brookes, Perdieu and Sanders. The capital entry has resulted in the raising of no less than Li 2s. 6d.

div.head: •Warrington Market.
div.p: •Warrington Market.

Wednesday. Wheat slightly firmer on the market, 6s. 3d. to 6s. 6d. per bushel of 701 b. being offered; there is a tendency of a further advance. The American markets are advancing steadily and are sure to affect our home supplies. , Oats- were steady at late rates, 3s. 6d. to 3s. a per 451 b. Clover hay maintained a good price, £5 15s. to £6 being offered for choice; inferior, £5 ss. to £5 10s. Straw (new), 325. 6d. per ton; old, 40s. XX flour, 38s. 6d. per 2801 b. Eggs, five and six 'for is.

div.head: Wounded Soldiers and the Cars.
div.p: Wounded Soldiers and the Cars.

At the Town Council on Tuesday Councillor Wilson said he-had been told that wounded men who did not happen to be wearing uniform had to pay the fare; in fact, he had come across a case of that kind. He felt it very keenly that a man who was on leave could ride free of charge. whereas a man who had done his best for his country, and had lost his leg, had to pay. Councillor Wilkinson promised to bring the matter before the committee. It was news to him that wounded soldiers are going about in civilian clothes.
Councillor Roberts: He is a discharged soldier.

The Pudding Lady. Miss Florence Petty, popularly known as "the pudding lady," is due to address a couple of gatherings on the 26th inst. in the Co-operative Hall. At the present time she, is fully occupied visiting various parts of the country giving demonstrations in war-time housekeeping. Last Monday she was lectaring to crowded audiences at Altrincham, when the Countess of stamford, Lady kl.aworth and Mrs. Hamilton supported by their presence. All the institutions, religious, political and philan- thropic, had combined to secure an excellent attendance, who were keenly appreciative throughout. The Camera In Western Norway.

The winter session of the Warrington. Photo- graphic Society opened on Tuesday with a lecture by Mr. J: Mansell, of the Liverpool Amateur Photographic Association. "Fosses and Fjords," or "The Camera in Western Norway," was the title of a most interesting lecture. Mr. Mansell travelled from Newcastle by the "Midnight Sun," and the cruise ex- tended from the Bukke Fjord to the Romsdal. as he took two cameras with him, one half- plate, the other quarter-plate, and would not trust to chance for his plates., but took them. all .with him a&); the trip dould not be entirely one of pleasure; in fact, the heat of a Norwegian summer, when the daylight lasts 24 hours per day, made it sometimes very hard work. The lecture was greatly increased in- interest by views taken of the country-folk. their dresses, es and scenes on market days, 11 H ? at Bergen, ardanger, Odde and Naas, ar!a excellent snapshots of the sports on board ship as they came home. The audience numbered 29—a good show for this "year of grace." The mover of the vote of thanks was Mr. W. LI Hartley, who has been over the ground with the Polytechnic Tours, more than olive. :Mt? vote was seconded by Mr. W. Brown. •
CORPORAL FRANGLE'PON
Wounded.

sorry to inform you that I was wounded in the right shoulder on Sunday night, September 26th. It was about 8.30' at night when I got hit. I was taken to a dressing station and then sent to France. Now lam in hospital at Shoon..- ness, but I cannot tell you how long I shall be there."

div.head: EXAMINER ,' OCTOBER 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER ,' OCTOBER 9, 1915.
PRIVATE ELIAS THOMAS
Killed

" A" Company, was fatally wounded on the 'night of September 30th by a piece of shell. lie was on duty as a stretcher-bearer with his company, the members ef which were, working r. short distance behind the trenches. I sympa- . _ _ . .
thise with you most sincerely. Private Thomas was one of the original company of stretcher- bearers, and during the eight months that the battalion has been out here he _performed his

work splendidly. I always regarded him as one of the best men amongst the stretcher-bearers. He helped to dress the injuries of many a • wounded soldier, and to carry injured men to safety, and to surgical aid. I know that his place will be hard to fill. He died doing his duty nobly, and perhaps having this know- ledge, you may feel a little Consolation in your sorrow. I am able to assume that he suffered no pain. From the moment he was hit he was ginconscious, and he passed away quietly and. peacefully. 'Major Cary, who is in command " A" Company, joins with me in offering to you every sympathy." This letter, written by Captain C. D. Law, conveyed to Mr. and. Mrs. John Thomas. of 10, IVehlfield-street, the news that their son, Private Elias Thomas, of !' A" Company, of the War- rington Territorials, had been killed in action. Private Thomas, who would have been 22 years of age on Thursday, received his educa- tion at Wycliffe School. Previous to the out- break of war, he was employed in the tablet department at Messrs. Crosfield's. He wor- shipped at the Working Men's Mission Church, Bank Quay, and was a member of the Young Men's Bible Class. He formerly played cricket for the church team. He had been a member of the Territorials for four years. The last
letter he wrote home was dated the day of his 'death, and it was received on Sunday.

Hoping you will find consolation in know- ing he died like a soldier and a man." Rifleman O'Day was in his 19th year. He received his education at St. Benedict's School, and was a regular worshipper at St. Benedict's Church. He worked in the box-room at Messrs. Crosfield and Sons' Soap Works, and far a couple of years was a member of the Crosfield Boy Scouts latterly holding the 'lnk of patroti leader.

The next day I was moved to my present pine's; .and here I went under a second operation, aria am doing as well as can be expected in . the circum- stances. I am lying in irons ht,re and will be for a long time yet, but I aral.llsoking forward to being home for Christmas.'

div.head: RIFLEMAN C. FLETCHER.
div.p: RIFLEMAN C. FLETCHER.
Pearson and Knowles' Mot*ler In Terrific Fighting.

Rifleman C. Fletcher, 11, St. BarnalSas'-place, brother of Mr. George Shaw, was woneded by an explosive shell in the knee at the Viit battle a fortnight ago. In the charge the 'Brigade suffered heavily. The fighting was so' terrific that for abost four hours Rifleman ]etcher had to lie in a downpour of rain. Then lie was found by stretcieT-bearers and taken to thie base hospital. After a few days he was removed to the Cambridge Hospital at Aldershot; and speaks highly of the treatment he is receiving there. He hopes to be ell right again in the course of a month or five weeks. When in Warrington he made his home with I..kfr. Shaw at the &have address. He was a keen ;follower of athletie games, both football Old ;cricket occupying a good deal of his spare time. ;Before enlisting he was employed as a moulder tat Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. As a boy he ;attended St. Barnalias' School, and for a few- years he has been a member of the Adult Class; .presided over by the Rev. I. Lister at the Cairo- ;street School. He was a valuable member of
the school cricket club, and was considered a olerably good bowler.

Mayers,. wheee photo- graph we reproduce below, haa written home tohiis parer tm who reside at 813) Orford-avenue, stating; that he has, been, awarded the D.C.M. fon oonspicuuns- bravery on the field of battle. At the commencement of hostilities he was woriting a& a, mine-sinlier Bed?Ordshir. e, but ithe call of dnty being strong to him, he en- liated in the 13edfords, and eventually was drafted ito I..rfance.. div.head: HOW THE AWARD WAS WON.
div.p: HOW THE AWARD WAS WON.
The gallant Lanae-Corporal thus reeerds the ;deed, which, won hint the coveted honour:—

"--- , we had' instructions to- undermine the :German trenches some little distance away, as vo.were, pesparing.,tota.ttack-... We had not quite completed the task when we found out that .!tile Germans-had' baoken. inta•the one that waa ,ready. I at once went to investigate, but had not proceeded far before I was shot at, but, .ifOrtunatery, owing to, the darkness, they ,missed their mark— I gave instructions to the men immediately to build up a barricade to .protect Mr lads. The neat question was how •to get the enemy out of the mine? There was no other course open but to blow them out! I obtained a bag of powder and went down to ithe bearicade and crawled on all fours for about thirty yards. I did not know / was so .near the Germans as proved to be the case, and. they again opened lire on me, once more with- out success. 1' crawled back again to the barricade and then the „officer commanding, after seeing me return safely, blew them up. , This was how I won the D.C.M." Previous to his being employed as a mine- sinker, Lance-Corporal Mayers was engaged by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co.,
D.C.M.
being well known and much respected bty bi workmates. He is a single man.
WANTS THE V.C. NOW!
In 11 letter to his sister the gallant Lance. Corporal says that having got the D.C.M. he will not be satisfied until he gets the Victoria Cross.

Four sons in the Army—two of them in ft French hospital, wounded; a third in ugland, also recovering from recently received wounds, and the fourth one still serving at the Front! Such is the record of the Kent family at 42 Hoyle-street. The two sons who are in hospit4 are members of tile Gor4oA Ei4lllo-114011,

div.head: Rejoined When War Broke Out.
div.p: Rejoined When War Broke Out.

Corporal Frangleton was formerly n the 2nd Scottish Rifles, with whom ho served through ;the South African War. He 'rejoined the +Colours in February ofethe present year. He is Married and has four children, and his home .address is 153, Church-street, Warrington. lie is a native of the town and by trade a plasterer. He has a brother, Joseph, serving in France, .also with the South Lancs. In his letter home the Corporal urges his wife rtpt to be uneasy abut him, adding that at the time of writing. he .was a great deal better, and that he was being well looked after. He adds .an appeal for "fags." The Military Hospital, Well Marsh, Sheerness, Sheppey, will find him shoul4 any reader desire to supplement his -.-wife's gift.

div.head: PRIVATE C. FORSTER.
div.p: PRIVATE C. FORSTER.
lilt After Doing "His Bit " hi " Land
Of -Nowhere."

Private Charles Forster, son of Mr. ancl Mrs. John Forster, of 12, Bramhall-street, off Liver- Pool-road, has received a shrapnel wound in the shoulder, and is 'row in a Birkenhead Hospital. Writing to his mother he says:—" I am glad to say that it is not serious. I have been in another charge—this time with our bomb- throwers. We were attached to the -while they charged. We took three lines of German trenches and a lot of prisoners. It iS a pleasure for me to see a bit of civilisation after eight months' fighting in the land of Nowhere.' Anyhow. I am glad to be able to saY I have done my bit." Five Years a "Terrier."
A single young fellow, twenty-one years of I,ge, Private Forster is serving his fifth year an the Battalion, and is attached to A Company. Ile. was educated at the people's College, and

Latchford. He was employed before the out- break of war as a tinsmith by Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd. He went to the Front in June, having enlisted in February last. He has proved himself a very good shot. He is nineteen years of age.
PRIVATE J. IIAMBLETT. Wounded.

div.head: "Still Living."
div.p: "Still Living."

Private Hamblett, writing to Ms mother on the 4th inst., says he is all right again, and hopes to be back again soon with his company. " I got hit a week last Saturday," hi, says, by shrapnel from a shell which burst only 15 yards away and a lucky devil I am not to be killed; I sttpose lam like a cat with nine 'lives. I thought I had lest my leg, as a piece of shrapnel as big as a penny went in about half an inch. It has been like hell this last week, but we are still living and can stand a bit more. Both officers and men are in the pink." "In The Thick Of It."

In a letter dated September 15th Private namblett wrote :—" Well, we were in the thick of it about a fortnight ago, but we are still in the hind of the living! We were under shell fire for about twenty minutes and it seemed like a week to me. Darky ' and I got knocked. on our backs twice through a shell bursting near us. I think I have been lucky so far." Writing five days later he said :—" I had a very near shave yesterday, but, I thank God, that I had my Prayer-Book in my pocket, be- cause a piece of shell hit it, bot did not go any farther. They may well call us the Unbreak- able Fourth.' I think we are the luckiest lads living! But wait until it is all over, and you see us marching down Sankey-street! Won't it be a time!"

div.head: PRIVATE H. BAILEY.
div.p: PRIVATE H. BAILEY.

"Another Bit Of A Scrap. With The ' Square-heads. " Mr. and Mrs. Bailey, 116, Battersby-lane, have received news on a field card that their son, Private Harold Bailey, of the Warrington Territorials is lying wounded in hospital. Writing subsequently from a Tunbridge Wells hospital, the wounded man said :—" I am sorry to say that I have been rounded in the left

div.head: NUR ATE J. PAIIRY.
div.p: NUR ATE J. PAIIRY.

An Unpleasant Surprise In The Dark. Private John Parry, who is a member of B Company, was wounded by a shell on September 2nd, while coming out of a wood in the dark. The Private, who is thirty-seven years of age, has been in the Territorials about five years. When a boy he attended the National School, and before the outbreak of war he was employed by Messrs. E. Forshaw and Son, iron founders. 110 is a married man.

div.head: PRIVATE J. J. SINGLETON.
div.p: PRIVATE J. J. SINGLETON.
Well-known Local_ Bowler Caught In
Ankle.

Private John Joseph Singleton, of the Territorials, and whose home address is 31, Scott- street, received a slight wound in the ankle on September, 3rd, whilst out trench-digging. He is a well-known local.bowler, having taken part in mains promoted by the National Independent Order of Oddfellows, and he is thirty-two years of age. He was formerly employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd. He enlisted in September, 1914.

div.head: PRIVATE THOMAS ROE.
div.p: PRIVATE THOMAS ROE.

Sleeplejack Hit And Now In Hospital. Mrs. Roe, of 14, Wilson-street, has learned that her husband, Private Thomas M. Roe, of Company Warrington Territorials, has been wounded, and is now in hospital. Private Roe, who was educated at Wycliffe School; is . twenty-seven years of age. He enlisted in October, 1914, having previously been employed as a steeplejack. He has helped to erect chimneys, at several lecal works.

div.head: PIHV.TE FRANK POTTER.
div.p: PIHV.TE FRANK POTTER.

Buried By Shell-Burst Whilst Guarding Prisoners. Mr. and Mrs. Isaac Potter, 27, Albert-terrace, Howley, were last week unofficially informed that their son, Private Frank, Potter, of the Territorials, was missing after the great charge. Since then, however, Private Potthr has written home from the base hospital, where he lies suffering from hurts consequent upon the burst- ing of a shell, which killed a number of Ger- man prisoners whom he was escorting to the back of the line, and buried him. He is now progressing favourably. Before joining the Territorials in September last year, Private Potter was employed by Messrs. Thewifs, Griffiths and Edelsten, Ltd. Ile was gassed by an asphyxiating shell early in June, and was for a short time in lidspital. Rifleman William Potter, his brother, is serving in France with the Rifle Brigade.

div.head: PRIVATE LEONARD ROBERTS.
div.p: PRIVATE LEONARD ROBERTS.
Shrapnel Causes Slight Wound In
Mouth.

Private Leonard Roberts, of the Warrington Territorials, son of Mr. and Mrs. Roberts, of 22, Thewlis-street, recently received a shrapnel bullet wound in the mouth. It was not serious. and did not necessitate his removal to hospital. Re has, however, been put temporarily on lighter duty, viz., that of an officer's servant.

Private Roberts was, before the outbreak of war, employed by Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd. He is a member of the Young Men's Bible Class in connection with, the Working Men's Mission, Bank Quay.

div.head: AMBULANCE MEN.
div.p: AMBULANCE MEN.

Further Batch of Certificates Earned. A week last night Dr. Manson presented am- bulance certifiCates to the following : • F. Massey, E. Higham, F. W. Wright, C. N. Rathbone, H. Glea,ve, J. Moore, J. Banner, A. Gartland, G. Rowe, D. R. Hodge, S. Twiss, J. H. Brown, A. Wright, jun., E. Delooze, W. Lamb, J. S. Allan, H. Plinston, C. Bradshaw, J. W. Wright, W. Street, H. Ashcroft, H. Seddon, W. Berry, S. Smythe, G. Fisher, J. Cairns, T. Evans.
Seven of the above are already serving the country.
At the conclusion Mr. Bradshaw, on behalf of the class, asked Dr. Manson (their lecturer) to accept a beautiful inkstand, and Mr. Baldry (the instructor) a silver-mounted walking stick.

div.head: FOR ACTIVE SERVICE.
div.p: FOR ACTIVE SERVICE.
The following left Warrington this week Private S. Rothwell, for the Navy at Ports- mouth; Privates J. W. Wright and J. Cairns, for R.A.M.C. at Winwick.

div.head: "COD BLESS HIM!"
div.p: "COD BLESS HIM!"

Owing to an unfortunate eye ailment, Mr. T. S. Steel, the well-known Warrington solicitor, has this week been compelled to wear an eye-shade. Passing through Market-street on Thursday afternoon two old gentlemen noticed him, and the following was overheard : First Old Gentleman: That young fellow's been to the Front, now. Second O.G. (turnip.; round) : Aye, God bless him!

div.head: RIFLEMAN J. HARDMAN.
div.p: RIFLEMAN J. HARDMAN.
Two Sons Lost Out Of ;The.

Rifleman John Hardman, of the 10th Battalion Rifle Brigade, and son of Mrs. Kate Bradshaw, 47, Scott-street, has been killed in action. The news was conveyed by Rifleman Harmer, a com- rade, who wrote home asking his wife to convey the news to his comrade's relatives that he was shot through the head. "I carriecrhim out of the trench and did my best for himr 'continued the letter, "but it was of no use!' Within the last two months Mrs. Bradshaw has lost two out of . her three- soldier sons, whilst she also has two step-sons-serving.

Rifleman Hardman attended when. a boy the Wycliffe School. Before joining up he was employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros. Ltd., as a galvaniser. He attended St. Ptiter's Sunday School: He was only eighteen years of age, and had been at the Front twelve weeks, having enlisted in November. Another sea is in train- ing with the reserve battalion • of the local Territorials.

fighttng on September 25th-26th. The news was conveyed in the following letter, dated September 25th, and sent by the sister in charge of No. 17 Casualty Clearing Station: "It grieves me very much indeed to have to send you very bad news. Youi son, Corporal Aikenhead, was admitted yesterday to No. 17 C.C.S., suffering from severe wounds in the legs.

div.p: Everything Possible Done.

"He was suffering very much from shock, and although everything was done that could be done for him, he passed quietly away to-night. He will be laid to rest in a quiet little cometerY, and a cross, bearing his name, regiment and number, will mark his grave. Ire will have a military funeral, and every respect will be shown his remains." Official informa- tion received from the War Office on Friday stated that he died on September 6th. The last letter which Mrs. Byrne received from her son was dated August 28th, and reached her on4September 19th. Private Byrne, who was twenty-five years of age, was educated at St. Mary's 8.C..
