div.head: Posthumous Scholastic Distinction.
div.p: Posthumous Scholastic Distinction.

• He was a member of the Sacred, Heart Guild, and the saeretary for the Study Club connected with the same. Also, for a long.' time, he had been an altar-boy. at St. Marrs, and more recently a chorister. At the Manchester School of Technology he had attended: in the evenings—indeed his City and Guild certificate has only reached his home sinte his death..

div.head: PRIVATE A. HAWTHORN.
div.p: PRIVATE A. HAWTHORN.
Succumbs To Spinal Injuries In Ranee.

Private Albert Hawthorn, 54, Lovely-lane, of the King's Royal Rifles, has succumbed to the 'injuries he sustaizml in the great advance, as reported in last week's "Examiner." He was shot in the spine and though he had every at- tention in the Australian hospital, Wimeranx, near Boutogree, he died on Wednesday this week. Private Hawthorn had an especially lovable nature, and he appears to have created a great impression among those who waited upon him in his last days in hospital, including Lady !Dudley. A military funeral was accorded him. His father (Mr. Thomas Hawthorn, who is !engaged in Crosfield's cement department) and 1 mother were wired for the day before he died, ! and, Mrs. Hawthorn being unable to travel, Mr. I Hawthorn and his daughter, Miss Emily Haw- thorn, went to France, but were too late to see I the patient before he died. They, however, had the satisfaction of knowing that everything ! that could be done had been done. Before going they had received several most sympa- thetic letters.

A " Dear, Brave Laddie.h Nursing Sister Denton at the Clearing Hos- pital, wrote:— " He was brought in by convoy late on Satur- day night with hundreds of other poor men straight from the field, and it was seen at once that he was dangerously wounded, the .spine being injured. He had very little pain indeed. .. . Such a dear brave laddie, he was; He
CORPORAL W. DANIELS.
Wounded.

dozing in and the man who dug me out said he thought it was all up with me. But I have only a few small cuts on the top of the halal. My pal, Sergeant Walker, got hit the same morning, but I hear it is not much." Corporal Daniels is thirty years of age and is a well-known player of billiards and, prize- winner at " Rylands's Rec." He was Lodge Master and treasurer of the Free Gardeners. Among the trophies he has sent home are two German helmets, one belonging to an offi- cer. He has asked that one of theta may be taken great care of, as there N% as "much excitement" when he got its

div.head: SERGEANT BLEASDALE.
div.p: SERGEANT BLEASDALE.
Injuries More Serious Than Reported
Last Week.

In last week's "Examiner" we gave an account of Sergeant Victor Bleasdale, of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers, and stated that he was wounded by shrapnel, in. the thigh. Since then, however, it has transpired that he is wounded in the thigh, hip, and also in both legs, his right leg being very badly shat- tered. The chaplain of the hospital writes almost daily to Mrs. Bleasdale, 24, Marsh-street,..stat- ing that though his wounds are very serious, the Sergeant is going on, all right. Visitor N. Burnett-Stuart, writing from a hospital at Boulogne, says 'Sergeant Bleasdale has been badly wounded in both legs and on his thigh and his hip by shrapnel. "He does not complain, but, of course, suffers a great deal of pain. He is getting on as well as can be expected, so do not worry any more than you can help about him. He is being well looked after here and will very probably be sent to England soon." How The Injuries Were Received.

The gallant Sergeant, writing to his mother on the sth inst., says " I will tell you how I received my injuries. I was taking part in the Great Advance on Saturday morning, September 25th. We went over the top about six o'clock and we got to the German trenches. They fled from their first trench, and I, in charge. of a party of 30 men, went bombing out their dug-outs, when one of them put his hands up and yelled for mercy. I soon put paid to him, and while I was going on with my successful exploit a shell burst about ten yards from us and it killed or wounded all the party. It caught me in my side, knocking me about ten yards, smashing my leg and fracturing my thigh, the shrapnel making a hole about four inches in my thigh and going right through, also burning my leg below. But, you know, I must not grumble, mother, as I am lucky to be living at all. Anyhow, aft& I was hit, there I lay in the drenching rain for twenty-four hours under

lines. There is no need to worry because mine is not a bad wound, and I shall soon be coming home to see you. I am glad that I am able to use a gun against the Huns, for if ever men wanted shooting it was them." • A Crosfield's- Employe.

Private, Rogerson, who was 'twenty years of age last Sunday, was, before the outbreak of war, employed by Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, in the box department. He received his educa- tion at St. Alban's School. He enlisted in September, 1914.

div.head: PRIVATE PERCY MARSH.
div.p: PRIVATE PERCY MARSH.

Private Percy Marsh, son Of Mr. James Williant Marsh, of 'the Railway Hotel, Latch- ford, was wounded in the right shoulder during the big advance. Soon after being wounded, Private Marsh was seen by Mr. William Pier- point (son of Alderman William Irierpoint)? who is serving at the Front as a dispatch rider. Writing home later, Mr. Pierpoint said:— " Just as I entered the German trench .we cap- tured, who should I see coming down but Percy Marsh (Railway Hotel) with a hole in his tight phoulder. I only had' tune to Wish him god d lAA, and had, to go on. I hope he will pull tiootio all right, though he leeked detidly pale; yet lie' Cotild manage to get along all right." . Private Marsh, Who is twenty-three years Of age, enlisted in the King's Own Scottish Borderers in August of last year. He was educated at. People's College, and previous to the outbreak •of war was employed by Mr. Arthur Clare, engineer ; ,Knutsford4oad. lie formerly played football for tre7t*F4st Church (Latchford) team. Ile ks' been at the Float., since April,
SAPPER PEVITT. Wounded.
second line of German trenches. I threw off my kit, and then happened to drop into the trench, where a pal 'dressed my wound.
Crawled to the Dressing Station.

"I then crawled for two hours to the dress- ing station, where they put me in an ambulance and I was taken to the field hospital, and then on to this place. r Here they operate.l on rte, and took the piece of shrapnel out, and I em a great deal easier now." Sapper Pevitt was educated at St. James' School. He was formerly employed by Messrs. Dolan's, joiners. He is also a .member of St. James' Church Choir. He enlisted in January, and had only been at the Front three weeks.,

div.head: 1111% ITE S. LYTHCOE.
div.p: 1111% ITE S. LYTHCOE.
Old Church Chorister Shot In The Hand.
Private Samuel Lythgoe, of the Northumber- land Fusiliers, son of Mr. Samuel Lythgoe, 158, Battersby-lane, is now in the Lord Derby Military Hospital at Winwiek, having been shot in the hand.

Twenty-six years of age and single, Private Lythgoe was educated at Hainilton-street School. He enlisted twelve months ago, having been previously employed by the Partington Steel and Iron Co., Ltd. As a boy he was first a member of Holy Trinity choir, and later of St. Peter's choir.
CORPORAL JOHN FINNERTY.
- Wounded.
Fusiliers a month after the war broke out, and is now in the Royal Engineers. Corporal Fin- nerty, we are glad to say, is sufficiently recovered to return to his duties. He is 23 years of age.
Praise for Kitchener's Men.

After rejoining his battalion he wrote to his .father saying that he felt a lot better, and hoped to be quite fit in a day or two. He also men- tioned that he had . been promoted to full cor- poral. He again wrote on October 2nd, as fol- lows: "I am pleased to say that both our Army and the French are -doing some fine work out here at present. liitchener'S Army has proved its mettle, for they haye doeplnlid? cl. deserve 111.1theplat;4 they get. Thq are driv- iDg the Germans back in fina style, null if they keep on we shall soon have the war at Ail ehei. I was in the big attack you ill have read about,. and .you can bet. that I shall never forget it. I am still in the best of health, and am living in hopes of seeing you all soon."

div.head: PRIVATE THOMAS WILLIAMS.
div.p: PRIVATE THOMAS WILLIAMS.
Private Thomas Williams, of the King's Royal Rifles, has been admitted into hospital wounded. Such was' the information received by his parents, Mr'. and Mrs. Charles Williams, 27; Fletcher-stre'et.

Private Williams, who is twenty-eight years of age, attended when a boy, Heathside School. He enlisted ilf.Tanuary, priorsto which time he was employed by Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and CO:.. Ltd. He has, played cricket and football forlotal clubs, ar,id While a memter of Rylands's Recreation Cricket lub, fie won two medals. His brother, Private johu Dutton. Williams, of the King's Own Senttlai' iforderers was killed in aetion' Di' Anglia:-

div.head: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
div.p: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
WOUNDED.
SIGNALLER W. MIDD.
Says The Big Advance Is Beginning
Of The End:

, In the Broadwater , llospittil at Ipswich, making a good recovery ,from nasty wounds received some little time back, is Signaller Walter Widd, the son of mine host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. Albert Widd) of the Roan Cow Inn, Bridge Foot, and brother to Sergeant Tom Widd, of the Warrington Territorials, who for a matter of nearly ten years has been asso- ciated with the civilian-inilitary forces: First Reported Seriously Wounded.

Signaller Widd is serving in the King's Royal Rifles, and at the time he received his wounds he was on duty in a communication trench. The first 'intimation his parents had that any- thing was amiss with him was an official noti- fication from the War Office to the effect that he was seriously wounded, a subsequent mes- sage from the same source greatly relieving his parents' anxiety by declaring him to be "past the stage of seriousness." The wounded plan is .23 years of age and he enlisted about a month after the war broke out. Prior to "joining up" he was employed as a carpenter in the London and North-Western Railway Wagon Works at Earlestown. He expects shortly to be transferred .to another hospital near London, there to undergo a course of electrical massage, with the hope of restoring to him the full use of his injured arm and leg. _ _ _

div.head: " Useful " Footballer.
div.p: A " Useful " Footballer.

Signaller Widd's favourite recreation is foot- ball, and at Earlestown he was regarded, in athletic circles, as a most useful man. He played for the Earlestown Y.M.C.A. When he first joined the King's Royal Rifles, Signaller Widd was made a °dispatch rider. Writing to his parents he describes how one of the Sisters of the hospital in which he is quartered is trying to teach him to walk once more, and, he adds, "I did very well for the first go-off !" He goes on to make sym- pathetic reference to the death of Private Dick Roberts, whose end, he says, was a noble one, worthy of so good a soldier. Writing of the war, the wounded man says that he regards the recent great advances as the beginning of the end!

div.head: PRIVATE C. lIIBBV.
div.p: PRIVATE C. lIIBBV.
Shot In Thigh By Turks It Big Advance.

Private Charles Bibby, a Warringtonian who enjoys much popularity with a wide circle of acquaintances, is lying woundeti, in St. Pat- rick's Hospital at Malta, a bullet having caught him in the left thigh during recent fighting in the vicinity of the Dardanelles. When home on leave shortly before sailinc, to meet the Turks, Private Bibby stayed with his sister, Mrs. Darbyshiro, of 10, Gorsey-lane. Prior to enlisting in the South Lancashire Regiment in August of last year, he worked for the Firth Mattress Co. He is a single man and is 25 years of age. He received his education at the National School, Church- street. Keenly interested in football, he played for the Firth Co.'s team in • the works' com- petition.

div.head: Succoured By Ghurkas.
div.p: Succoured By Ghurkas.
Writing to his sister to acquOnt her of the fact that he had been hit, Private Bibby says:

"We did have a rough_ time! We had advanced about three miles when I got hit. I had to scramble back the best way I could until I met some Ghurka stretcher-bearers, who took me to the dressing station.. But I was not safe there, for the Turks started shelling the place, and so the R.A.M.C. men soon had the other wounded and myself on a boat and out of harm's way." Mrs. Darbyshire has another brother with the Colours, viz., Private William Bisbby, who is in training with the Warrington Territorials in Surrey.
RIFLEMAN W. BENTLEY.
Back Injured By Bursting Shell.

Mast week Mrs. Bentley, of 26, Wilson-street, received a field card bearing the news that her husband, Rifleman William Bentley, of the King's Royal Rifles, had been wounded. Later the injured man wrote two letters. The first one stated:—" I am getting all right now, and can consider myself a lucky man. Don't upset yourself, as I only got buried by a shell bursting, and I have only hurt my back a little. I expect that by the time you get this I shall be fit and well, and ready to have another ' go ' at the enemy.'" _

In the second -letter he said: '. / am the luckiest man in the world to come through what I did. For quite an hour and a quarter I lay on my face in a field until I .lecidA to make a final attempt to get to cover." Rifleman Bentley, who, up to three ears ago, lived at Manchester, has been in the Army twelve months. He had previlu4y worked as a driver for Messrs. Peter Walker And Son. Ltd.

div.head: SERGEANT EDWIN SYKES.
div.p: SERGEANT EDWIN SYKES.
Roy al Estate-Warringtonian Wounded
In France.

Another native of Warrington who has been wounded in France is Pioneer-Sergeant Edwin Sykes, of the Northumberland Fusiliers—son of Mr. and Mrs. E. Sykes, of 25, Willis-street. By his brother the news was received at the end of last week on a field-eard, which said he was going on well and would write at the first opportunity. Further news is not yet to hand. A_;;;;;1 thirty-eight, Sergeant Sykes was edu- cated at Heathside School, under the head- mastership of the late Mr. Finney; and attended St. rites churlt and Sunday School. For three years actatrardn he Inut to work its a tinsmith for Mr. Johngoii, Pridge Foot, and Oen enlisted in the Grenadie Onatds-- transferring later to the Northumberland Fusiliers. Atter .seven, years' military service, having been lièl, he made his home on the Royal Estate ai t!iffdlsoi Oreat Park, where lie has since remaia6l4:- ,

He has two children, and a brotitef ancer ft_L, Sergeant-Major in the Northumberland Fug- liers. Another brother, having been dts- charged from the. army, is now engaged at' munitions.
Fought At Omdurman.
Sergeant Sykes fought in the last Soudanese War under Lord- (then Sir Herbert) Kitchener and was ,present at the Battle of Omdurman, He wears both Vie- &Will* and -the; E`eptian Medals for this war.

LAID TO REST.

div.head: SOLDIERS' LOSS.
div.p: SOLDIERS' LOSS.

At the Warrington Cemetery early on ,Mon- day afternoon the late Rev. Father Thomas Oswald Swarbreck, rector of St. Benedict's Church, was laid to rest amid tokens of wide- spread affection and sorrow. At the graveside not only were other denominations represented, but also there were present several wounded soldiers from the 'Lord Derby War Hospital, ViTinwick—at which Father Swarbreck had earned great respect and popularity by his services as chaplain. . In the new Orford-lane church the funeral was preceded in the morning by solemn Requiem Mass. The whole . atmosphere was impressive and still; the altar bare in its sim- plicity; the Archbishop's stately throne and faldstool in the sanctuary draped in purple. In the middle of the church, before the high altar, rested the 'coffin, Upon it lying the priestly emblems—the stole, chalice and paten. On all sides it was surrounded by beautiful wreaths; .otherwise no flowers were to be seen..

div.head: HUNDREDS OF PEOPLE.
div.p: HUNDREDS OF PEOPLE.

Fourteen weeks ago, amid scenes of splendour and rejoicing—scenes unprecedented in War- rington's religious history—this imposing new edifice was opened in state by Cardinal Bourne, of Westminster. Upon the priest to whom was the credit, but who took no ostentatious part, congratulations were showered by unanimous consent. Six days ago hundreds of people again assembled. There ivas the Archbishop and the Abbot, with their deacons; the black-stoled priests; the Mayor and other representatives of the Corporation; military officers and men; 'the wounded; school children and their teachers; men and women, young and old, of all classes and shades. To that same priest they had come to pay-the last tribute. In solemn Gregorian tones the organ pealed out; all heads were bowed. Through the stained-glass windows the sun shone upon a moving scene.

div.head: BEREAVED CLERGY.
div.p: THE BEREAVED CLERGY.

In the presence of the Archbishop of Liver- Pool, the Requiem Mass was sung by the 'Abbot of Ampleforth. The assistant priest' was the Very Rev. .T. P. Whittle (Warrington), the deacon the Rev. B. Gibbons, and the sub-deacon the Rev. J. P. Wilson (Warrington). The remaining clergy present were: The Revs. Canon Bothwell (Urmston), Dean Clarke (Appleton, Widnes), J. Almond (Widnes), J. T. Walshe (Liverpool), W. Rockliff, J. • Murphy, Tallon and .McVeigh (Warrington), Donohoe (Croft), and Kelly (Crouton); and the late Father's brothers in the Benedictine 'Order— the Very Rev. J. I. Brown and Rev. J. W. Darby (Parbold), the Very ReV. J. A. Wilson, Revs. G. B. Cox, W. Pearson, A. J. Macdonald, T. I. Barton, G. S. Ryan and E. Mullany (Liver- pool), IL M. Campbell (Woolton), S. A. Parker (Grassendale), J. C. Almond (Brindle), H. P. Turner (Hindley), A. Coyle (Ormskirk), C. E. P. Griffin (Netherton), and N. V. Wilson, R. B. PrimaveSi, B. Mawson, J. M. Dawson and G. C. Jackson (Warrington). The organ music was Provided by the Rev. T. A. Hind (Warrington). The family mourners were: The Rev. Charles Swarbreck, of Ditton Hall, and Mr: William Swarbreck (brothers), Miss Swarbreck (sister), Miss A. Swarbreck, of Bedale (cousin), Mr. j. Lynch and Miss Lynch, of Glascoed (cousins). "LIFE THAT HAS BEEN LIVED."

In a brief address to the congregation, the Abbot of Ampleforth referred, to the work of the dead priest, and said: "You, rather than anyone else, will know the virtues that belonged to him and that made him dear to you. Every soul that is sent into this world is seat by the good God to represent Himself and to silo* to Others some of the virtue which belongs; to' Unself. And so, on such an occasion as this,. -`„ think it is well ,for us to remind *ourselves :init we can learn something in our own lives 'trom. the life that has been lived amongst. us,, and 'which is now ended. There were certain Characteristics about Father Oswald which endeared him to everyone. There was, first of Lai% his almost- universal sympathy, and then his burning •zeal. Though there were Many Points about him that one could cavil at and Criticise, they always ended by our saying, Well, he means well, and he is doing the work for God.' He never thought about himself. I remember, when he was quite a boy, asking him to do something that really was quite be- yond 'him. He did not understand what he was writing at all, but lie did it most loyally and thoroughly and excellently well. And so one hears constantly of instances, of the interest he has taken in individuals in whom others did not take any interest at all. He has followed up that interest, not just for a week-or for a Month, but for years, and he has rejoiced when it has borne fruit and a soul has been brought nearer to God. He had a great sympathy for souls and for individuals. It was not an attrac- tion towards them, but a sympathy with their Wants. And so, when this war began, his whale heart went out to the poor soldiers, and you know how he spent himself, 60 that some of You would no doubt think he was neglecting 'you, because he gave so much time to them. It was a sign of his sympathy for those who re- quired help. He had known in his own life- What a priest meant to a soul. He had, known, When he was living a gay life, what it meant to have a friend to whom he could go fa sup- port, strength and comfort. When he himself became a priest, he determined to give every Power that he had for souls. It was his pre- vailing passion, one might say.

div.head: "Pray For Him."
div.p: "Pray For Him."

" So I would beg of you that you would, in sour kindness, pray for him; because, though he was good, and though he showed to us some of the sympathy and kindness of the good God, still he was human, and we know what that is. We know how he required our prayers. There is no soul that can stand before God without prayer to back him. No soul, however holy, eau stand before the pure God with confidence, unless he is helped by the prayers of those who love him. There was one thing his heart was in—this church. He brought it to perfection; the last workman had left it when he took, to his bed and died. It was the work which God had given him to do—for you; and the least- You can do is not to stand in the way of his successor, but .to support him as fully as you tan, that Father Oswald's work may be free of debt and encumbrance—that it may be, as he wished it to be, a pure gift handed to God for the salvation of souls." In conclusion, the Abbot asked the priests at least not to forget the late Father at the altar: 'lie had a great devotion to the Holy Mass— devotion that endeared him to Inc, very much. Ile was a dear friend. He had many faults, loany peculiarities, but at the same .time he Was full of zeal for God and sympathy for As such may he soon enter into his test, and may he, wheii. be has come to the tompanioaship of God, look down upon, us and. help us in our necessities. May he not forget °lle single soul," A MILITARY PROCESSION. _

- - „By desire the procession to the Cemetery took shortest route—via. Marsh v House-lane. under Lieutenant R. B. Cahill, the Band of ~..the 2nd South Laneashires headed it, playing ‘;hopin's stirring "Marche Funebre." div.head: FLORAL TRIBUTES.
div.p: FLORAL TRIBUTES.

Beautiful wreaths were sent by: The. Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peacock), Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Meekly (Thelwall), Mr. and Mrs. H. P. Den Sham, captain Matthew Honan, Mr. Leonard G. Davies, 'Mr. and Mrs. John J. Whitley, Mr. and Mrs. E. Gaskell Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Vere Beamont Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Louis A. Voisey, Mr. and Mrs. Charles H. Tinsley, Dr. and Mrs. McKee, J. and A. THE NEW RECTOR.
We understand that Father Swarbreck's eel- league, Father G. C. Jackson, will be appointed the new rector of St. Benedict's.

div.head: •R• . FREDERICK DAINTITH.
div.p: •R• . FREDERICK DAINTITH.
Popular Assistant School- master's Death.

"We record with deep regret the 'death of Mr. Frederick Daintith, which took , place at his 'residence, 31, Alexandra-street, during the early hours of Saturday last. He was born on the 28th August, 1877, the eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. William Daintith, 114, Manchester-road,

div.head: LATE MR. DAINTITII
div.p: THE LATE MR. DAINTITII

and received .his early education at the War- rington Parochial School, under thd late Mr. John Dewhurst, with whom also he served his pupil teachership. In 1896 he entered the Chester Training College with a first-class Queen's- Scholarship.. On the completion of his college career, which was a brilliant tone, Mr. Daintith returned as an assistant master to the Warrington Parochial School, where, with the exception of three years at the Boys' Home, Regent's' Park-road, London, he served until the time of his illness.

Mr. Daintith was a man of strong personality. He had a very high sense of duty, and anything he undertook was carried out in a thorough and wholehearted manner. Outside his school work, which was his first consideration, his chief hobby was horticulture, which he followed with much skill and interest. In 1904 Mr.; Daintith married Miss E. Jane Andrews, Only child of Mr. John Andrews, of Church-street, Warring- ton, who is left to mourn his loss. By his colleagues and friends he will long be remem- bered for his unfailing devotion to duty, his frankness, his unfaltering faifh, and his loyal friendships. Mr. Daintith was a member of the "Gilbert Greenall " Masonic Lodge.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The blinds of all the houses in Manchester-road we're drawn, and there was a large assembly at the graveside. div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.
War Work In Canada.

• The amount of voluntary war work cheerfully undertaken by the women of the Dominions is incredible, and perhaps scarcely relished in the Mother Country. Sonic idea of the mag- nitude of their labours is afforded by the immense quantities of medical stores that arrive every week at the headquarters of the Canadian Red Cross Society in London. The Quebec Provincial Branch sent -retently fifteen thousand bandages, twelve thousand dress ings, nearly three thousand khaki handkerchiefs, the same number of towels, fifteen hundred khaki shirts—surgical and convalescent—seven hundred pairs of socks, five hundred Pillow cases, over a hundred bed jackets, and sixty convalescent suits. In addi- tion there were numerous sponges, quantities of old linen, and absorbent cotton,'-stores of sheets, nurses' aprons, bed-pads, pyjamas, sur- gical Pillows, and about ninety comfort bags. These contain toilet requisites, stationery, sweets, cigarettes, playing cards, and needles and thread.

div.head: Mittens and Mufflers.
div.p: Mittens and Mufflers.

A central organisation is now being formed in London, which will from time to time issue instructions as to what to make for the soldiers at the Front, and for the sailors with the Fleet. , This it is hoped will save over- lapping, and help more effectually the men who. will be in sore need of. comforts during the coming winter. As the British Army is very 'much larger than it was last year, more comforts will be required. Women who can- not leave their homes to take up outside war work can help by knitting socks and warm garments at home, and thus minimise the ordeal of suffering that lies before the brave men facing the foe. At present the central organisation announces that mufflers and mit- tens are in great demand. • Mufflers shotild be made of fleeced wool in drab shades and must be fifty-eight inches, long and ten inches 'wide. Mittens should have short thumbs, no fingers, measure eight inches from wrist to knuckles, and match. the muffler in •colour.

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suggestions.
The Economy of Good Materials for Jam.

She who is able to differentiate between true and false economy will not for a moment enter- tain the idea of using inferior materials, but sound fruit in good condition and preserving Sugar of the best quality. An inferior quality of sugar will be found more expensive in the end, for there will be there waste in .the form of scum, and the jam made with it will neither have a good colour nor keep long. Rather econo- mise on the method of making, and here the invaluable hay-box stands our friend. A Plain Tapioca Pudding. Soak four tablespoenfuls of pearl tapioca over- night in water to. cover. Drain in the morning, add a quart of sweet milk to it, and put in the double boiler or a pail set in a kettle of hot water on the. stove. Boil until creamy, stirring occasionally. Add a cup of cream, half a cupful of sugar. Beat the yolks of four eggs and stir in with the flavouring of lemon, orange or vanilla. Turn into a pudding-mould or pan, and bake three-quarters of an hour. About ten minutes before taking from the oven, beat the whites of the eggs to a stiff meringue with four table- spoonfuls of pulverised sugar; draw the pudding to the edge of the oven, and pile the meringue carefully on top. Set back, leaving the oven door partially opened if too warm, and dry. slowly until there is a thick golden glaze. Serve hot or cold. Semolina Cream.

div.head: Women Salvation Officers.
div.p: Women Salvation Officers.

Women have always been regarded as the equals of men in the Salvation Army. That wonderful organisation did a great and much- needed work among the British and Boer soldiers 'during the South African War, and its influence to-day extends to every corner of the Empire. Sir john French and his officers speak most highly of the work done by the Salvation Army among the troops at the Front. In the domestic and social sphere, women Sal- vationists have always taken an _.important part, but since the war broke out their labours have exceeded all previous records. Ensign Mary Booth, Brigadier Mary Murray, and Mrs. Commissioner Higgins are especially revered by British soldiers and sailors. The last-men- tioned of the three ladies controls the distribu- tion of parcels of clothing and groceries among British prisoners of war in. Germany. Brave Quakeresses.

Many brave women belonging to the Society of Friends are doing noble work in the devas- tated districts of France and Belgium. But courage and contempt of danger in prosecuting good work have ever been marked character- istics of the sect. The records of Quakerism show that in times of persecution almost ~every female member of the Society was a heroine, and not a few earned the martyr's crown. Margaret Fell, who married George Fox, and, of course, Elizabeth Fry, are the most ,prominent historic, Quaker women, although the lion- hearted Elizabeth Ilooton, who dared to testify before Charles 11., deserves to be classed with the two former. Charles and his brother James 11. were both inclined to be lenient towards the Quakers, but this did not save the members of the Society, from frequent persecu- tions and confiscation of their worldly goods.

Italian Colours and Styles. Italian influence may be noted in dress and millinery for the autumn. The vivid green used as a contrast to black velvet on a nuniber of new hats is one of the colours composing the Italian flag. The wearing of coral has been revived, and this also is a compliment to Italy. The striped skirt and plain coat, so much worn during the summer, as well as the laced peasant bodice all come from Dante's beloved ountry. Gold with velvet is an Italian combination in VOlille during the Middle Ages, and still popular. Genoa and Milan continue to send their beauti- ful velvets to this country, for the looms of

Told by the Hair. (;irls with blue eyes and straw-coloured hair generally have a far calmer and happier life, as a rule, than those with big dark eyes and olive complexions,

The fai& girl is almost-sure to be level headed in her lofe affairs, and to make a sensible mar- riage, but she will be much more fickleTnan the dark girl, because her feelings will not be so deep and passionate. Dark girls are more emotional; love means so much to them that their feeling is deeper and more lasting than the love of fair girls, or so the learned in such matters say. It is said that fair children are easier to bring up than dark .ones, as their ailments are less likely to be serious, and they have more vitality to. resist disease.

Auburn-haired people must be judged alone. The mother of a daughter with ruddy gold locks and dark eyes must be on the look-out for trouble. The course of true love rarely runs smoothly for the dark-eyed auburn-haired girl.

Revival of the Ostrich Tip. Ostrich feathers and tips rival ribbons as trimmings for large hats. When tile latter are of the Charles Duval typo, long, graceful plumes are lavishly used, although the " line " is of more importance than the decoration. Smaller hats of the Watteau type are trimmed with full, beautifully curled tips, several colours being effectively arranged on the brim of a hat, or under it. Some winter models droop slightly at the sides, others are tilted at the back. The latter provide an excellent opportunity for the introduction of the tip, that has been neglected for some considerable time, but has now returned in full array. Quite a novelty are gold, silver or copper tip, and in order to thus colour them they Are dipped in a metalic liquid and dried immediately. The silvered feathers look well on grey velvet or felt. Steel ornaments in the shape cf large cabachons, give much the same effect and are enjoying a vogue just now on black velvet hats. Fashions in Muffs.

It is quite impossible to decide as yet whether the big or the small muff will lead this winter. Both are shown, and every style and shape are represented in the furriers' department. The small barrel worn during the Early Victorian era, will probably have a vogue, for it goes very well with the new fur tippet of the same period, which is also among this winter's revivals. A pretty set consists of a collar and barrel muff, a large bow of ribbon to match the hat trimming resting jauntily on he left side of the latter, and taking the place'of last scaSon'•ls bouquet. Persian lamb sets will be worn this season, the only drawback being the price, which is high. Stoles are flat in shape, and consist of one animal's skin thrown over the shoulder. At present furs are very low in price, as the Germans have bought none this year. They will be much dearer later on, and should be secured at summer prices which still prevail.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular Language.

The Common Bilious Attack. It ought to be obvious to anyone that the stomach of a person suffering from a bilious attack requires immediate rest, but most people seem to think that it is necessary to go on feed- ing, lest the patient should become weak and emaciated. Skipping two or three meals and drinking water freely is the best means of bringing about prompt relief. If there has not been sickness and there is any evidence of un- digested food in the stomach, give a pint or more of lukewarm water and tickle the throat with a feather to induce vomiting. A little mustard added to lukewarm water makes a good emetic. Vomiting should be encouraged until the stomach has been completely relieved of its foul contents. The application of hot fomentations or a hot water rubber bottle to the stonmch will relieve the pain. The, headache is usually relieved by a full warm bath which has a decidedly soothing effect. The application of hot fomentatiOns to the head, or alternate hot and cold compresses, will also relieve the ache. In some cases a hot foot bath gives prompt relief. Fomentations to the spine are helpful, and a hot abdominal pack, is even more efficacious than the fonientations. At night the wet girdle or heating compress may be applied to the abdomen. It is of almost equal import- ance to give .attention to the bowels, and if necessary give an • enema and also a dose of salts. In many cases constipation of the bowels is one of the predisposing causes in bringing on a bilious attack. After a bilious attack the diet should be very simple and abstemious for a few days, and food should not be taken more than two or at the most three times a day.—A.' B. Olsen, M.D., D.P.H., in "Good Health."

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell asked whether any- thing was being done to lessen the number of inmates of the Workhouse. He noticed from the papers that other Unions had succeeded in getting friends and relatives of inmates to take them out of the house for the time being. Un- doubtedly many of the workers at the present' time were better off than they were before the war, and it occurred to him that something might be clone in the way of suggesting to such of them as had relations in the house that they might relieve the rates to the extent of giving them a home for the time being. Of course, later on, when things returned to their normal con- dition the people taken out of the house would be readmitted, if the relatives considered that necessary.
The Chairman suggested that the reverend gentleman should bring the matter before the next meeting of the House Committee. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell said he would act on. the Chairman's suggestion.

The Chairman: We wiint to be, very •careful how we do anything of the kind suggested; it might be so easily misunderstood and regarded as an attempt to treat some of the poor people in a manner of which, I am sure, none of us would approve.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
Corporal Tombs's Father.

So Corporal Tombs, V.C., is in hospital. I trust his complaint may not be at all serious, and that he may soon be all right again. He is the son of one of the oldest and most ex- perienced Liberal agents in the country, and evidently inherits from him the qualities of pluck, endurance and an unconquerable spirit. When. I made his acquaintance, Mr. Fredk. Tombs, the father of our V.C., now Liberal agent in Cheshire wEts acting in that capacity in the Sower by Division of the West Riding of Yorkshire. Candidly, he was not a favourite at the Revision Courts, for he would tight out every case openly on its merits, whereas prior to 'his advent much time had been saved by a give-and-take arrangement between the party representatives in prelimin- ary conference. Ho took his work very seriously, and was always desperately in earnest. He was familiar with the law, and whenever challenged on a Point which he had liaised was ready with chapter and verse. A somewhat frivolous revising barrister who came his way years ago chaffed him most un- reasonably, but none of these things moved Mr. Tombs. The doughty Liberal agent was the only passive resister to the 1892 Educa- tion Act I know of successfully to defy the authorities and outwit the police. His home was veritably besieged for weeks, but they never succeeded in effecting an entrance or distraining on any goods of his. While the family lived in that district (they were there between eight and nine years), Corporal Tombs attended the Wesleyan Chapel and was a member of the Young Men's Class in the Sunday school, which his father taught on alternate Sundays. The latter was an in- patient at Chester Infirmary when he heard that his gallant son had joined the Army, hav- ing himself had the misfortune to be knocked down by a motor cycle, his lower jaw being broken in two places, his teeth dislodged, and his right leg severely injured. I heard last week from my indomitable old friend, and am glad to be assured of his recovery. " Abide With Me."

Last week's mention of this fine hymn as having been sung by a soloist at the Working Men's Mission Church, Bank Quay, reminded me of an incident to which I may possibly have referred in this, column on some former oeca- 'lion, though I have no recollection of that. A popular and eloquent Baptist layman on the East Lancashire border once told me that he had gone to one of the village chapels to assist at special services which were being conducted by a lady. The lady invited him to take charge of the preliminaries, where- upon he suggested that she should select the opening hymn. She promptly turned down a leaf, and handed him the book closed. "And," said he, with serio-comic air, " You may imagine the turn it gave me, a widower, when I discovered her deliberate choice to be 'Abide with me ' ! " Blind Preachers.

I have met with a few blind organists, but only one sightless minister besides the Rev. J. S. Morley, who preached in Warrington as reported in last week's issue. He was an American Bishop, ancl fulfilled two or three engagements in a district in which I resided somotbing over. 30 years ago. He took the entire service, and his recital of the Scripture lessons was especially impressive. For this purpose he chose some of the finest passages from Isaiah, the Psalms, and the Acts of the Apostles, and the effect was remarkable.

Origin of " Movies." was much interested in the account of the origin of moving pictures in last week's " Ex- alhiner." As a youngster I was the happy possessor of a " wheel of life" therein called the " soetrope," though our name for it in those far-off days was zeotrope. A similar effect was obtainable by a like arrangement of figures on slips attached by a holder at the top and moved in rapid succession by the thumb. Next in the evolutionary process came the mutoscope, into which one looked as through a stereoscope while the operator kept the pictures rotating. At a sort of " dime museum" in a shop at the top of Market- street, Manchester, I thus witnessed (tell It not in Gath I) a reproduction of a prize fight.

div.head: Tea.
div.p: Tea.

The writer of the sketch " In Northern Russia" has a reference to this. I had always understood that the Russians drank more tea per head of the population than any oilier nation; but a young Colonial who dropped in to .tee me the other day (his grandparents, distant relatives of my own, emigrated to Australia when I was a youngster) tells me that the people of Melbourne and neighbour- hood, among whom he has always lived, drin4 enormous quantities of tea daily, taking it at every meal. After all, when one comes to think of it, might not one almost say the same of Lancashire people, particularly the opera- tive class? If my observation goes for any- thing, most of the mill *orkers in Lan,la- shire and West Yorkshire could feelingly sung with the dame in the old song, "I owns I likes my tea." "The Bibles What It Is."

This was the Rev. Irvine Lister's subject at Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday. lam not for the moment concerned with the rev. gentle- man's treatment of it. The advertisement of the fact somehow reminded me of certain things that. were written about it during the celebration of the tercentenary of the Jacobean translation. G. K. Chesterton made a characteristic contribution in the course of which he thus expressed it in his inimitable way : " What we are celebrating is a triumph of our own language. The English translation of the Bible has one real claim to be English. . . . It is in this immense sense national, that it is anonymous. The translation, as a translation, is as English as the ballads about Robin Hood, which were written by everybody and nobody. . . . It is impossible to point to a single great man who is responsible for this masterpiece of verbal music. At the very - time when the translation was being made there were in England greater literary men than she is over likely to see again. But by no conceivable trick or turn of circum- stance can Bacon or Burton, Jonson or Shake- speare, have had anything to do with the translation of the Bible. It was done by bishops—simple and well-meaning men. . . . England wrote it; no mere Englishman could have done so."

" The Simple Diet." Thus a paragraph in last week's "Hints on Health.' Dr. Johnson was wont to say in his shocking way, "He who does not mind his belly will mot mixid anything." But what to eat, drink, and avoid—aye, there's the rub! I have a relative who has repeatedly crossed the Atlantic, and who will take a frog's leg with her meals on the liner, finding it some- what like chicken.; I have also a soldier friend who, asked out to tea in Calais, was appalled when snails were served as a dainty. Well, that again depends. I have somewhere read that Fulvius Hilpinus fed his snails on wine, honey and flour, " so that they became whole- some and delieious to the palate." One of these days I may give the interested reader a few, extracts from my copy of "Good cheer: the romance of food and feeding." Mean- while, simple livers who imagine that we have fallen on evil times in respect of the habits in question may perhaps profitably consider the ways of one Francesco de Medici, a Grand Duke of Tuscany in the sixteenth century. In "Enchanters of Men," Ethel Colburne Mayne gives the following account of this worthy's tastes at table -
" Everything he ate was mixed with the most fiery condiments, ginger, pepper, nut-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
GREAT RECRUITING RALLY.
INarrington's Part In National Effort.

div.head: MEN IN KHAKI AT PLAY.
div.p: MEN IN KHAKI AT PLAY.

On Saturilay and Sur day Warrington played its part in the pleat national recruiting effort; an effort that was put forth in all the big centres of population, and which partook of a novel character, in that it did not consist of street- corner meetings and rhetorical appeals to the patriotisni of the young men passers-by, but took the form of parades and marches, with a gymkhana, a military tattoo and a drum-head religious service following, the principal idea of the promoters being to attract those who are still capable of- service and yet are not serving, by unfolding for their edification a picture of the attractive side of soldiering. It is sincerely to be hoped that the effect aimed at was achieved and that as a result of Saturday's and Sunday's rally still more Warringtonians will flock to the Colours and thus add additional 1-4,stre to the brilliant patriotic record of the old town. The day's proceedings began at 11.30 a.m. with a general assembly of all the troops in the town on the green sward fronting the Town Hall, the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) addressing to them a few suitable words of encouragement and thanks. The troops consisted of the 12th South Lancs. (the Bantams)—who had marched down from Orford Barracks with the band of the 2nd South Lancs.—and the 4th South Lancs. —who, headed by the band of the 2/4th South Lanes. had come from the Drill Hall. An hour or two after the assembly at the Town Hall, soldiers and bandsmen marched to the Warring- ton Football Ground, at Wilderspool, where the gymkhana was held, whilst in the evening they took part in the military tattoo in front of the Town Hall, and on Sunday attended the drum- head service.

Still a good crowd got off ht the crack ,of the pistol, but the usual weeding out process ensued, and in the last two laps the issue was confined to five runners. Getting away with a fine spurt in the last time round the track, Private Naylor ronaped home a winner by some- where between 25 and 30yards.
During the afternoon Sergeant-Major Davies, of the 3/4th South Lancs., gave an exhibition of sword swinging.

MAYORESS PRESENTS THE PRIZES. At the elose of the sports the Mayoress, who was accompanied by the Mayor, graciously dis- tributed the prizes, being awarded a vote of thanks and a hearty round of applause for her pains'. The vote was proposed by Mr. W. Peter Rylands and seconded by Alderman Tinnion, the Mayor acknowledging the compliment on behalf of his wife, remarking that she was only too plehsed to do anything she could for the happiness of the soldiers and the furtherance of the British cause in the war.

div.head: ATHLETIC " TommIES "
div.p: ATHLETIC " TommIES "
Compete For Prizes On Football
Ground.

The military gymkhana and sports were a decided success from the soldiers' point of view —and, after all, that was the only point of view that mattered. They were Ills° a considerable success from the " civviee' " viewpoint, for the competition was of that friendly, cleanly, unre- lenting description that distinguishes British athleticism the whole world over. The crowd that made its way to the Football Ground at Wilderspool on Saturday afternoon might have been larger—and no doubt it would have been but for the unconscionable and uncomfortable coldness which an unaccommodating Clerk of the Weather saw fit to inflict upon this particu- lar part of the globe over whose climatic destinies he rules. Still the crowd was quite a good-sized one—one couldn't help wishing that it had been of cup tie proportions !—and any- thing it lacked in the way of the numbers one had hoped for, it certainly made amends for in its enthusiasm.

div.head: GOOD AFTERNOON'S SPORT.
div.p: A GOOD AFTERNOON'S SPORT.

" Tommy " saw to it that a good afternoon's sport was provided, and the crowd saw to it that the deserved expressions of appreciation were not lacking. The difference between a sports meeting and a gymkhana seems, to the lay mind, to consist in the fact that the last-named is, whilst considerably the same, more interest- ing. Your avbrage sports_ meeting supplies you with a succession of events—" miles" and "half miles," "two hundreds" and "hun- dreds." and "hurdles," and what not !—in which, unless you happen to be muscularly en- dowed or particularly sportingly inclimAl, you can have but passing interest, and concerning which it must be either a gift, or an effort, to raise any great degree of enthuqiasm. But a gymkhana is different—there's more variety about the events; there's more of them, and, generally speaking, they are more interesting; save possibly, of course, to your—pot "hunter." GENEROUS WINNERS AND SATISFIED LOSERS.

Surely there never was a sports meeting where a greater degree of cameraderie was shown! Why, even the winners, flushed from their efforts, came up to the table of the recording— er—angels and almost apologised for their suc- cesses. "Couldn't Corporal This or Private That have another go in the next heat, as, if he hadn't ittumbled when he wasn't expecting to give at the knees, he would have won !" There were never more generous winners and more sat- isfied losers—and yet every single competitor did his best; there was no giving anything away, but every competitor who went off at the crack of the pistol put as much into it as if he were going for the Germans, instead of merely for a photo frame or a set of carvers—or some other little reminder of his prowess.

div.head: THOSE IN AUTHORITY.
div.p: THOSE IN AUTHORITY.

The officials were: Clerk of the course: Mr. W. Mason; starter: Mr. M. Curbishley ; judges: Colonel J. A. Moggridge, Lieut.-Colonel D. E. Mocatta, Sergt.-Major Quick, Alderman D. Henshall, Lieutenant Dick. son, Lieutenant and Quartermaster Boardman, Second-Lieutenant Tymms, Cogncillor E. Osborne, Messrs. T. F. Barber, T. Bunch, T. Barnes, J. Winstanley, J. T. Sampson, W. Hill, W. Mason, J. F. Foster, T. Pemberton, T. P. Bradshaw, E. A. Sanders and 11. Hayes.

The Bands of the 2nd South Lancashires and of the 2/4th South Lancashires were in attend- ance, one being quartered in the members' stand and the other in the stand on the public side. They played selections alternately—the one "doing the popular stunt"—" Are we down- hearted?' "Good-bye, Isabelle," and the like— and the other the semi-classic, so that most prts of musical tastes were catered for. The afternoon's programme opened with a military display by the Bantams, who went through the usual Swedish exercises, and mlny others, in a manner that must have convinced every beholder that a man sft. 4in. is capable of becoming quite as smart and useful a soldier as a man at sft. 441 n.! It's grit and not stature that tells!

div.head: BIG MILITARY TATTOO.
div.p: BIG MILITARY TATTOO.
Impressive Night Speetacie Out.
side Town Hai!.

Saturday's proceedings were wound up with a military tattop in front of the Town Hall, a feature which attracted a huge crowd of on- lookers, the spacious lawn which stretches away to the ornamental wrought-iron gates on Sankey-street being black with people. The two military bands which had rendered such yeoman service throughout the day once again supplied the indispensable music, reaching the Town Hall by devious and different routes. Thus the band of the 2/4th South Lancs., accompanied by a strong detachment of-the 4th South Lancs. Regiment, with whom were Boy Scouts, Church Lads' Brigadiers and members of the local Cadet Corps—their way lighted by numerous torch- bearers—made the journey from the Drill Hall, via Sankey-street, -Horse- market-street, Scotland-rood A.•aftviny-street and Bridge-street; whilst the band of the 2nd South Lancs., followed by the Bantams (whose official style and title is the 12th ,South Lancs.) wended their way from thei'r head- quarters at Orford Barracks and eventually, meeting their comrades, united in making one big, imposing procession of it. The combined march through the streets formed a striking spectacle, and a stirring one; but the scene in front of the Town Hall, when. the massed bands drew up and the torch-bearers and all the khaki- clad men and boys stood at attention in serried ranks was more striking and stirring still. The bands, responsive to the baton of Mr. Cahill, opened the tattoo prpper with rousing march music, after which the Bantams gave an entertaining display of "fiery figures." Next the 2nd South Lancs. musicianly performed the over- ture to "The Gondoliers," which, if not the most ear-haunting of the Gilbert Sullivan light operas, is certainly one of the most interesting.

A PLEASANT SURPRISE FOR tHE CROWD. "Short speech by the Mayor," the programme announced as the -next item on the programme, and as he stepped forward to fulfil his " turn " it was noticed that his Worship was not only accompanied by the Mayoress, but that on his right hand were Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield, the honour conferred by whose unexpected presence wa's greatly appreciated on all hands, the crowd showing their pleasure in the time- honoured manner.

His Worship said that his duties were very light that evening; all he had to do was, at the request of the recruiting officers, to call upon Sir Arthur Crosfield to say a few words with a view to stimulating recruiting in Warrington.
"TIME TO BE UP AND DOING." Sir Arthur Crosfield And The Appeal For Recruits.

Sir Arthur, who was cordially received, said he was going to follow the Mayor's example and not inflict a lengthy speech upon those pre- sent, because they had had a good many speeches 'lately on the subject which was uppermost in their minds that day. The leading citizens of Warrington and the officers present that night had not spared themselVes in the efforts they had put forth to encourage and stimulate recruiting. And now, after all the talking they had had, came the time for them to be up and , doing. He did not think there was need for any Englishman to labour the appeal for , recruit's at the present moment; one had only got to look at the news. Whether they turned to the west front, or Whether they looked to- wards the Gallipolan Peninsula, the news that met them was enough to make every man who had the chance go and offer himself, to his country without delay. Of course, it was not everybody who could be spared, but there were still many who had the chance of serving—of taking part in the greatest piece of work that the men of any nation had ever set their hands to.

div.head: Chance In Hundreds.
div.p: A Chance In Hundreds.
They, heard that there was a great .deal of hardship to be faced, but hardship never yet discouraged Britisher. And there was one fact

which they might bear in mind, and it was this: That their descendants for hundreds; per- haps, thousands, of years to come would not have an, opportunity of serving their country such as that which presented. itself to the men of Britain °in these days. .This war was the greatest task to which the people of the nation had over set their hands, and the victory which was to be theirs would be the greatest achieve- ment in the history of the race. "By the million," continued Sir Arthur, "our fellows have flocked to the task and are getting on with it in a manner which ,stirs our blood, and, as we read the accounts of their heroism, fills us with pride.in them. "Go And Back Them Up."

• "To the men who can go I say, 'As those who have gone have done so much for you, I appeal to you to go and back them up.' I am sure that the appeal will not fall on idle ears; I am sure you will go, and go with a brave, a full heart, always keeping in mind the fact that it is only by a determined effort, that we shall achieye not merely a patched rp peace, but a genuine and permanent peace, which shall be for the godd of the world at largo. I will conclude' by reading you three lines from a letter written by a German in Berlin to another German fighting at the Front. 'I recognise fully,' wrote the German, 'that if John Bull and Jacques Bonhomme were capable of the German effort we should be done for. But they are not capable of it! Therefore be of good courage; remain firm to the end! Deutsch- land über alles !' It is up to every man in this country who has the opportunity—and I say this with all seriousness—to prove to the Germans that this country is capable of the effort required, and, being capable of it, that we mean to put it forth, so that, at the end, it shall not be a case of Deutschland über alles !' but of 'Britain to the fore !' " Sir Arthur concluded his brief remarks amid ringing applause.

div.head: CLOSE OF A LONG-TO-BE REMEMBERED
div.p: CLOSE OF A LONG-TO-BE REMEMBERED
EVENT.

The brief speech-making concluded, came a rousing performance of Tschaikowsky's im- mortal overture " 1812," descriptive of Napoleon's retreat from Moscow—" the great miscalculation that presaged the end of Bonapartism." The famous composition was dramatically treated by the massed bands, added effect being supplied by two firing parties, liberally supplied with blank cartridges. "If you think the Germans have come "--said the, programme apropos of the fusilades and for the benefit of the enlistable among the crowd— "enlist on Monday !" A pot-pourri of Hie national anthems of the Allies and the sound- ing of "Lights Out" by the buglers—a signal for the torch-bearers to "douse their glimel " brought a long-to-be-remembered event )f o a close.

div.head: DRUM.HEAD SERVICE.
div.p: DRUM.HEAD SERVICE.
War Of Hatred Against Friend- ship, Says Rector.

On the Sunday afternoon came an impressive drum-head service in front of theNTown Hall. In addition to a. large concourse of the general public it was attended by the merebrs of the 4th South Lancashire Regiment at the time quartered in the town; the 12th South Lanca- shire Regiment, now undergoing training at Orford Barracks, the Boteler Grammar School Cadet Corps, the Latchford Cadet Corps, .and the Church Lads' Brigade. Practically all those on 'parade, in addition to "the soldiers of the King," wore the omnipresent khaki, and the scene which confronted one as he gazed down from the altitude of the steps fronting the Town Hall was an inspiring one in the extreme. _ _ _ _

The rails at 9ie head of the' steps were draped with a large -Union Jack, behind which the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), bareheaded and wearing his vestments, stood to conduct the service, which was brief and most appro- priate'in character, the special form of ritual including supplications for the King, for his soldiers, and for victory for our arms— prayers which, despite his weight of ygars, the Rector intoned in a clear voice, the "Amens" being 'reverently sung by the khaki-clad wor- shippers and the big throng in the background. The service opened with that fine old hymn "0 God, our help in ages past," the singing of which was led by the Band of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment. After the prayers came the hymn "Fight the good fight," and then a short address by the Rector, which was listened to with profound attention.
WHAT WILL HISTORY'S JUDGMENT BE?
A War of Might Against Might and Right.

He was, the Canon said, very pleased to respond to the invitation which had been given him to speak a few appropriate words that afternoon. He felt it to be a great privilege to have been asked, but also a vtry great respon- sibility, because it was a great opportunity. They were engaged in the greatest war that the world had ever known; a war which had lasted now some fourteen months. For the last few months this country and some of her Allies had been stationary, in the trenches in the west, whilst other of her Allies had been retreating in the east. But on Sunday last a great change took place, and, in the opinion of competent judges, the Allied Forces were at present passing through a very critical period. That afternoon it was his intention to speak to the soldiers and others present ars earnestly as he could upon three points—firstly, the nature of the war; secondly, the judgment of history; and, thirdly, the duty of all in the matter. To take the first point—the war was one of might against might and right.
_ - Enemy Strong, But Allies Will Be Stronger.

Twenty millions and more of soldiers were now engaged in it. The numbers on each side were probably about equal; there were ten millions of ,the enemy and about ten millions of the Allies. The enemy was very strong, but they believed that eventually, even if they Were not so now, the Allies would be stronger, and, being stronger, would prevail. Lord Kitchener had said that he believed the Germans had almost shot their bolt. As he (the Rector) had said, the Allies had not only might, but also right on their side—the consciousness that their war was a just one. It was a war of hatred against friendship; no doubt they had all heard of, or read, "The Hymn of Hate "—unmiti- gated hate. Seeing all the hatred that existed on the other side, he could not help being struck by the fact that, notwithstanding all that had passed, he had never heard British soldiers, or British civilians, speak in terms of hatred of the Germans. They had been triends —the Britons and the Germans—and they had wished still to be friends. Another point which occurred to him waEi' that this was a war of lies against truth. One of Germany's Many Lies.

need only mention one of the enemy's lies;• that first, initial lie to the effect that the British nation prepared, planned and began the war. All present that afternoon knew that that was not true; knew, instead, that this country was taken by surprise and that Germany had been preparing for the war for forty years or more. To take another aspect of the matter, the 'war was one of cruelty against kindness. When he made that statement .he was not going by \hearsay, but was going by Lord Bryce's report—a report, which they could all trust. He also went by the papers which had just been published by the 'French Foreign Office, and after reading the report to Which he had referred and those papers nobody could doubt that the outrages alleged against the Germans were perfectly true. The war was a war of tyranny against freedom. The Ger- mans wanted to be the— conquerors of the world, whereas the people of Britain wanted to be free and wanted everybody else' to be free. .A Life and 'Death Struggle.

Lastly, the war was a struggle of life or death for .the enemy and for this country. The enemy realised that fact, and he hoped that the people of this country realised it also. What would be the judgment of history concerning this-great upheaval of the nations? The war was too present; too close at hand for them to express an opinion at present, but they could speak their opinion concerning the past. Com- paratively recently this. country had been keeping two centenaries—that of the Battle of Trafalgar and that of ;the •Battle of Waterloo, Let them for a moment think of three great figures of the past—Napoleon, Wellington, and Lord Nelson. The late Lord Acton, a foremost historian, had written that, whilst Napoleon Bonaparte was a very great man, he was not a good man; in fact, they knew that he was a tyratt. Contrast that finding with the findings of history concerning Wellington and Lord Nelson. They knew what history, led them to think of those two great men, and ever in their
minds, especially at a time like this, there echoed the words of Nelson's famous signal: "England expecte every man to do his duty." What Will Posterity Think of the Kaiser ?

What would be the judgment of posterity on the happenings of the present times? What would the future think of the German Emperor? Ho (the Rector) honestly thought that the people in the distant days to come would look upon him as a monster, morally. Aye, the Kaiser would be handed down to posterity as a man who knew what was right and yet did what was wrong. On the other hand, what would posterity think of Britain's gracious Sovereign, the Sovereigns of their Russian, Belgian and Italian Allies, and of the Ministers of their great French Ally? What would it think of the soldiers and sailors who were fighting in the cause of justice and freedom, and what would it think of the workers of this generation? The names of the great men of the allied nations would be handed down from generation to generation as the names of men who have been worthy of ;their nation. The name of 'every soldier or sailor who played his part, or of. every worker who did his share, would, of course, not be known to posterity; only the representative , names would be recorded but the gallantry of the fighting men and the assiduity of the workers at home would never be forgotten. ' There were lessons that the people of this country could learn from the Germans in these times of crises.

div.head: Lesson To Learn From Germany.
div.p: A Lesson To Learn From Germany.

One thing was that they were all as one; all of one mind and purpose—men and women, boys and girls were all doing their utmost for their country. That was one lesson that the people of this country could learn from their enemies, and he trusted that the verdict of posterity would' be that every one amongst the Allies had tried to do his duty at this difficult time. That gave rise to the question that must often be in the minds of many: What is it we can do? Well, all could offer their ser- vices—either to fight, or to work, or, at any- rate, to do something; for everybody, could do something, even if it were only giving—giving in proportion as God had blessed them. Then they could all speak words of encouragement to everyone about them. Let them not be depressed, but let them be brave and kee% up a good heart. The brief service concluded with the first verse of the National Anthem, prior to which those present joined in singing "Onward, Christian Soldiers!" and the Rector pronounced the Benediction.

div.head: 10,000 PINK FORMS.
div.p: 10,000 PINK FORMS.
Praise And Thanks For The
Voluntary Workers.

The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), in a report to the General Purposes Committee, which was laid before the Council on Tuesday night by the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), said that the returns required by the Registrar- General under the National Registration Act, 1915, were completed and dispatched within the prescribed time. "I am forbidden by the Registrar-General," says the report, "to publish the information supplied to him; but it may be of interest to know that upwards of 41,000 registration forms were distributed and collected, and the same number of registration certificates prepared and distributed. About 10,000 of the celebrated pink forms and about 5,000 other forms had to be prepared. "I wish to express my acknowledgment and thanks to Mr. W. H. Woodcock for the very able assistance he has rendered to me in the work. By means of his registration books the work was greatly facilitated, and his thorough know- ledge of the ward areas and the arrangements for the preparation of the voters' lists greatly reduced the labours I was called upon to per- form.

"My thanks are also due to several members of the Borough Treasurer's staff, to Mr. Essen- high and other members of my department, to Mr. Elliot of the Education Department, and to Mr. McAdam of the Museum Department; but, perhaps, more especially are my thanks and the thanks of the town due to those gentlemen who undertook the duties of supervisors of the differ- ent wards, and to the many ladies and gentle- men who rendered most valuable voluntary ser- vice either in clerical work in the central office or in acting as enumerators, the whole of which work was very willingly and creditably per- formed without any expense to the town.

"The President of - the Local Government Board has forwarded to me an autograph letter of thanks to all the voluntary workers for their kind co-operation in the arduous task of prepar- ing the register, a copy of which will be for- warded to all those who assisted in the work in this borough; but I think the thanks of the Town Council might also be extended to them."

The Council resolved: "That the thanks of the Council be tendered to the officials of the Corporation and to the several ladies and gentle- Men who voluntarily assisted in the enumeration and completion of the register and that the Council record its warm appreciation of their kind and valuable co-operation in the arduous work."

div.head: REGISTRATION IN • RURAL DISTRICT:
div.p: REGISTRATION IN • RURAL DISTRICT:
Local Government Board Tender Thanks To Voluntary Helpers.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council on Wednesday afternoon, the Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) reported that the Permanent Secretary to the Local Government Board, wrote that the Presiclent of the Board desired to express his appreciation of the work performed in connection with the National Registration Act. ' The Right Hon. Walter Long realised that the responsibility and novelty of 'the duties which had fallen to local authorities imposed a considerable burden upon the clerk and upon lnembers of his staff, and he recognised the promptitude and thorough- ness with which the work had been, he be- lieved, very generally carried out. Mr., Long would be obliged if a letter of his thanks to those who volunteered their assistance be given to each voluntary worker. He (the clerk) had applied for and received copies of Mr. Long's letter and he proposed, with the approval of the Council, to add a short expression of the Council's thanks to each helper. The recipients in the Council's district would consist of non- official country persons acting as ellimerators and otherwise attending at the Council's offices to render a helpful voluntary service, which was Much appreciated. Late Hours And Sunday Work.

Completion of the work involved the neces- sity for Mr. Burnedge (Mr. Newcombe's assistant) and his own personal assistant (Mr. E. J. Sutton) working late hours, and also on Sundays, beyond the personal general super- vision and action olk the Surveyor and himself. The Clerk added that he was now in reript of an important communication from the Registrar-General, who commenced his letter with the words "The Act lays the duty upon local regi6tration authorities not only of com- piling, but of maintaining the register, for their respective areas."

div.head: TRAM SHELTERS.
div.p: TRAM SHELTERS.
Dissatisfaction With Cemetery
Gates Erection.

At the Town Council on Tuesday night, the Electricity and Tramways Committee reported that they had resolved, "That the tender of the Lion Foundry Co., Ltd.; for the supply and erec- tion of a tramway shelter in Rylands-street at £55 be accepted, and that the resolution of this committee of the 19th January, 1915, accepting the tender of the Lion Foundry Co., Ltd., for the supply of tramway shelter No. 3 (Bridge- street) at £B5 16s. ad., be rescinded."

Alderman Bennett expressed the hope that the committee would not make the same mistake in Rylands-street as they had made with regard to the shelter at the Cemetery Gates. He had not heard a single person in that densely populated district of Fairfield Ward who had not. said the shelter was put in the wrong place. Councillor J. T. Locker said he would like to support /Alderman Bennett in saying that a great deal of dissatisfaction had been caused by the-placing.of the shelter in its present position. The Mayor: We camMt help that' now. The work is done.
Councillor Locker; Well, e opposed it at the time,
