div.head: ELECTRICITY FINANCES.
div.p: ELECTRICITY FINANCES.
Councillor Gough's Attack And Councillor Roberts's Defence,
AN "ABSOLUTE FARCE."

The only "passage" at the brief meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday took place over the annual report of Mr. Mathias, electrical and tramways engineer, upon the work of his department. The report stated that there had been a slight decrease in the consumption of current for both lighting and power purposes, due to the effect of the war. During the last part of the financial year the demand , became much more active. A considerable quantity of new mainstwere laid during the year. The new turbine and boiler plants were put into com- mission during the year and are proving bene- ficial to the undertaking. The weight of coal burnt was 9,772 tons, as against 10,526 last year, making 3.981 b. of fuel per unit, an improve- ment of approximately 6 per cent. "Rates and taxes" is the sum of £1,942, representing an increase of .t 963 over last year. If to this be added the contribution of £l,OOO made to the rates by this department, a sum approximating £3,000 is obtained; this figure,. on a turnover of £25,000 is a fairly large percentage, and tends to demonstrate the value of the department as an asset to the borough finances. The gross revenue amounts to £25,41955. id.; working ex- penses, £16,858 3s. 5d.; leaving a balance of £8,561 is. Bd. Out of this has been paid: Interest en loans, .£2,926 16s. 2d.; contribution' to sinking fund, £4,184 ,10s. 5d.; leaving a net profit of £l,BlB 19s. 9d. The revenue from private lighting and power consumers is £19,131 15s-. 10d., representing 3,664,026 units, a decrease of £149 14s. 7d. and 120,503 units less than last year; 680 consumers are now connected to the mains; the increase is equivalent to 6,750 8 c.p. lamps during the year. The average price obtained is 1.29 pence per unit. The contribution to the sinking fund is £4,184 10s. 5d., an increase of £l2O 103. 11d. The interest on the loan account is .22,926 16s. 2d., an increase of £365 4s. Ed.

div.head: An Anxious Year.
div.p: An Anxious Year.

"A considerable number of men from the department," adds Mr. Mathias, "have joined the Forces; in fact, in view of the large amount of power being supplied to a great number of firms working on important Government con- tracts, as many as can possibly be spared. The past year has been one of considerable anxiety and responsibility due to the progress of exten- sions and, abnormal conditions, and I have to thank the Chairman and committee for the confidence and unfailing support they have in variably accorded me, and for the loyal co- operation and assistance of my staff."

div.head: " MYSTERY " AND A "FARCE."
div.p: A " MYSTERY " AND A "FARCE."

Councillor S. Gough said he would more readily have supported this report if the Engineer had stated the number of units gener- ated by each dynamo. The Engineer did not say how many lay-by dynamos we had on hand, 'nor how many were obsolete. The Council had no information on which -to judge whether the new turbine And boiler plants—which, it was stated in the report, were proving beneficial to the undertaking—were justifying the expendi- ture upon them. The undertaking had made a profit of £l,BlB during the year, and the Engineer considered that that\vas a reasonable sum on a turnover of £25,000. If they looked at the capital outlay, however, they would find that no less than £128,000 had been spent upon the undertaking since its commencement. "This undertaking," he said, "to my mind, is a mysterious thing. (Laughter.) I. question whether there are very many members of the committee who know much about it and" who are not relying absolutely upon the Engineer for information."

Councillor H. Roberts: Really, Mr. Mayor, 'I don't know whether it is worth while saying anything in reply to such criticisms. To any ordinary individual who has the slightest elementary knowledge of accounts, the state- ment that the profit on the 'undertaking is £1.,818 is an absolute farce. The profit on the undertaking-is 0,561, but out of that there have been paid: Interest on loans nearly £3,000, and contribution to sinking fund £4,184. The in- terest on loans is equivalent, in a commercial concern, to the payment of n dividend of that amount on the share capital. The other sum of £4,000 paid into the sinking fund would, in a commercial concern, be a contribution to- wards the reserve fund or depreciation. On the top of that, there is a net profit of £l,BOO. Yet here we have an attempt to raise a discussion on an absolutely silly issue or, at any rate, on an issue that is not germane to the facts at all. -(Hear, hear.). .

Councillor Wilkinson did not reply, saying amid laughter, that Councillor Roberts had done so for him in the arguments he himself would have used. (Laughter.) Councillor Gough's speech, he added, was quite as mysterious as he alleged the manufacture of electricity to be. (Laughter.) The minutes were approved.

div.head: BOOKS AND WAR.
div.p: BOOKS AND WAR.
Libraries' Bulwarks Against Prussian-
'sing. of Intellect.

Mr. John Upson, as representative of the Museum Committee, who attended the Confer- ence of the Library Association, held in London in August and September, reports to his com- mittee that the Conference was severely prac- tical and was pervaded by an atmosphere of seriousness. The President, Mr. J. W. Y. Mac Alister, Y.S.A., dealt with the intellectual enslavement of Germany, an enslavement so complete that Germans had forgotten the,very meaning of liberty. Libraries were the great bulwarks against the Prussianising of the intel- lect, and librarians the patriots who could best lead the resistance to the subjection of the mind and soul to an organised process of drill- ing, forcing and moulding. The intellectual en- slavement of Germany was the root-cause of the horror overshadowing our civilisation. Cblonel Sir E. W. D. Ward, K.C.8., read a paper describing the work of the Camps Library. This, since the war started, had distributed a million, books and magazines to our soldiers and sailors. He described how the .Postmaster- General had come to the aid of the organisation so that those wishing to send books or maga- zines to our troops had only to hand them, un- addressed, untied and without packing, over the counter of any Post, Office, and they were for- warded to the Camp i Library's Headquarters for distribution.

"What public libraries can do during and after the war," by Mr. L. S. Jast, was the sub- ject of perhaps the best paper of the Conference, and moved somewhat along the line of the Presidential address. Briefly, the library was, he said, first the great agency in fighting intel- lectual Germany ;- secondly, it provided avenues of escape from too much thinking about theo war; and, thirdly, it could draw up and circu- late a bibliography of books suitable for reading in war time. One session was given up to five papers on the "Report on Library Provision and Policy" made to the Carnegie Trustees by Pro- fessor Adams. The need of collaboratiov and co-operation among library authorities was em- phasised, the danger of overlapping in some dis- tricts was pointed out, and a National. Scheme, or at any rate a County Scheme, of Library Organisation was advocated.

Five papers on the Literature of the War were read, and some of them were accompanied by annotated lists of the best and most suitable books for library purchase. There was a fine exhibition of books on the war. These were in English, French, Italian, and Spanish. Already nearly 2,000 books and pamphlets have appeared in English, and libraries such as ours can only hope to have a selection of the best. Every side of the war—professional, political, financial and ethical—is dealt with by a bewildering number of books.

A resolution,iwhile admitting the present need df economy, stated that libraries had been estab- lished with great trouble and at small cost to the ratepayers, and went on to say that "main- taining the public libraries .at the highest point of real efficiency was never more important than now, when the public was anxious to have the fullest and most reliable information and guid- ance on many subjects of the most vital conse- quence to the nation."
A decent man will always carry life insurance —it gives his wife's second husband such a good start,

div.head: – • ult N^^ 7?
div.p: - • ult N^^ 7?
ECONOMY.
Corporation Save in Manure Department.

The Military Works Committee recommended to the Town Council on Tuesday night that the price of the manure for. the ensuing season be fixed at .25 10s. per ton, with a discount of 55. per ton for lots under five tons, and is. 6d. per ton for lots of five tons and over; that for the ensuing season the whole of the sales be con- ducted through the office of the Borough Collec- tor, and that is. per ton be allowed for ex- penses; and that the Manchester and District Farmers' Co-operative Association be offered the manure at £5 per ton net cash on Ist June, 1916. Councillor Wilson, proposing the adoption of the recommendations, explained that Mr. Bailey, Wilderspool-road, had been their agent for the sale of manure for 28 years: They ap- preciated Mr. Bailey's services very highly, but the Government had called upon the Corpora- tion to exercise economy in every possible way. and dealing with these sales direct was one of fhe ways in which they could comply with that request, although they regretted it very much. Councillor'Chriffies seconded, and the minutes were passed.
NVYCLIFFIANS
IN KHAKI.
Letters From P.S.A. Members On Active Service.

At a recent gathering of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood, extracts from a number of letters wcre read from members who have donned }LL uniform and are at present either actuallY the Front or are preparing to go out.

div.head: JUST THE SORT OF LIFE.
div.p: JUST THE SORT OF LIFE.

Lance-Sergt. F. Andrews, who is in training with No. 2 Company of the sth Battalion of the South Lancs. Regiment, "somewhere in the Eastern Counties," wrote: "The life we are at present living is more varied than that we have recently experienced, and, consequently, it is more interesting. It is just the sort of life to keep a man in perfect health, provided he con- ducts himself as a man and lives a sober, clean life. Of course, the temptations in a camp like this are many, but the influences for good are as stronk, and chief among the latter are the influences which radiate from the Y.M.C.A. huts. . . . If the Association's huts in France are conducted on the same lines as they are here, then, I am sure, the " Tommies " find them a priceless boon. At the huts here the mon are always made welcome and are encour- aged to come again, and the fact that the huts are packed full at the free concerts which are given twice and, sometimes, three times a week, shows that the men appreciate all that the Y.M.C.A. does for them." "Mr. James," the writer adds, "could not have done any better work than to assist such a fine body of workers." TWENTY-ONE-DAY SPELL IN THE TRENCHES.

Writing from France, Sergeant A. Spencer, of B Company of the 10th Lanes. Fusiliers, made reference to the fact that Mr. James had been out in Flanders, and regretted that he had not had the opportunity of coming across him. "We have," he adds, "been out here sinco July.'. . . Although we have not been exactly in the thickest of it we have had our share. The first time we wont into the trenches we did twenty-one days off the reel. Then we had eight days out and wont back for another spell of eleven days. At the time of writing (Septem- ber 23rd) we are back in the trenches again. There are a lot of Warrington lads here !"

CONVALESCENT! Private Joseph Bond, of the Warrington Territorials, who was recently wounded end who is now in hospital at Barnet, Herts, wrote :—" I am now convalescent, and have been so for a couple of weeks."

div.head: FEW LINES FROM THE TRENCHES.
div.p: FEW LINES FROM THE TRENCHES.

A letter from Private Harry Kent, who is in France, says that he was "in the pink of con- dition," and added that he had heard that Mr- James had been out to the Front, but had no,t, had the pleasure of meeting him. "I have, lie continues, "been in the trenches five or silc times. When we come out for a spell of rest we go into billets and those spells are, needles; to say, much looked forward to. This letter 1015 been written in the trenches. .. . I often IviBlh this war was all over!" .

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
ALIENS' RESTRICTION.
Additional Charge For Drunken _knd
Disorderly Woman.

Monday's Police Court Bench—The Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Jas. Evans and Smethurst, and Messrs. W. Furness and T. Locker—considered the case of Sarah Lewis or Keirns, widow, no settled abode—who was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Friars'-green at ten on Saturday night. It was stated that she called after Detective Skelton, and when told to go away said with much bad language that "She was a Welsh woman, and her blood was up." Under the Aliens' Restriction Act she was further charged with giving kfalse name. The Chief 'Constable stated that Are had been living at the lodging-houses, 14, Ship-yard, and 5, Stanley-street. She had been up at Manchester. Liverpool and other places 36 times previously for lirunkenness and other offences. The Bench -could never allow her to go back to her ordinary associations. _ _
Irhe sentence was two months' imprisonment

div.head: RAILWAY TOWELS.
div.p: RAILWAY TOWELS.

'Visitors From Hereford Do Not Remember Taking Them. •Jane Thorpe and George Thorpe, of no settlea .libode, were charged at Wednesday's Police 'Court with having been drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane -And at the Police Station respectively; also on suspicion of having stolen 'two towels—the property of the Great 'Western 'Railway. Ca. Superintenaent Williamson said the prisoners «ame by the four o'clock train from 'Hereford the previous afternoon and took lodgings, where two towels marked " Great Western Railway" were placed under the bed. The woman's head had been badly damaged. Both man and woman declared they did not remember anything at all about any towels. Pending inquiries, they were remanded for a week.

div.head: PUGILISTIC SOLDIER.
div.p: PUGILISTIC SOLDIER.
Fought His Friends Instead Of His Enemies.

At Wednesday's Police Court Mr. C. Jackson ' Holmes presided, and Mr. W. T. Williams was also present on the Bench. Private Edward Moore, of the ,fith Manches- ;,,, ters, was charged with having in Winwick-street the previous afternoon been drunk and dis- orderly, and also with having assaulted Acting- Sergeant Jas. Hewitt. Sergeant Hewitt said he found the man arguing with P.C. Ballard and approached. Whereupon Moore knocked him in the chest -with both fists. - All the way to the Police Station he used the most filthy language, and wanted to fight witness. P.C. Ballard corroborated, and said he came upon Moore arguing with a woman. He cleared the woman along, and was trying to per- suade the soldier to go back to -his billet and not disgrace his uniform. He struck the Sergeant withce.at the slightest provocation. Lieutenant J. Beswick said the man's general character was bad; they could not do any good with him. Superintendent Williamson: And I understand 'that when a man's character is bad in the Army 'it is bad! The Chairman (to prisoner): We are very sorry to See you here in this position. You 'have an important duty to perform, although .you are not engaged at the Front. We are sorry we cannot overlook it, as it is a very serious offence. You will be fined 20s. or 11 'days.

div.head: "TRESPASSED FOR GAME:"
div.p: "TRESPASSED FOR GAME:"
Two Warringtonians In Trouloae At Houghton Green.
At the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday morning, Mr. Charles E. Parker presided, and _Messrs. J. Bailey and J. Ball 'also occupied the Meneh.
James Eaves, of 353, Winwick-road, Warring- ton, and John Robson, of The Fold, Orford, were summoned with trespassing in pursuit of

game. Evidence showed that on' the morning of Sun- Any, September 19th, a gamekeeper named (George Ashley was passing RadleY Wood, lioughton Green, when he heard voices and stopped. He then saw the two defendants with two ferrets and also seven new nets, which they placed over some rabbit holes. He waited for live minutes and then went into the wood. There ensued some discussion. Each defendant was fined 40s. or one month's imprisonment.

div.head: CROFT FARMER AND THE
div.p: THE CROFT FARMER AND THE
HARE.
"A Trivial Case.'

At the Warrington Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, before Mr. C. E. Parker (in the chair), Messrs. J. Bailey and Joshua Ball, Walter Monks, farmer, of Croft, was sum- moned for carrying a gun without a licence and killing a hare without obtaining authority. On August 3rd defendant was seen by George Ashley, a gardener, in th,e employ of Mr. Knowles, solicitor, Myddleton, Croft, to shoot a hare in a field belonging to Mr. Monks, farmer. Ashley subsequently informed a constable. In cross-examination by Mr. Steel, who de- fended, Ashley admitted he was looking. round on the instructions of Mr. Knowles. He thought - it was his duty to ask the defendant for his authority, although the hare was not shot on the land owned by Mr. Knowles. P.C. Duffy admitted to Mr. Steel that when he asked the defendant for his authority he told witness that Mr. Monks had asked him to shoot a hare for him. , For the defence, Mr. Steel contended that the prosecution was toe paltry for words. Nominally it was. a police prosecution, but .it really eman- ated from' Ashley, who was the understudy of Mr, Knowles. He was instructed that Mr. Knowles was jealous that the land in the occu- pation of Mr. Monks was taken from him. The gun lic.ence expired on Saturday, July 31st, and would have been renewed in the course of the following week. With regard to shooting the hare, it was only a technical offence. 'Mr. Monks, the farmer, ought to have given permission to the defendant in writing instead of verbally. The whole prosecution was too paltry and too mean for wOrdS. The magistrates decided that the circum- stances surrounding the case did not warrant the imposition of a fine, and the ease would be dismissed. The magistrates were of the opinion that the circumstances were Somewhat trivial.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
THURSDAY. Before Mr. J. Rymer Young, Messrs. W. Roberts, A. J. Jolley, W. T. Williams, and Dr. /STaden.

Two Months for Theft.—Ann Jane Hickman, Gough's Yard, Winwick-road, whose husband is serving with the National Reserve, was sent to gaol for two months for stealing or receiving bed linen and clothing 0 the value of 35., the Pre- .perty of Mary Govan, lodging-house keeper, Hill- street, On Monday afternoon Mrs. Govan, on returning .to her house, met the accused with ,a bundle under her arm. Later she discovered the articles.were missing. A search at the pris- oner's house by Detective-Sergeant Reddington revealed the stolen property.—Prisoner denied having stolen the articles, and said they were given to her by an " unknown " woman.
He Could Wait.
"Has your husband an old pair o' pants that he ain't usin', ma'am?" asked Wareham Long, respectfully removing from his head the shape- less remnant of a hat. -

"No," shortly answered the woman of thct house, eyeing him suspiciously. "My husband has only one pair of trousers, and they'll last him six months yet." "All right, ma'am," he rejoined, taking from an inside pocket a soiled Scrap of card- board and making a memorandum on it with the stump of a lead pencil. "I'll be around agin six months f'm to-day. Afternoon, taa'ant."-

div.head: MAID AND MISTRESS.
div.p: MAID AND MISTRESS.
Grave Allegations That Were Not Substantiated.
THE VILEST ADMISSION.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, Mary Mumby summoned for persistent cruelty —by reason of which she sought a separation— her husband, Frederick Mumby, fish dealer, of 224, Orford-lane. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the . complainant, and Mr. Arthur Browne defended. Both parties were respectably at- tired.. _ _

Air. Steer said the pair had been married about eleven years and had four children, whose ages ranged from 10 to 4. They lived happily together until about two years ago, when the husband started to drink very iheavily out of doors, and also to keep spirits. in the house. When he came home drunk at night he still kept going downstairs to " replenish " himself. He ,continually assaulted his wife and had said, he was tired of life and would finish himself. During the last three months he had been drunk nearly every night.

div.head: CASES OF CRUELTY.
div.p: CASES OF CRUELTY.

Mr. Steel then alleged several :instances of cruelty. On August 30th the parties, went to the Hippodrome together, and- on their return found the servant at the front gate talking. to her young man. The defendant said to hr:• ". The back door is the place for you.— When they got inside Mrs. Mumby- remonstrated with him for saying that in the presence of the maid's young man and he caught her by the throat and struck her, the children hearing him.' Amongst other instances he said "he had been watching her" and locked her out. Recently he told her "she shouldn't swank about with her jewellery," and took it from her. Again, he said. she should have no more meals in the house, and at night tried to throw her out; he affected her heart and the maid had to give her some brandy. "I understand," .concluded the solicitor, "that defendant is going to allege mis- conduct against his wife. This, I suggest, is only to cover his own misconduct, and I am assured there is nothing at all in such an allega- tion. She has often been urged to apply for a separation on account of his brutality; and I think the case is one of gross cruelty."

div.head: BANDMASTER AND THE CHILDREN.
div.p: BANDMASTER AND THE CHILDREN.

Mr. BrOwne, for the defence, alleged that mis- conduct on the part of the wife liad taken place, and remarked that the maid who had been so friendly with Mrs. Mumby, and had been with her six years, now declined to do anything for her, but appeared against her! Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, Mrs. 3efumby said the girl had been telling her husband things all along, and she had only just found out. She bought a wristlet-watch and, though she did not tell her husband, he saw it. A local military bandmaster int passing the house, accidentally knocked down one of the children. He called to apologise and gave each of the chil- dren a threepenny bit. That was how she got to know him.

Mr. Browne wondered why a strange man should give her children money. Complainant further 'tldmitted that she re- ceived a letter from "H.," a friend of the maid's young man, addressed to "Dear May," and further that she had also received from him a postcard to the effect that he was looking for- ward to seeing her 500 n... She did not know why he had written to hr like that. She had never been with a certain Woman to a house in Stock,. 'ton Heath. She did not remem- ber watching for the bandmaster to pass With the •band and sitting at the window with the maid and smiling at him and he at her. She never told the maid she had arranged for him to came to the house the day after first speak- ing to 'him; he came about a week after to ask for rooms, .and was not in half an hour, during all of which time the maid could see them.
She denied other suggestions made by Mr. Browne.

Mr. W. B. Forshaw said he represented the bandmaster (who was present), and denied the allegations. CHAIRMAN ASKS FOR "FOUNDATION." The Chairman (Councillor Roberts) said he did not like allegations of the kind that were being made unless there was some real founda- tion for them. As far as the letters were con- cerned, they might have been indiscreet, but they were nothing Worse. A letter Mrs. Mumby sent to her 'maid was perfectly fit and•proper. He had always made it a rule never to let any- one 'blacken a woman's character unless there was :substantial evidence to corroborate the allegation. The charge was per- sistent cruelty, and he did not think it right to listen to all this attack unless they had very substantial evidence.

After consultation with the Clerk, however, the cross-examination was proceeded with. - Mrs. Mumby went ont to say she did not give the girl a shilling to go out to the pictures with the child, but the girl had intended to go out a walk and 'did so. She was not in the house alone with the bandmaster for more than ten minutes. She 'told him she would ask her hus- band about his having rooms. He. called a week later and asked if she had done so; she replied "No," because she did not think it would be wise to have anyone in the house. She had never met him round Orford or up Win- wick-road, or anywhere outside; she swore it. The Saturday afternoon following she met him in town, and he asked her what the bother was about; the maid was there all' the time. He did not ask if she had admitted anything but said he would go to his solicitor, Mr. Jenkins. ;` think," added complainant, "it was a case of that girl wanting my place all the time!" She daresay her husband had marks as well as her, for she hit him in self-defence when he hit her. The girl continually had to come between them, and said if she would go in for a separation she would be her chief witness. There was not the slightest ground for any charge of misconduct with the bandmaster at all. Apart from two chance meetings she had never interviewed him outside. She presumed the. letter was from a friend of the maid's young man who had often been to the door with him. He had no right to write her that letter at all; she was quite sur- prised by it, and had there been Anything between them she would have burnt it first thing, instead of giving it to the maid to keep. Mrs. Amy Bennett, 208, Orford-lane, cor- roborated Mrs. Mumby!s statements.

div.head: WHAT CAUSED BAD TEMPER.
div.p: WHAT CAUSED BAD TEMPER.

Mr. Browne pointed out it was only when Mrs. Mumby had gone out, or bought jewellery, that her husband had It his temper. He had been chaffed in the stets by numerous persons, who shouted "how's the bandmaster?" and so on; subsequently there had been assault on both sides.

div.head: DRANK FOR SEVERE COLO.
div.p: DRANK FOR SEVERE COLO.

Defendant., in the course of long evidence, said he only took the rum when he got a severe colds and did not drink heavily. He continu- ally asked his wife if .there was any truth in the rumours he had heard and she said "No." When he told her he was convinced there was something wrong she told him with much bad language that he could do what he liked, and find out where she went and what she did. He had often' found her at the gate talking to a soldier, but said nothing offensive to her. She said it had nothing to do with him. He offered to forgive her if -she would confess, and she promised to have absolutely nothing to do with the bandmaster. • That was the first happy meal he had had for months. He did not kno* the bandmaster at all and didn't want to; he thought he was taking the right course when he wrote to him. He would have taken the letter himsof, only he had a train to catch. He had never ben told till yesterday afternoon that the maid never delivered a letter he gave her to take from him to the bandmaster. On the occasion when he locked his wife out, he had come up on the 'bus and noticed his wife get off at Amelia-street and go round home the back way; she ran off when she saw he had got in through the front before her. He had never kicked her in his life.

div.head: SERVANT'S EVIDENCE.
div.p: THE SERVANT'S EVIDENCE.

Millie Gleave (21.)—the servant upon whose evidence the allegations were principally made —said Mr. Mumby did not get exactly Alrunk. It was not true that the bandmaster knocked down the boy, but he did give 4 the children threepence. By arrangement the bandmaster visited the ,house and she showed him into the front room. He and Mrs. Mumby sat together on the couch for about an hour and a half. She could see them through the glass partition from the kitchen. Mrs. Mumby afterwards told her

what she had denied in her evidence, and that he had arranged to call again. Upon hearing this she (the maid) said that when he came she would either go out or upstairs. The band- master came a week afterwards—on the Wed- nesday afternoon—and was shown into . the middle room. She went upstairs. He remained till 3.45, and afterwards Ails. Mumby spoke to her.

div.head: SPIRITED PASSAGE.
div.p: A SPIRITED PASSAGE.

After the maid had given a mass of further evidence, including alleged admissions by Mrs. Mumby, The Chairman said: When Mr. Mumby asked you to deliver that letter to the bandmaster you promised you would? Tho Maid: Yes.
He never made any inquiries after whether you had done soP.---No; he trusted that I had taken it.
You' are perfectly certain he didn't-aek you? —Yes. -

.' Why didn't you take it?—Well, • they had agreed to forgive and forget, and f thought it would be better not to. So I took:. ;t upstairs to Mrs. Mumby and opened it, and *4 both read it aloud and then I tore it Up. yesterday I admitted I had not taken it. You Anew what the bandmaster was gding to call again for?—Yes. In other words, you yourseff assisted ih what you knew to be gross immorality between this gentleman and your mistress?—'No; it had nothing to do with me. Then your idea of your auty is that it does not matter twopence to you what goes on in the house so long as you don't see it?, . . . If that is your idea of it I don't think much of your statement. Mr. Steel: I might suggest that nothing at all took place and that all this' has been made up since! "VILEST ADMISSIO.N EVER HEARD." The Chairman (to the maid): Your's is the vilest admission I have ever heard made in the box, and I have been in the Police Courts for twenty-two years. Mr. Browne: The girl is young, sir.

The Chairman : Young! It she has let all this go on there isn't much she doesn't know. A word from her to Mr. or Mrs. 3lumby might have prevented all this unhappiness and misery —assuming that her. statement is comet, which I don't believe!
Mr. Steel: I can go further and give a reason why she has concocted the story if you think it necessary.
DENIED ON OATH.
Cross-examined by Mr.:: Rirshaw, the band- master, Mr. Cahill, denied on oath and in their entiretly all the allegations made against him. Such relations had never been in his thoughts:
A separation order was granted, the allow- ance being £1 a week and a guinea advocate's fee.

div.head: "TOEING THE LINE."
div.p: "TOEING THE LINE."
Curious Allegations In Domestic
- Trouble Case.

At Tuesday's Police Court—before Councillor IL Roberts (in the chair) and Messrs. C. Jack- son Holmes and T. Locker—Florence Hunt summoned her husband, Percy Hunt, a well- spoken man of 41, Lythgoes-lane, for aggra- vated assault.

Mr. T. S. Steel represented defendant, and pleaded not guilty. - • Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of complainant, said on Saturday night; September 20th, Mr. and Mrs. Hunt went up town at about eight and met his:brother-in-law, Mr. Richard Smith.. They went into an inn and had a:drink. After a short time the husband and wife returned hoine and' she began to get supper ready; a Mrs. Massey from' next door came in and told ler about a military instructor who had been on leave to see his mother. When they sat down to supper her husband said: "Fancy having a one-eyed 'He's doing a good man out of a job." His wife said: "Don't talk like that about anybody's eyes." "0h" he replied, "who are you dictating to?" "I'm not dictating to anybody," she 'said. He then re, took a piece of chalk out of the cupboard, drew a line across the middle of the hearthrug, and said: "You toe that line." Mrs. Massey was afraid and went out, and Mrs. Hunt locked the doors and went straight upstairs to bed. The husband followed her and hit her, and his mother said: "You will be murdering that girl some of these times when you are assaulting her." He went and got hold of both his wife's arms and began to bite her all over the breast: She shouted " Murder " out of the window,, and a crowd gathered outside. He kept hitting her for hours. Next morning he remarked upon her black eye and asked if he had done ;that. Defendant had written asking his wife to meet him and come home.

Mrs. Hunt gave evidence and said she pulled the curtains down to shout through the window. She never closed her eyes till about four o'clock in the morning; her husband had a quart of beer, and was continually drinking. Next morning he asked "What is the matter with your face?" and she told him he had done it.

div.head: " Would She Marry Again?"
div.p: " Would She Marry Again?"

Mr. Steel asked if there was not also a Mrs. Gallop in the house at? the time, who asked her if Percy were to die would she marry again; whereupon she replied "What, after twelve years with that, I marry again?" Complainant: There was nothing of' that sort of conversation went on. X put it to you that your husband was annoyed at what' you had said, and ordered a woman out of the house?—No, he didn't.
Didn't some people stand outside shouting?— No. Mrs. Massey Was in and saw the blow struck.

Didn't you rush at him and scratch him over the face for turning the woman out?—No. Mr. Steel,: I put it to you that he lever touched you except to push you in the bedroom. Maggie Massey, wife of a soldier, gave evidence corroborating that of Mrs. Hunt, and denied having shouted from outside: "Summons him Florrie, and I'll come as witness."

Defendant—a pipe-fitter's labourer at Long- ford Gas Works--went into the witness box and denied assaulting his Wife. , Mrs. Georgina Hunt—the aged mother of defendant , and an invalid, .said her son's wife was the principal cause ~qf the ,row. In the 'bedroom he was pushing her because she wanted to go out downstairs; and then when he would not lei her she ,tried to jump through the win- dow. There was not a..erowd ouiside. Mrs. Appleton said she saw the marks on Mrs. Hunt's chest on Monday, and was told they were bites.
Mr. Laws (the Police Court missionary) said the wman's eye had been very, much dis- coloured. The Chairman said the Bench were satisfied there 'had been an assault, and the fine would be 20s.

div.head: Separation Case Adjourned.
div.p: Separation Case Adjourned.
Mr. Browne then applied for a summons against the husband under the Married Woman's Jurisdiction Act, Mrs. Hunt saying her life with defendant was a misery. She had tried for a separation before.
A seven dnys' adjournment was decided upon.

div.head: HOW BRIDGES AND RAILWAYS ARE DESTROYED.
div.p: HOW BRIDGES AND RAILWAYS ARE DESTROYED.

The public hardly realise the tremendous amount of destruction that nowadays can be wrought by a retiring. force en the permanent way, embankments, and bridges of a railway line. The'sleeperS call . burnt, and the rails, -"made red .hot in the fires," can be 'so twisted laterally that it. is _a practical impossibility- to "-straighten them out again: The ,foundations on which the piers sof the bridges are based can be. blown up, and the approach embankments to the bridges can be similarly destroyed, so that not only may it take weeks to replace them with temporary trestles of timber, but the work an only be pursued from one end at- a time, because once the muddy season sets in, the heavy tini- bers, the rails, sleepers, and in fact every heavy detail 'of the whole equipment can only be brought up over the rails as they are relaid to- wards the front. When really heavy rain sets in, the banks .of newly thrown up. earth will 'settle, the trestles of the bridges are liable to link, and the whole line becomes so" unsafe that , trains carrying the immense loads now required •(a siege howitzer weighs 89 tons without its car- riage or platform) can only proceed at a snail's pace over the bad places; and it is, Of course, these which determine the carrying power of the whole • line.—Colonel F. N. Maude, in Abe October `! Contemporary Review."

At a N.U. meeting Mr. E. 3. Mee (Warring- ton) was appointed to act as referee in the St. Helens Recs. v. Wigan match, to be played on Saturday next. Young, the Warrington half-back, again turned out for Rochdale Hornets on Saturday, and assisted them in lowering the colours of the Wigan Club. According to the critics Young played a sound game, and made most of his opportunities. Two other Warrington lads—C..Povey and H. Povey—who are playing with Broughton Ran- gers, received special mention last week-end. In their match against Salford the Rangers lost by the odd point in eleven, but the Poveys made an ideal wing, and defeat might have been turned into victory had they .been given the ball oftener.

div.head: INTERMEDIATE LEAGUE.
div.p: INTERMEDIATE LEAGUE.
RESULTS FOR LAST SATURDAY.
Parochial, -18 Points; lieathside, 0. Rylands's Rec., 3; Sarecl Heart, 0. St. Mary's; 6; St. Thinnas', 0. Beamont, 13; Whiteemss, 0.
St. James', 7; Silver-street, 5. The match Wycliffe v. Bolton was not played, owing to many of the latter team being engaged on Government work.
PAROCHIAL OLD BOYS OUTPLAY HEATHSIDE.

Great interest was taken in, last Saturday's match at Victori4 Park between the. Parochial and Heathside teams. The old champions, have still clearly• got their old form; for the match ended in .a victory for the Church-street lads by 18 points to nil. Moreover, they have scored 96 points this Season without having had a single point scored against them. W. Brandwood,.the Parochial full-back, has done great 'service td the teituu. but has been called away to work on munitions, and his place was taken by H. Challinor, who played a fine sound game. - Heathside wen the toss and played with the wind at their backs. Mathews set the ball rolling and after five minutes' struggling on the Heathside line Mathews -scored a splendid try, which was improved upon by Wilcocks. Play was very even until. the Parochial were awarded ,a free-kick, but there was not much gain g 0 by it. Griffiths, the Heathside full- back, was forced to mark close to the line. The Heatbside forwards broke away with the ball, but Challinor came to the rescue and made a fine save. At the interval Parochial led by five , points to nil..

- The second half started in favour of the leaders, and after a short time Broadhurst scored, Brown improving. At this stage play became a little scrappy, and Breese, of Parochial, and Bailey, of Heathside , were ordered to leave the field. With a ten points lead. the Parochial forced the attack and Litherland scored a try. The goal points were added by Brown. Play was again brought to midfield, but the Parochial forwards soon broke away and Gibbs added another try to the list. The goal-kick failed. Result: Parochial, 18 points; Heathside, nil. The most prominent players were Griffiths, Ashton, Dillon and HaAer for Heathside, while Challinor, Broadhurst, Brown and Gibbs played a fine game for Parochial. The scorers were : Tries : Mathews, Gibbs, Broadhurst and Lither- land (one each); goals: Brown 2, Wilcock Heathside team deservedly, paid the penalty by turning up three players short. Two re- serves were brought into the team, but Heath- side played twelve men tbronghout. The game was unusually strenuous, not to say rough, and the ',referee—Mr. Bibby—had to send off a player Of each team.- ,While the Heathside Players' efforts were disjointed, the Parochial lads showed' a clever knowledge of the game, and often combined in beautifully-timed pass- ing movements. Parochial.-711. Challinor; H. Malkin, H. Brease, B. Brown(capt.) and W. Broadhurst; Wilcocks and T. Robinson; T. W. Cook, W. Mathews. S. Stretford, D. Gibbs, J.. Litherland and A. Roberts. Reserve, G. Clare.

div.head: RYLANDS'S‘REC. v. SACRED HEART.
div.p: RYLANDS'S‘REC. v. SACRED HEART.

This match took place on the Gorscy-lane enclosure, on Saturday. Both teams were at full strength. Dumbell winning the toss, "Hearts" kicked off against a slight breeze. Archer returned the ball to the centre, where Baker fielded and made an opening for the "Hearts," 'which was badly mulled. From a scrummage the " Hearts' " half-back kicked the ball across, and Ratcliff took it, passing to Grady. That player repassed to Ratcliff, who made a fine opening for Rylands's wing man to score. Dumbell failed at goal. Rylands's again came to the attack, Savoury eluding man after man. His final pass broke down a yard from lie line. Half-time arrived with the score :—Rylands's, 1 try (3 points); Sacred Heart, nil. ' Dumbell kicked off in the second half and the game was played at a ,terrific pace. Play was kept in the centre of the field until Baker, the "Heart?" left wing, made a dash and carried play, to the Rylands's line. On the whole the game was give-and-take and there was not much difference, between either teams, who were too anxious. Baker and Titchard were the pick of the visitors, the former being an putst'anding player who got through a lot of,,wOrk; while Rylands's were best represented by Archer, Ratcliff, Grady and Durnbell. Result :—Rylands's Rec., 1 try (3 points): Sacred Heart, nil. ST. JAMES' v. SILVER-STREET.

St. James' and Silver-street met in Victoria Park, St. James' winning by 7 points to 5. The score by no means represented the general run of the game, for St. James', although playing twelve men after fifteen ,minutes, were easily better • than their- opponents. After twenty minutes' play Heesem dropped a. goal for St. James'. Early in the second halt SilVer-street put on a try and a. goal, quickly followed by a try and a gold -for St James': throUgh Smith and Rigby. Silver-street were best represented at right- centre, while for St. James' the custodian was easily best. •

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
Season Opens With Two Well-Fought
Games.

Last Saturday the clubs comprising the above League opened their season's fixtures under rather dismal conditions. Some slight showers in the morning were followed - by threatening skies during the afternoon, and no doubt had something to do with the sparse attendance of spectators al the games which were played.

Paddington were the visitors to the Hollins Green Club and a match for the opening of the season's fixtures between keener rivals locally could not be wished for. The Green men were represented by players who constituted their team last season, whilst the visitors had several fresh faces among them. Horrocks, in goal, last season played the Rugby code; Lord, at centre-half, has previously played for the Oughtrington Clubs; Rothwell, at centre-for- ward, last season played for the Earlestown St. John's Club; and Greenwood is also from the Earlestow-n district. The remainder of the team were playing members last season. -

It was a disappointment to the Paddington- ians to have to return home with a defeat; and thejlollins Green team were very fortunate to gather both points, as on the general run of the game a division-Of "points would have been more representative of the play.

- The other game in the competition was be- tween the Elmwood Congregationalists and Warrington Central, and both had fairly repre- sentative elevens in the field, the former intro- ducing several of last season's reserve players, whilst the Central were composed of all their regular players with one exception. They in- cluded O'Neil, who has previously played for the Excelsior's and St. Barnabas'.

div.head: AN AMALGAMATION.
div.p: AN AMALGAMATION.

We are informed that the Fairfield United and the Orford White Star Clubs have amal- gamated and have sent in an application for membership to the League Secretary. They will now be able to put a strong team in the field, as they will probably be able to hall upon Millward, Meachin, Ilankinson, Woodhouse, Potter, Gleave, .Lewis, Kelly, Ditchfield,- Gif- ford and Pilling'. Mr. H. Clayton has consented to. take up the secretarial duties.

div.head: LAST SATURDAY'S LEAGUE GAMES.
div.p: LAST SATURDAY'S LEAGUE GAMES.
SANKEY ATHLETIC v. WIDNES ST. AMBROSE.

Played at Sankey. The home team attacked, but were soon repulsed. The visitors made a great effort, but were well held by the home defence. After 25 minutes E. Taylor scored for Sankey with a high, drooping shot. Half-time: Sankey Athletic, 1 goal; Widnes St. Ambrose, none.

The visitors made several attempts to score on resuming, but could not make headway against a splendid defence. Sankey now had a turn and the Widnes goalkeeper saved three successive shots from Kenyon. The home team continued to hold the upper hand to the end. Result :—Sankey Athletic, 1 goal; Widnes St. Ambrose, none.
HOLLINS GREEN v. PADDINGTOii.

The above clubs opened their season's League 'fixtures on Saturday, on .the ground of the former club, the following players taking part: Hollins • Green: Blundell; Millington and Clarke; Buckley, Savery and Cleworth; Green, Taylor, Muskett, Etchell and Atkinson. Pad d ing ton : Horrocks; Garnett and Holmes ; Marsh, Lord and Pritchard; Horrocks, Derby- shire, Bothwell, Wrench and Greenwood. Referee, Mr. S. C. Essenhigh. The visitors won the toss and played up the slope. Muskett set the ball rolling, and the first advance, came from the home team, but their final efforts were wide of the goal. Directly after Garnett had to kick into touch in order to check Atkinson. The visitors then became more aggressive and attacked the home goal very keenly. A strong appeal was made for a goal, but the referee's ruling was against the point. Good play •by Clarke and Cleworth cleared the danger away. Muskett, gaining possession, broke away, eluded the attentions of Garnett and Holmes, and beat Horrocks with a good shot after twenty minutes' play. The visitors quickly retaliated and within a couple of miniites Greenwood .equalised the score with a splendid shot. The game was now keenry contested, and after Horrocks had made a couple of grand saves play was transferred to mid-field. Muskett scored an offside goal for the home team and then Greenwood forced Blundell to concede a corner. This proved fruitless, and the interval arrived with the scores one goal each. On resuming, the game was very keenly con- tested and the visitors were quickly in the home goal area, but good defensive play by Clarke and Millington saved the situation. The home team made a raid on the visitors' goal and a splendid centre from Atkinson was mulled by Horrocks and Pritchard in the visitors' defence. Taylor availed himself of the opportunity and put the home team in front by scoring an easy goal. The visitors now made strong efforts to get on equal terms, and Both- well skimmed the bar with a splendid shot. • At the opposite end Atkinson hit the inside of the upright, but Horrocks eventually cleared his lines. , Play was very evenly contested in mid- field for a while, and then the visitors' forwards became more .dangerouS and Bothwell beat Blundell with a good shot, but the referee dis- allawed the point for some infringement of the ,rules. Horrocks,.was equal to the .occasion by clearing finely from Savery. From now to the clos4,- of play: the visitors Made repeated attempts to make the scores equal, but failed to break down the home defence. Scores : ' Hollins Green, 2 goals; Paddington, 1 goal.
ELMWOOD CONGREGATIONALISTS V. WARRINGTON CENTRAL.

The above teams opened their season's League fixtures on Saturday on the King and Queen ground, before a moderate attendance of spec- tators. The following players turned out Elmwood Congregationalists: bolt; Joe Phe- nix and Smith; Main, Hazeldino and Oxley; W. Phcenix, Molyneux, Ashton, Kendrick and Wells.
Central : Ashcroft; Sankey and Glover; Pot- ter, Gilbert and Williams; Mason, O'Neil, Brown, Hands and Mason. Referee, Mr. Harry Clayton. _ .

The game .started- with the Central having the slope in their favour and they were quickly attacking. The visitors .were, having the best of the exchanges, and owing to the weak clear- ances of the home backs they scored their first goal after seven minutes' play, O'Neil doing the needful.. Directly after, Mason, on the right, gained possession and.. beat the home defence and registered the second point. The home team, now- had. more of the game and made several attempts 'to reduce their arrears. They- succeeded in getting the ball past Ashcroft, but the referee ruled. the point offside. The interval arrived with the Central' leading by 2 goals to none. - The game was evenly contested for a while in the second half, but gradually the Congrega- tionalists were seen to better advantage. They forced the visitors' defence to concede a corner- kick. This was Swell placed by Wells, and W. Phoenix headed the ball through. During the remainder of the game the Congregationalists had slightly the better of the exchanges; but ,failed to get on equal terms with their oppon- ents. Result: Central, 2 goals; Elmwood Con- gregationalists, 1 goal.

div.head: Second Round.

div.head: N.A. Centre.
div.p: N.A. Centre.
There has been an improvement in sport'all round, the Gowy and Shropshire Union Canal in particular, and members May give these places more attention, now that the match season is over. . .

div.head: HOY ON CUPS.
div.p: HOY ON CUPS.

. The Cooper's Arms annual brought the coi- tests to a close. 'The- distribution .a prizes Of the above club took place last week, and the secretary, Mr. A. Swarbrick, had some very nice prizes for his members to select from. There was a prize for all who caught fish, so the novice was well catered for, and the membership should grow considerably next season. A most pleasant evening was spent at the distribution. The cup Mr. S. Donoghue presented to the club was won by the veteran, F. Jolley, who is hot on cups and medals. He also won the massive cup for the largest roach caught in the match. This cup becomes his own property, and he says it is nOt for sale. We cannot let our readers know the size, but Mr.. Jolley will be pleased to show it to anyone who gives him a call.

div.head: GOWY PROVIDES GOOD SPORT.
div.p: THE GOWY PROVIDES GOOD SPORT.

Angling on the Gowy has been very good of late by the upper reaches near Waverton, where roach up, to 11b. have been taken, and dace 10Ioz:; above the mill at Mickle Trafford, roach 11b., dace 90z., gudgeon loz. 11dr.; Shaker Bridge way, ,roliTch 11b. loz. and: dace 9oz. sdr. On Sunday last Messrs. Green, Jolley and Trigger were responsible for good bags of class fish. Mr. Trigger tried for the best plate of four roach, , but just failed to draw the scale. Re, has top weight for the mill side of the Gowy;

div.head: SHROPSHIRE UNION.:
div.p: SHROPSHIRE UNION.:

The canal has fished fairly well with our mem- bers lately, although none has come from here to upset the Gowy roach of 11b. 7oz. 10dr. One member brought a bag of dace of about 10th.; three others have had roach over 11b. iind dace up to 10oz. The other places—Norton, Chester, and the Weaver—have had fair catches lately, but no weighers. THE SEVERN.

A member who is holidaying on the Severn sent over this*. week three chub, the heaviest being 11b. 156 z. 15dr. He reports good sport, bra no specimens. He has had half a dozen chub over 111). in one day and dace galore. He reports river low and clear.

EMPLOYERS AND BUDGET.
Some Criticisms And A Few Suggestions.

Mr.. W. Peter Rylands presided over the monthly meeting of the Central Executive Com- mittee of the Employers' Parliamentary Associa- tion, held in Manchester. The President (Sir Charles W. Macara) was absent in London. The Budget proposals were carefully considered, and the following resolutions were unanimously adopted:—

div.head: Halfpenny Postage.
div.p: Halfpenny Postage.

That this committee view with regret the pro- posed abolition of the halfpenny postage, as they lean to the opinion that it would involve more loss to the trade of the country than is com- mensurate with the presumed gain to the Exchequer- _

div.head: Excess War Profits.
div.p: Excess War Profits.

That this committee approves of the prin- ciple of taxation of extra-ordinary: profits made in consequence of the war, and forbears to criti- cise the Chancellor's proposals until the details of administration of the scheme are to hand. We respectfully suggest, however, that in order . to give practical effect to theproposals advanced with a minimum of individual hardship an Appeal Tribunal should be formed- whereby- manufacturers and traders can. apply for pro- tection when the presence o? any special circum- stances does not warrant the imposition of the full amount of the tax; and venture to recom- mend the utilisation of the Surveyor? and In- come Tax Commissioners in this capacity. Incidence of Taxation in Particular Cases.

The Central Executive were also of opinion that in the imposition of the excess profits tax careful attention should be devoted by the Government to eases where the giving of prac- tical effect to the letter of the Chancellor's speech would operate unfairly. In this connec- tion two resolutions, inter alia, are worthy of note.

In the case of a firm whose profits in any one of the financial years upon which the assessment is based suffered from any abnormal conditions outside its control, such as strikes, fires, explo- sions, resulting in a reduction of profits in such year or years, provision should be made for the exclusion of such year or years in the calcula- tion of the datum assessment and such combina- tion of years shall be taken as may seem just. That .in the case of a new company assessed for income tax upon_ actual trading for less than three years the datum should be 10 per cent. upon the capital invested. Anent the dates within which the proposals were to take effect, the committee were of opinion that it was unjust that a firm whose financial year ended a month after the out- break of war should be assessed equally with a firm whose financial year ended perhaps after 11 months of war.-
Co-operative Societies.

While this committee adhere to their view that the whole profit 4 of co-operative societies should be-liable to income tax in the same way as other industrial concerns, they desire •to record their strong opinion that even if divi- dends distributed amongst co-operators must be exempt from taxation for reasons of administra- tive convenience, it is highly improper that allocations of profits to reserve and capital pur- poses should not be liable to the same taxation as similar allocations made by trading firms with whom they compete.

div.head: MUNITIONS TRIBUNALS.
div.p: MUNITIONS TRIBUNALS.
There was also a considerable discussion ag Tgards the industrial situation, and the follow- ng resolution was put on record:

• This comniittee welcomes, the constitution of the local tribunals 'appointed Under the 3/1111i- tions Act, containing, as they do, equal numbers of employers and employed, for the settlement of differences arising out of the Act, as embody- ing the principles of the Industrial Council, the utilisation of which has been so long advocated by this association. •

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1915.
SECONDARY SCHOOL HEADMASTER.
Mr. Broome, M.Sc., Selected.

4 The School Management Committee of the Education Committee have made a wise selec- tion in appointing a successor to the late Mr. E. S. A. Robson, headmader of the Secondary School and Technical Institute. Their choice has fallen upon Mr, James Spears Broome, M.Sc., who ihas been second master of the school since November, 1911. During Mr. Robson's soMewhat protracted illness Mr. Broome was largely responsible for the man- agement of the school, and the extraordinarily gratifying results at the last Senior Oxford Examination, when a large number of students passed with honours and gained many distinc- tions, demonstrated beyond doubt that Mr. Broome and his staff were working well and satisfactorily together. When it was made known yesterday that the committee had de- cided to confer the 'post upon Mr. Broome there was a Tespeotful demonstration on the part if the pupils at the Secondary School, and those of flip: upper forms were among the first to congratulate their new headmaster upon his promotion. We add our Congratulations, with the confident hope that the school may proceed along its successful course.

div.head: DISTINGUISHED CAREER.
div.p: A DISTINGUISHED CAREER.

Mr. Broome, who resides at Penshurst, Hill Cliffe, is 33 years of age and married. He was educated at the Salford Central nigher Grade School and the Salford Pupil Teachers' Centr:-? and the Manchester University. In his earlier school days .he showed marked promise of the scholastic success that was to follow. In 1895=S he held the Board of Education Science and Art scholarship; in 1900 he gained a first-class King's scholarship, with distinction in geo- graphy, history, science and drawing. In 1901 he matriculated first claSs and won the Herbert Memorial Scholarship, taking in the following year his Intermediate B.Sc. in mathematics, physics, chemistry and English literature. Then followed a highly successful University career, in which chemistry stood out promin- ently as one of Mr. Broome's subjects. In 1903 he passed B.Sc.,- and in the following year he gained first class honours in the same degree. In 1907 he took his M.Sc. During these event- fill years he was awarded the Mercer Univer- sity Scholarship for distinction in chemistry at the Honours B.Sc. Examination (being the top man of his year), and he was prizeman ;n technological chemistry—the chemistry of the synthetic dyestuffs and their. intermediate -pro- ducts.

In 1904 Mr. Brodme was awarded a first-class teacher's certificate by the University for work in history, theory and practice of education, and a first-class in history and administration (college examination). Mr. Broome took a course in metallurgical subjects at the Manchester. Municipal School of Technology, and made researches in ammonia salts, dyestuffs, gums and pure organic chem- istry. He took first-class honours in cotton, bleaching and finishing; cotton dyeing; and coal tar products in the City and Guilds examina- tion, 1906. He also took the Board of Education certificates in inorganic and organic chemistry. Mr. Broome has spent a considerable time in Germany, studying the higher educational system of that country. Facilities Were afforded him-of acquiring a thorough knowledge of school work in Berlin. He has subsequently had wide experience in the training of stUdent teachers. Among the appointments Mr. Broome held prior to coming to Warrington were: Assistant master, Pendleton Higher Elementary School, 1904-5; science master, Salford Secondary School for Girls, 1905-11; besides which he held the followinq evening school appointments: Mathematics and science lecturer, Salford Tech- nical Institute, 1906-8; head of the chemical de- partment, Radcliffe Technical School, 1908-11. In addition to all his successes and qualifica- tions, Mr. Broome could point to the fact that he had had four years' practical work at the Warrington Secondary School in circumstances to which we have referred, circumstances that were within the knowledge of the School Management Committee. During the 'first two years at Warrington he was responsible for the mathematics and general elementary science taught in the Secondary School and the Techni- cal Institute; more recently he has had charge of the chemistry department. Of great importance in the head of such an establishment as the Secondary School is the fact that Mr. Broome is keenly interested in athletics and the social side of school life. He is an athlete in practice as well as theory, and during his residence here has been a prominent member of the Warrington Cricket Club.

The position Mr. Broome has now attained is worth £3OO a year, rising to £4OO a year by annual increments of £25 a year. There were applicants from all over the country, who were reduced by a selection committee to six, and the final choice was made on Thursday at a full meeting of the School Management Committee.

div.head: GLOWING TESTIMONIALS.
div.p: GLOWING TESTIMONIALS.

So 'recently as last March, when he was a candidate for another post, Mr: Broome received a testimonial from his then chief, Mr. Robson, who spoke of the "very efficient manner in which he has discharged his duties. As a teacher," wrote Mr. Robson, "he has exhibited in a marked degree power to maintain the in- terest of his stidents and to stimulate .their interest in the practical application of their studies. . . . As second master he has .had the supervision of the entire work of the school during my absence, and I cannot speak -too highly of the loyal and conscientious manner in which he has discharged his duties." Professor Dixon, Manchester University, :and chairman of the Royal Technical Institute, Salford, said that Mr. Broome was .one of "the most able of his students." After mentioning Mr. Broome's successes as a student, the Pro- fessor continued "Mr. Broome's work at War- rington has brought into prominence his organising and stimulating power. I know the high esteem in which he is held by the students who have dome from him to our University, and I know no one better qualified by attain- ments and experience for the position he seeks." Another equally glowing recommendation came from Mr. G. W. Stone, M.A., principal of the Salford Secondary School for Girls, who described Mr. Broome as "sympathetic, full of energy," and as one who "always makes the interests of his pupils his first consideration."

div.head: CASE FOR THE CHURCH.
div.p: CASE FOR THE CHURCH.
The Rev. J. G. Lockhart Lectures A
Legh-street.

bn Thursday a visit was paid to the Legh- street Primitive Methodist Church by the Rev. J. G. Lockhart, of Manchester, who preached in the afternoon and in the evening lectured on "The Case for the Church." Mr. E. Wallington presided. The lecturer said to some the Church repre- sented men, money, intellect, power. The ecclesiastical idea was that the Church must prosper by what is brought, to it, but these represented but the small things. Wherever men congregate for high ends and combine for progress and the advancement of the ideal, the Christian Church stands for the great things in each group. Religion had been the greatest creative force in history, the mightiest force in the progress of the past. Benjamin Kidd had said that all progress in its beginnings had ultra-rational sanction. The Renaissance was 'an exclusively intellectual movement which made no social change; the Reformation a dis- tinctly religious movement, established our commonwealth, and through it came the Eng- lish democracy, behind which. lies a great -religions impulse. The Christian Church stood for the Bible; no higher ideal has ever been pre- sented than that presented in Jesus Christ; no better dynamic for progress and ideals will be found; it holds a supreme place in the world's literature. The study of comparative religion, while enabling -us better to .understand the great world religions, has not lessened our reverence for Christ, but with new conviction we recognise , that the Christian Churck stands for Jesus Christ, the greatest figuM in religion. But , above all the Christian Church stood for the greatest thing in life—character—redeemed character, saved men, transformed lives. The lecturer claimed that the Christian Church stood for the supreme things, for sublimity, and the man who was loyal to his Church stood for the bighest of all possible things.
An unbappy marriage is like an electric bat. ;ery—it makes you squirm, but you don't let go.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.
DR. BALLARD AND THE WAR.

A Deluded And Infuriated Nation. During last week-end Dr. Ballard paid a visit to the Padgate Wesleyan Church. A good muster of people assembled on Sunday morning to hear him give an address from. the words: "When I remember God I am troubled," and "We ourselves are comforted of God." Why, he asked, did God permit evil? Having made us what we are, with our own wills to use in whatever direction we chose, God could not unmake us. If the Almighty thought of intervening, He might have intervened when , He gave His only Son to be "a propitiation for our sins." The afternoon meeting was presided over by Mr. E. Lunt, and Dr. Ballard spoke on "The Kaiser and His Bible." Not only did the Kaiser possess a Bible, but what was of more importance, he read it. The Kaiser and his German professors argued that their cause was right and, in-accordance with the Divine Will. The Kaiser saw in the Old Testament assur- ances of the Divine favour on'the side of all the most terrible atrocities of this awful war, acts more terrible than those of our enemy being held to be righteous. Such views were, however, according to the New Testament, entirely wrong. A reorganisation of Christian ideas would most surely take place after this war, and the only guide in such an organisation would be the New Testament. In the evening Dr. Ballard took as his sub- ject "Conversion," at the close of which a dis- cussion was held, Dr. Ballard answering the questions put to him by the congregation. Special music was rendered throughout the day by the choir. In the morning they gave the anthem "If ye love Me," Miss B. London taking the solo. Miss A. Ball took the solo in the anthem "0 worship the Lord," rendered lat the evening service. Mr. W. J. Bate was the conductor and Mr. W. H. Ward the organist. CHRISTIANITY AND WAR: FIRST THING TO BE CONSIDERED. On Monday evening Dr. Ballard gave a lecture on "Christianity and the War." Mr. C. E. Parker, who presided, said as was glad to see his old friend, Dr. Ballard, among them again. He (Mr. Parker) was especially interested in the subject of the lecture. This war .had been to very many Christian people a great intellectual and spiritual burden. Many had not been able to reconcile their idea of duty with the action of their country in regard to our participation in this great war, and any- one who could show us the connection between' the war and Christianity would do them a great service. (Applause.) Dr. Ballard said the Germans were a people, who had been fed upon lies. They knew not, the difference between right and wrong so long as they were destroying their enemies. The Allies, therefore, had to deal with a deluded and infuriated nation, and absolute unity of conviction and purpose was necessary in order to prevent all that was worst in Germany's ambitions. After long, careful, treacherous and complete preparation, Germany had plunged Europe into the most terrible war the world; had ever known. We did not want the war; if' we had wanted it would we not have been prepared? We entered into this war for honour's sake; we were not going to stand aside and watch a little country trodden down under the heel of a cruel invader. Germany's methods of warfare were frightful; for proof of this we had only to think of that once fair country of Belgium—a country which had earned the name of the "Garden of the Lord," and was now only a mass of ruin, and a scene of desolation. Not only the welfare of Europe, but the -wel- fare of the whole future of nations was at stake. It was not the mind of Christ that such terrible things should happen on the Continent. Some people had asked "Why does not Chris- tianity end this 'war?" That query could be answered by the following question being asked back again: "Why does not the goodness in Warrington put an end to all the badness in Warrington?" (Hear, hear.) - Christianity would stop the war to-day, but men and women would not let it. True Christian love did not necessarily mean that we must not fight our enemies. The welfare of the human race should be the first thing to be considered. It was out of the cause for humanity and not for blind hatred against them that our soldiers killed the Germans. in conclusion, Dr. Ballard said it was marvellous how the people of this country had collected the thousands of pounds for the different relief funds, &c., during the war but there still remained a great deal to, do. There were many sufferers who needed everything that could be done for them, both with heart and hand. (Applause.) The Rev. A. J. Morton proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Dr. Ballard for his interesting and instructive address, and th Mr. Parker for presiding. Both were carried with hearty applause. The collections, which were in aid of the Trust Funds, amounted to £l6 17s. Id.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
GRIFFITHS-LEWIS.
First Marriage At The Grappenhal Independent Methodist Church.

A wedding which created considerable interest took place at the Independent Methodist Church, Grappenhall, on Thursday afternoon, in the presence of a large congregation, the bridegroom being Mr. Arthur Griffiths, son of Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Griffiths, of Ontario, Canada, and employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros. The bride was Miss Bessie Lewis, third daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Lewis, of " Marthlyn," Leigh Villas, Grappenhall. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a charming gown of champagne satin, beauti- fully mad, and she wore a Leghorn hat, prettily trimmed with pale pink dahlias, veiled with silk. She carried a sheaf of fine Madonna lilies. The bridesmaids were Misses Marie and Blanche Lewis (sisters of the bride) and "Little May" (niece). The two sisters were charmingly attired in pale blue voile, Leghorn hat, trimmed with red dahlas and silk net; pale pink voile, Leghorn hat, with pink roses and black velvet, respectively; whilst "Little May" looked chic and winsome in a dress of pale pink voile, with pink hat to match. The best man was Mr. George E. Edwards. ,Councillor Robert Henshall, of " Sunnyside," Knutsford-road, officiated, and Mr. W. Barton (uncle of the bride) presided at the organ, giving a fine rendering of the hymns "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "How welcome was the call." After the ceremony a reception was held in the Schoolroom adjoin- ing, when the bride and bridegroom were the recipients of hearty congratulations from a host of friends.
It is interesting to note that this ceremony is the first to be celebrated at this new church connected with Friars' Green.
The catering arrangement S were by Mr Roland Prince, Sankey-street, Warrington.
