div.head: HARVEST THANKSGIVING.
div.p: HARVEST THANKSGIVING.
ST. GEORGE'S MISSION.

Harvest thanksgiving celebrations were com- menced at St. George's, Mission on Thursday evening, when the preacher was the Rev. A. H. Johnson, of the Parish Church, Wigan. Taking for his text the Prayer-Book version of the seventh verse of the ,126th Psalm—` He that now goeth on his way weeping, and beareth forth good seed, shall doubtless come again with joy and bring his sheaves with him " the reverend gentleman said some people were to-day sowing good seed, and some were sowing bad seed. Those who were sowing bad seed were making this war an excuse for slackness in their- religious life, while those who were sowing good seed were using this time as a time in which they could get into touch with God.
The collection, which was for the Assistant Clergy Fund, was very satisfactory. The choir ably rendered special music, includiu an anthem.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
Vicar To Pay Flying Visit From The
Front.

Harvest celebrations were commenced at St. Paul's Church on Thursday evening. The special preacher should have been the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, principal •of the Training College, but, owing to indisposition, he was unable to attend. His place was taken by the Rev. W. Hendy-Cock, vice-principal Of the Training College, who, touching upon the war, said the seed which was now being sown in France, Belgium and Russia, would in the future most surely come to a harvest that would be reaped in joy, for the good of honour and civilisation.

Special music was rendered by the choir, in- cluded among it being the anthem "0 Worship the King." The Rev. E. Downham (curate of the Parish) and the Rev. E. Gunner assisted in the service. The celebration will be con- tinued to-morrow, when services will be held at 10.30, 2.30 (for children), 3.15 (United Bible Class Meeting), and 6.30. The preacher at all these services will be the Vicar (the Rev. Wm: Bracecamp), who has been acting as chaplain to the Territorials at the Front. He left France on Thursday, arrived in Warrington this morii- ing, and will leave again for the Front on Tues- day.

div.head: BEWSEY ADULT SCHOOL.
div.p: BEWSEY ADULT SCHOOL.
llow Money Has Been Over-Estimated.

The harvest festival of the above was held on Sunday, when Mr. Frank V. King, of Ain- tree, was the speaker. In the morning he spoke on "Money, Labour and Life," in which he pointed out that Labour was the all- important factor. Money had .been over- estimated in its importance. Money they could do without by means of a great State arrange- ment, but Labour never. In speaking about Life, H. G. Wells was quoted as writing: "I want to know and feel for the sake of knowing and feeling. I want to go round corners and see what is there, to cross mountain ranges, to open boxes and par- cels. Young animals at least have that dis- position, too. Much more to me than • the desire to live is the desire to taste life; I am not happy until I have done and felt things." The gospel of H. G. Wells was a true gospel. ' They must touch and .see and examine things, or they could not live. It was this gospel which made it essential that they should touch Men. Things could not be known a great way off. Men tried to interest themselves in their fel- lows at a distance. It was too poor. It .was asserted "We must see the need, we must apply the gift.' Contact was necessary. Life was not lived nor known by algebra, nor by reading newspapers, nor by confinement in a motor car. Jack London, Stephen Graham, Walt Whitman, and Tolstoy had touched the life they told us of, and therefore they touched us. The speaker urged the need of real self- expression and attacked many of the artificial Phases of present day society. One of the great problems of industrial life was to so recon- struct society that individual workers could find means of better self-expression. In the evening Mr. King addressed a packed meeting on "The Wayside and the Field," giv- ing a well-thought-out exposition of the law of supply and demand in Nature. Mr. King em- phasised the fact that the supply, no matter how abundant, was uselesS unless there Masi need and a demand for it, .

div.head: LOCAL AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: LOCAL AMUSEMENTS.
tACY REVUE AT ROYAL COURT.
A merry medley of music and mirth:— lavishly ladled out by a bevy of beautiful girls and a coterie of droll dogs of the other sex— occupies .the boards at the Royal Court Theatre

this week. It bears the title. of "The Silver Lining," and is presented, per programme, in "eight scenes of sunshine "—and bright and frolicsome the scenes are, like those who ap- pear in them and keep the fun going from beginning to end! Good audiences have been the order throughout the week. The produc- tion is excellently staged; one scene, the Coral Grotto, being among the most entrancing stage settings • ever seen in this theatre. The piece is played with a swing from beginning to end, experienced artistes having charge of the "speaking parts," and a large and well-trained chorus backing them up right loyally. Intro- duced °its a speciality are Francis Laidler's "Little Sunbeams," a finely-trained and attrac- tive troupe of juveniles who dance prettily, sing naturally and look more than attractive. Those who like song and joke, colour and costume, will be well advised to take one of the two remaining opportunities of seeing this blithe- some trifle. Domestic Drama Next Week.
A pleasing_ drama _will form the fare to be
provided at the Royal Court Theatre next week and the authors of the play may be congratu- lated upon having avoided several of the most troublesome melodramatic pitfalls. .The hero-

me certainly loses her character in the eyes of the world, but not too much stress is laid upon the incident, and throughout the whole story there is a welcome absence of that super- villainy which revels in every variety of crime. Even the war, it should most certainly be added, receives only an incidental thention, and although there is a sufficiency of the kind of pathos which appeals to the audience, there is nothing at all which need harrow the feel- ings. "Somewhere a Voice is Calling" is,
indeed, just a domestic story. There is some good dialogue and some agreeab!e humour, and the piece is deserving of a hearty reception.

div.head: FINE ACROBATS AT THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: FINE ACROBATS AT THE HIPPODROME.

The outstanding turn in this week's fine pro- gramme at the Hippodrome; is supplied by the Michael Richardini Troupe, who give a clever display of physical culture, executing several really turprising feats of strength and endur- ance on a pair of rings and a trapeze. Sharp's Tramboneers provide a novel musical ,turn, and one that is also most attractive, their playing of classical numbers evoking the warmest ap- plause from all the audiences which have this week been privileged—for it is a privilege—to hear them. Much fun is caused by the sketch "The Fool" presented by Mr. Murry Leonard, the well-known American comedian, and his company. At a set-off in quite another vein the playlet "A Baby's Shoe," presented by Mr. T. Norman Akeroyd and his company, is a 'decided success. The Avolos score heavily with a novel turn, in the course of which they perform breath-catching feats on a series of perpendicula; poles. Robb Gilmore is a quaint comedian, and Gordon and Lassie give a charming musical turn; whilst Mina Bax proves to be a youthful and dainty dancer. Interesting war pictures go to make up a tip- top programme.

div.head: Spendid Programme Next Week.
div.p: Spendid Programme Next Week.

Next week's bill at the Hippodrome promises to eclipse even the excellent one that is being given this week. It will be headed by the Two Anartos, a pair of first-rate comedians, and will include Cooper Mitchell, the versatile entertainer, in song and story, at the piano. The Ryewodes Trio will present their refined and artistic scena, "Music Awakes "—a speciality that no lover of good music should miss—and Hastings Lynn and Sydney Lynn will present the dramatic comedy "The Awak- ening," which has scored a big hit up and down the country. Jas. Farrow and Zonny Fiske, in eccentric comedy; Eric Clifford, in character and chorus songs; and Lily Flex- more, comedienne and dancer, will go to the making up of an all-star programme.
SOCIAL PROBLEM-DRAMAS AT STAR KINEMA.

During this week's first three days, capital Star Kimena bills of fare include: "Birds Feed Their Young," a most instructive and pretty Nature film. "A Sad Dog's Story" was a comedy-drama with a novel setting. " Pathe's Animated Gazette" depicted all the, latest fashions, war news, .&c., whilst the "Star Kinema Roll Of Honour " was added to by several photographs. Graphic war material was also contained in a special "Around Tracy- le-Val." A fine social drama, full of plot and problem and excellently staged, acted and pro- duced was "When It Strikes Home." "The Story of a Glove," featuring Mr. and.. Mrs. Sidney Drew, -elicited roars of laughter by its whimsical quaintness.
During to-day equally powerful programmes obtain. The film principal is "Life's Whirl- pool "—another' telling Aocial drama. Talking Pictures Next Week.

The bio. 'attraction on the first three nights of next week will be Edison's Talking Pictures, which have been secured at considerable cost, and will doubtlessly nrove a great draw. For the week-end " The Lion's Cubs" will be the Premier film.

div.head: PRISONERS OF WAR.
div.p: PRISONERS OF WAR.
A AA'arrington Scots Guardsman's Letters Home.

Sydney Thomas, 12, Platt-street, off Fennel- street, is a prisoner of war in Germany and has been since the battle of Mons Two years before the war broke out he joined the 2nd Battalion Scots Guards, having up to that time been engaged in the netting department at Messrs. Rylands Bros. The latest letters received from him show that he is receiving parcels regularly that are sent from Parr Hall and by his mother, and that he is receiving 3s. ed. a week wages from his captors for work he does for them.

div.head: "ADOPTED" PRISONERS.
div.p: "ADOPTED" PRISONERS.

'This week's dispatch of parcels numbered 127. These men are .in need of comforts now, and with the close proximity of winter their needs will be greatly intensified. The following have each "adopted" a prisoner to whom they undertake to dispatch parcels fortnightly: Staff, Hamilton-street School; Mrs. Bracecamp, St. Paul's Girls' Friendly Society, and Mr. T. W. Fletcher, Misses Barker and Jackson, Misses Price (Manchester-road), Miss Ewart (Manchester-road). Fairfield School have adopted two additional prisoners, making for this school four in all. Hamilton-street School (Girls' Department) have adopted three prisoners. CATHOLIC SUPPORT.

, The Secretary of St. Mary's Catholic Young tlllen.'s Society has handed to Mr. Spinks 10s. for the Prisoners of War Fund. This amount was part of the proceeds of a recent whist drive and dance organised by the committee of the society.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
Raddon Court.

Another Pound Day will be held in connection with the Raddoxi Court Hospital on Thursday next, when gifts of groceries, money, &c., will be most thankfully received, special needs being tea, eggs, vegetables, Poultry, dried fruit and blankets. Farmers are specially asked to bear in mind the request for vegetables, eggs and poultry.

div.head: THEATRE ARTISTES AT WINWICK.
div.p: THEATRE ARTISTES AT WINWICK.

On Thursday afternoon the members of Mr. Francis Lawler's super revue company, along with the Royal Court Theatre bandsmen, visited the Lord Derby War Hospital at Winwick, and entertained the wounded soldiers. Songs .and concerted pieces of ,vocal music were given. interspersed with orchestral selections, to the great delight of an appreciative audience. Mr. Croke, the manager of the revue company, and Mr. H. L. Warburton, the 'resident manager of the Royal Court Theatre, took charge of the party and saw to their comfort in transit and at the hospital, and Mr. Waters, of Winwick, stage-managed the concert arrangements.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT- HOUSE, • KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 18th day of OCTOBER, 1915, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Altrincham, Buck- low, Dukinfield, Middlewich, Sandbach, Congle- ton, Northwich, Prestbury, and Stockport, form- ing the Knutsford district, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the COURT HOUSE, KNUTS- FORD, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 18th day of OCTOBER NEXT, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT • will be Adjourned to the CASTLE OF CHESTER on WEDNESDAY, the 20th day of OCTOBER, 1915, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be erupannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broxten, Chester Castle, Daresbury, Eddisbury, Nantwich, Run- corn, Winsford, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners 'com- mitted from the last-mentioned Divisions, will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the CASTLE OF CHESTER at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 20th day of OCTOBER, 1915, at• Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatine of Chester. Chester, 28th September, 1915.

KILLED. 'PRIVATE ELIAS THOMAS. Faithful Streteher-Bearer INIto Died At Duty. "It is with the deepest regret that f have to inform you that Private E. Thomas, No. 1,490,

was formerly employed at the Sankey Wire Mills. In June last he was in hospital for six- teen clays, suffering from the effects of gaff poisoning. PRIVATE It. PEMBERTON. Buried Alive In Trench, But Dug Out. Private Robert Pemberton, of the Warrington Territorials, a married man, residing at 26,

Winwick-road, was wounded while taking part in the great charge. In a letter to his parents Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Pemberton, of 98, Hood- lane, he said We were in that charge at on Saturday. We had to take our part as bombers to the - and take three lines of German trenches. We sat in our own trench all through the bombardment, and then the word came down to get ready, and over the parapet we went, taking the first German trench in three minutes, and then we took the second and third. Shells Like Hailstones. "Then the fun commenced. They sent shells at us like hailstones, and we had to retire to the first trench. We had just got to it when a 'Jack Johnson came and blew in our trench, burying me and a corporal. Thanks to the lads who dug us out, we just got our senses back when it came along the trench that we were cut off. .. . We went across 200 yards of open gl•ound while they pelted us with shells. . . . I got just a slight shrapnel wound on my finger, and when I got back the first thing I did was to go down on my knees and thank Gi]rd. that I was left alive." Private Pemberton, who is thirty-two years- of age, attended as a boy, St. Ann's School. Before the outbreak of war he was employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd. He rejoined the Territorials a year ago, when the war broke out, having served in them previously. PRIVATE J. lIAMBLETT. Nineteen-Year-Old Soldier Who has Proved A Good Shot. SAPPER T. PEVIIII. "Still Alive And kicking—With One Leg!" Mr. and Mrs. Pevitt, of 37, Oldham-street, have received news that their son, Sapper Thomas Pevitt, of the Royal Engineers, has been wounded in the leg. A field card con- veyed the intelligence, while later, from the 2nd Canadian Hospital, France, Sapper Pevitt sent the 'following letter:—" I am still alive and kicking (with one leg). lam going on fine now, and hope to be sent to England in a day or two. I .was hit the first time I went into action; indeed, I believe I was the first one in the • company to be hit. It was on a Sunday afternoon, when we were going to the first line. The 'Jack Job nsons ' and shrapnel shells were falling like rain around us. Suddenly, 'some- thing struck me—just as we were over the

likely be the last letter for at least one week, but don't upset yourself. I suppose you have an idea as to what is going to happen." . In Winwick Military Hospital. . Mrs. Middleton this week visited her son at the Winwick Military Hospital, and found him in excellent spirits, despite his wounds. • Private Middleton, who is eighteen years of age, was, before the outbreak of war, an employe of Rylands Bros. He was educated at the National School, Church-street, and attended St. Cleinent's Mission Church.. He enlisted on the 2nd September, 1914. PRIVATE NI. ROGERSON. Describes How Trenches Were Taken And Lost. Mr. Matthew Rogerson, 146, Longford-street, forgeman at Bew,sey Forge, has been officially informed that his son, Private Michael Roger- son, of the Rifle Brigade has been wounded and is now in hospital in the homeland. After landing in England, Private Rogerson sent a Postcard and a letter to his parents. " Mercy English—Good Comrades!" The letter, which was dated September 31st ran as folloWs:—" I am once again in dear old England. . . . We went into another charge, and it was like hell itself! We got into the trenches as usual, and in the morning, at 4.25, our guns opened a murderous fire on the German trenches. Then we started to crawl forward while the shells were dropping on all sides. We had just got near the enemy's trench when we saw them coming towards us with their hands up, shouting 'Mercy, English— good comrades!' An Attack in Force. "We took their two lines of trenches and be- gan destroying the second one when reinforce- ments of the enemy rushed upon us in thousands and drove us back to the first line, where we remained until 4.30 p.m., despite the fact that for a long while we underwent a terrible bom- bardment. Then the enemy came again and drove us back, and we had to retire to our own lines. GASSED. CORPORAL JOHN FINNERTY. Rejoins Regiment And Hopes To Be Fit Soon. Corporal John Finnerty, an employe at the Latchford Tube Works, son of Mr. John Fin- nerty, 14, Portland-street, who is engaged at Crosfield's, was gassed during the operations on the 25th ult. He enlisted in the Lancashire

LANCE-CORPORAL THOMAS FOY. A field card conveyed to Mr. and Mrs. John Foy, of 4, Winwick-road, the news that their son, Lance-Corporal Thomas Foy, of the Bth Battalion King's Own Scottish Borderers was wounded and in hospital. Single, and twenty-three years of age, Lance- Corporal Foy was educated at St. Alban's School. Before the war he was employed by Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., as a pipe- fitter, for whose football team he formerly played. PRIVATE J. H. WARBURTON. Private J. H. Warburton, of the King's Royal Rifles, who in peace times resides with his parents • in Fairclough's-avenue, has been wounded. Nineteen years of age, Private Warburton was educated at Silver-street School; Before enlisting twelve months ago, he was employed by the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd. He worshipped at the Parish Church. His favourite hobby is boating.
